temperate.name: Tomatoes
temperate.tagline: The crop every garden ends up with too many of at once — and the one most worth putting up.
temperate.frostNote: Tomatoes die at 0 °C. If frost is forecast, pick everything with any blush of colour and anything full-sized and glossy green, and ripen it indoors out of the sun. A sheet or row cover over the plants buys one light frost, not a hard one. Pick before the frost, not after: fruit from frost-killed vines is fine to eat fresh but should not be canned — the canning guides are explicit about it.
temperate.ready: Full colour for the variety, slightly soft to a gentle squeeze, and it comes off with a light twist. A ‘mature green’ tomato — full size, glossy, pale or whitish at the blossom end — will ripen off the plant; a small, dull, dark-green one will not.
temperate.pick: Twist or snip with the calyx on. Pick every two or three days in August; a ripe tomato left on the vine splits after rain. Never refrigerate a tomato you mean to eat fresh — below about 10 °C the flavour compounds stop developing and the texture goes mealy.

store.how: Stem end down, one layer, not touching.
Wrapped singly in newspaper in a box, or spread on trays one layer deep; check twice a week and pull the ripe ones. Light is not needed — warmth is what ripens them.

temperate.preserveNote: Tomatoes are the home canner’s classic, but they sit right on the acidity line: every tested canned-tomato recipe adds bottled lemon juice or citric acid to each jar, and that is not optional whether you water-bath or pressure can. Whole tomatoes freeze well with no blanching — the skins slip off under the tap as they thaw — which is the fastest way to deal with a glut on a weeknight. Cherry and paste tomatoes dry beautifully. What does not work is a sauce you have thickened with flour or loaded with extra peppers, onions and oil to taste: the added low-acid vegetables change the safety of the recipe, so follow a tested salsa or sauce recipe exactly. Green tomatoes are more acidic than ripe ones and can be canned by the same recipes, with the same added acid.

seeds.how: Tomatoes self-pollinate, so an open-pollinated or heirloom variety comes true from saved seed (an F1 hybrid — it will say so on the packet — will not). Squeeze the seeds and gel from a fully ripe fruit into a jar, add a splash of water, and leave it 2–3 days somewhere warm until a mould forms on top: the fermentation removes the germination-inhibiting gel and kills some seed-borne diseases. Pour off the floating pulp and hollow seeds, rinse the good ones in a sieve, and dry them on a plate or coffee filter (not paper towel — it sticks) for a week. Label and store cool and dry. A few metres between varieties is enough; potato-leaf and currant types want more.
seeds.viability: 5 years comfortably; often 10 if kept cool and dry.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: not where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant or tomatillos grew in the last three years if you have the space, two at minimum, to keep early and late blight down. Full sun, steady water, and a cage or stake from the day they go in; 45–60 cm (18–24 in) apart. Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost; plant out one to two weeks after it, once nights hold above 10 °C. In zones 3–5 pick varieties under 75 days to maturity and have a green-tomato plan for September.

sow.outdoors: Transplant 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once nights hold above 10 °C.

faqs.q: Will green tomatoes ripen indoors?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are mature: full-sized, glossy, and paler at the blossom end. Keep them at 13–21 °C out of direct sun — a windowsill is too hot by day and too cold at night. A ripe banana or apple in the box speeds things up with ethylene. Small, dull, dark-green fruit will not ripen; use it green for chutney or fried green tomatoes.

faqs.q: Do I have to add lemon juice when canning tomatoes?
faqs.a: Yes. Modern tomatoes vary in acidity and some sit above pH 4.6, the line that makes botulism possible in a sealed jar. Every tested recipe adds 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice (or ¼ teaspoon citric acid) per 500 ml (pint) jar and 2 tablespoons (or ½ teaspoon citric acid) per litre (quart) jar, whether you water-bath or pressure can. Bottled, not fresh — the acidity is standardised.

faqs.q: Can I freeze tomatoes without blanching?
faqs.a: Yes. Wash, core, and freeze whole on a tray, then bag them. The skins split and slip off under warm water as they thaw. They are soft when thawed, so use them for sauce, soup and chilli rather than salads.

faqs.q: Can I can tomatoes picked after a frost?
faqs.a: No. The canning guides say not to can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines, because their acidity is no longer reliable. Eat them fresh, cook them into something you freeze, or make them into a tested relish. The fix is to strip the plants the evening before the frost, not the morning after.

faqs.q: How do I save tomato seeds?
faqs.a: From an open-pollinated or heirloom variety (not an F1 hybrid), scoop seeds and gel into a jar with a little water and let it ferment 2–3 days until mould forms. Rinse, dry on a plate for a week, and store cool and dry. Good for 5 years or more.

faqs.q: What should kids know about tomatoes?
faqs.a: Ripe tomatoes are safe to pick and eat straight from the plant, rinsed. The leaves and stems are not food — they contain solanine-type alkaloids and can upset a stomach — so the rule is fruit only. Picking cherry tomatoes is one of the best first garden jobs for a three-year-old.

faqs.q: When do tomatoes ripen in Canada?
faqs.a: Late July to the first frost in most of southern Canada, with the main flush in August and September. In zone 3–4 gardens the season is short enough that early varieties (55–65 days) and a green-tomato plan matter; in zone 6–7 the plants can go on into October.

temperate.name: Sweet peppers
temperate.tagline: Slow to colour, quick to freeze — the pepper harvest is a race between the plant and the first frost.
temperate.frostNote: Peppers die at 0 °C and sulk well before it — a few nights near 5 °C and the plants stop doing much. The evening a frost is forecast, pick every full-sized fruit, green or coloured; peppers do not ripen after picking, so a green one stays green and you may as well eat it that way. A sheet over the plants gets you through one light frost if you want to gamble on a few more coloured ones. If the plant is loaded and the forecast is bad, pull the whole plant and hang it upside down in the garage for a week — the fruit stays firm while you work through it.
temperate.ready: Full size for the variety, thick-walled, glossy and firm; it snaps off cleanly rather than bending. Green peppers are simply unripe fruit and are perfectly good — bells, jalapeños and most frying types are picked green by the tonne. Leave them on the plant and they turn red, yellow, orange or purple and get sweeter, but each one takes two to three extra weeks and the plant sets fewer new fruit while it waits.
temperate.pick: Cut with scissors or secateurs, leaving a short stub of stem; pulling tears the brittle branches and often takes a chunk of plant with it. Picking green keeps the plant producing; letting a few colour gives you the sweet ones. Handle gently — a bruised pepper rots in days.

store.how: In a perforated plastic bag or an open box with a damp towel over it. Peppers want cool and humid, not cold.
In a perforated bag. The fridge is colder than peppers like; after a couple of weeks the skins pit and soften.

temperate.preserveNote: Peppers are the easiest vegetable in the garden to freeze: wash, core, slice or dice, and bag them raw — no blanching needed. Raw-frozen peppers stay crisper than blanched ones and go straight from the freezer into a pan, a soup or a stir-fry. Roasting first is the other great option — blister them under the broiler at 200 °C (400 °F) for 6–8 minutes, peel, and freeze the strips. Pickled peppers and pepper relish are classic and safe when you follow a tested recipe exactly, because peppers are a low-acid vegetable and the vinegar ratio is what makes the jar safe. What does not work is canning plain peppers in a water bath, or making your own ‘peppers in oil’ for the pantry: plain peppers must be pressure-canned (35 minutes for 250 ml or 500 ml jars at 10 psi, weighted gauge, near sea level), and oil-packed peppers are a botulism risk unless they are made by the tested NCHFP Marinated Peppers recipe, water-bath processed as written.

seeds.how: Check the packet first: many of the big blocky bell varieties sold in Canada are F1 hybrids and will not come true. From an open-pollinated variety, let the fruit go fully coloured and just starting to soften, then scrape the seeds out, rinse, and dry on a plate for a week or two until one snaps when you bend it. Peppers mostly self-pollinate, but bees do move pollen between plants, and sweet peppers cross with hot ones — a sweet pepper grown next to jalapeños can give you a hot ‘bell’ next year. Keep varieties 90–500 m (300–1,600 ft) apart, or bag a few flower clusters in organza before they open and mark those fruit for seed.
seeds.viability: About 3 years.

temperate.nextYear: Nightshade family — not where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant or tomatillos grew in the last three years. Full sun, the warmest spot you have, fertile soil that holds water, 45 cm (18 in) apart. Peppers are slow: start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat (they germinate best at 27–32 °C), and plant out two weeks after the last frost once nights stay above 10 °C — set out cold, they stall for the season. In zones 3–4 choose early varieties (60–70 days from transplant), use black plastic or a dark mulch to warm the soil, and plan on eating most of them green.

sow.outdoors: Transplant about 2 weeks after the last frost, once nights hold above 10 °C.

faqs.q: Will green peppers turn red after picking?
faqs.a: No. Peppers are non-climacteric, which means they do not keep ripening once they are off the plant — that is why green bells sit next to red ones in the shop. A pepper picked part-way through its colour change may deepen a little on the counter, but a solid green one stays green. Pick green ones to eat green, and leave the ones you want coloured on the plant as long as the frost allows.

faqs.q: Can you freeze peppers without blanching?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best way to do them. Wash, core, slice or dice, spread on a tray to freeze, then bag. Raw-frozen peppers keep a better texture than blanched ones and are ready for anything cooked. A whole, cored pepper frozen on its own makes a stuffed pepper in February.

faqs.q: How do you store peppers after picking?
faqs.a: Cool and humid, not cold: 10–13 °C in a perforated bag in a basement or cool room keeps them two weeks. The fridge crisper works for a week or two, but after that the skins pit and soften because peppers are sensitive to cold. Do not wash them until you use them.

faqs.q: Can I can peppers at home?
faqs.a: Yes, two ways. Pickled peppers and pepper relish are water-bath canned by a tested recipe with 5% vinegar — never cut the vinegar. Plain peppers are a low-acid vegetable and must be pressure-canned: 35 minutes for 250 ml or 500 ml jars at 10 psi (weighted gauge) near sea level. There is no safe water-bath method for plain peppers, and no safe pantry method for home-made peppers in oil.

faqs.q: How do I save pepper seeds?
faqs.a: Only from an open-pollinated variety — many bells are F1 hybrids. Let the fruit colour fully, scrape out the seeds, and dry them on a plate for a week or two. Peppers cross with other peppers, hot ones included, so isolate varieties by 90 m or more or bag a few flowers. Seed keeps about three years.

faqs.q: Are peppers a good crop for kids?
faqs.a: Sweet peppers are one of the best: no thorns, nothing poisonous on the plant except that the leaves are not food, and a ripe red one eaten in the garden like an apple wins over most four-year-olds. The only rule is to check with a grown-up before biting into any pepper, because a hot one looks a lot like a sweet one and the heat does not wash off a tongue with water.

temperate.name: Hot peppers
temperate.tagline: A handful of plants gives a year of heat — dried on a string, pickled in rings, or fermented into sauce.
temperate.frostNote: Hot peppers die at 0 °C like any pepper. The evening a frost is forecast, pick everything full-sized: green jalapeños are what you pickle anyway, and red ones that are already turning will finish colouring a little indoors. Fully ripe red cayennes and Thai types are the ones to string up and dry. If the plant is still loaded, pull it whole and hang it upside down somewhere airy — the fruit keeps colouring and drying on the dead plant for weeks. Wear gloves for the whole job.
temperate.ready: Full size, firm and glossy. Jalapeños are picked green and shiny, often when fine tan ‘corking’ lines appear on the skin; cayennes, Thai and habanero types are picked when fully coloured and just starting to soften. Heat climbs as the fruit ripens, so a red jalapeño is hotter than a green one from the same plant.
temperate.pick: Snip with scissors, stem on, and wear gloves — the capsaicin is in the seeds and the white ribs, and it gets on your fingers through the stem end when you twist fruit off. Do not touch your face, and wash your hands with soap and warm water afterwards; water alone does not shift it.

store.how: In a perforated bag or open basket. Thin-walled types start air-drying on their own, which is fine.
In a perforated bag. Expect soft spots and pitting after that — turn them into something before it happens.

temperate.preserveNote: Drying is what hot peppers were made for. Thin-walled kinds — cayenne, Thai, chile de árbol, small red annuums — can be slit, threaded on heavy string and hung somewhere airy for three to four weeks; a ristra is just that, done neatly with fully ripe red pods (green ones shrivel and go a dull orange). Thick-fleshed jalapeños and habaneros mould before they dry in a Canadian October, so give them a dehydrator: 60 °C (140 °F) for two hours, then 54 °C (130 °F) until they are leathery to brittle. Pickled jalapeño rings and pickled hot peppers are tested water-bath recipes — 5% vinegar at the stated ratio, 10 minutes for 500 ml jars near sea level — and so is a cayenne-style pepper sauce made with vinegar. Fermented hot sauce is the current favourite and it is safe done right: a measured salt brine, peppers kept under the brine, three or four weeks at 20–22 °C until the bubbling stops and a pH strip or meter reads 4.6 or lower, then refrigerated. What does not work is treating a ferment as shelf-stable, or canning plain hot peppers in a water bath: fermentation on its own does not make a pantry-safe food, and plain peppers are low-acid and must be pressure-canned. Freezing is the lazy option and it is fine — whole, stems off, no blanching.

seeds.how: Many hot varieties — jalapeños, cayennes, Hungarian wax, most habaneros — are open-pollinated and come true if they have not crossed. The problem is that they cross readily with each other and with sweet peppers when bees move between plants, so a mixed pepper bed gives mixed seed. Isolate varieties by 90–500 m (300–1,600 ft) or bag a few flower clusters in organza and mark those fruit. Take seed from fully coloured, slightly soft fruit, up to two weeks past ripe. Wear gloves and work outdoors or by an open window: the dust from dried hot-pepper seed is unpleasant to breathe. Dry the seed on a plate for a week or two.
seeds.viability: About 3 years.

temperate.nextYear: Nightshade rotation — not after tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant or tomatillos for three years. Full sun, the hottest and best-drained bed you have, 45 cm (18 in) apart. Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat; the Capsicum chinense types (habanero, Scotch bonnet) are slower than jalapeños, so start them at the early end. Plant out two weeks after the last frost when nights stay above 10 °C. In zones 3–4 grow jalapeño, cayenne and Hungarian wax types in black pots or against a south wall — habaneros rarely ripen outdoors there without a tunnel.

sow.outdoors: Transplant about 2 weeks after the last frost, once nights hold above 10 °C.

faqs.q: How do you dry hot peppers at home?
faqs.a: Thin-walled peppers like cayenne and Thai: slit each one, thread on heavy string through the stems, and hang in an airy room for three to four weeks until brittle. Thick-walled ones like jalapeños: halve or slice and dry in a dehydrator at 60 °C (140 °F) for two hours, then 54 °C (130 °F) until leathery to brittle — they mould on a string in our autumn humidity. Store dried peppers whole in a jar away from light and grind as you need them.

faqs.q: Is fermented hot sauce safe to make at home?
faqs.a: Yes, with a few rules. Use a measured brine — roughly 1 to 3 tablespoons of salt per litre of water — keep the peppers fully under the brine, and ferment at about 20–22 °C for three to four weeks until the bubbling stops and a pH strip or meter reads 4.6 or lower — if it is still above 4.6, keep fermenting and check again every day or two. Blend, bottle and keep it in the fridge (up to about 9 months); a home ferment is not shelf-stable on its own. If you want jars for the pantry, use a tested vinegar-based pepper sauce recipe and water-bath it.

faqs.q: Can you freeze hot peppers?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the fastest way: wash, pull the stems, and bag them whole or chopped with no blanching. They thaw soft but the heat and flavour are all there, so slice a frozen jalapeño straight into chilli or salsa. Label the bag — frozen hot peppers look a lot like frozen sweet ones.

faqs.q: How do you pickle jalapeños?
faqs.a: Follow a tested recipe exactly, because peppers are low-acid and the vinegar is what makes the jar safe. The NCHFP pickled jalapeño rings use about 1.4 kg (3 lb) of jalapeños to 1.8 L (7½ cups) of 5% cider vinegar with a little water and pickling salt, after an 18-hour pickling-lime soak and three rinse-and-soak cycles exactly as written, processed 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath for 500 ml (pint) jars near sea level. Never dilute the vinegar to make them milder — pick a milder pepper instead.

faqs.q: How do I save hot pepper seeds?
faqs.a: From an open-pollinated variety and a plant that was not next to other peppers — hot and sweet peppers cross freely through bees, so isolate by 90 m or more or bag a few flowers. Take seed from fully ripe, softening fruit, wearing gloves, and dry on a plate for a week or two. Keeps about three years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about hot peppers?
faqs.a: Grown-ups pick and cut hot peppers, not kids. The heat is an oil called capsaicin that sits in the seeds and white ribs; it does not wash off with plain water, so rubbing an eye after touching one hurts for a long time. The rule in our garden is look, do not touch, and nobody tastes a pepper until a grown-up says which plant it came from. Harvest day is a good day to wear gloves and show them why.

temperate.name: Cucumbers
temperate.tagline: Eaten within a week or pickled within a day — a cucumber has no middle option.
temperate.frostNote: Cucumber vines collapse at 0 °C and the fruit left on them goes water-soaked and soft. By the time frost threatens most vines are finished anyway from mildew and beetles; if yours are still going, pick everything usable the evening before and cover the vines with a sheet if you want one more week. There is no ripening indoors — a cucumber is picked immature and stays what it was.
temperate.ready: Pickling types at 5–10 cm (2–4 in) for gherkins and 10 cm (4 in) for dills; slicers at 15–20 cm (6–8 in), dark green, firm and still slightly bumpy. Too late looks like this: pale or yellowing skin, a fat belly, big seeds inside, and a plant that has stopped setting new fruit because it thinks it has done its job.
temperate.pick: Cut or snap the stem just above the fruit every two days in August — missing one for a week costs you a dozen more. Pick in the morning when they are cool and crisp, and do not pick when the vines are wet, which spreads disease. For pickles, pick and brine the same day: cucumbers go soft fast, and the pickling guides say use them within 24 hours.

store.how: In a perforated bag or a box with a damp towel. Cucumbers like cool and humid, which is colder than a kitchen and warmer than a fridge.
In a perforated bag. Pitting and soft spots after a week are cold damage, not age.

temperate.preserveNote: Pickling is the only real way to keep a cucumber, and it comes in two flavours. Fresh-pack (quick) pickles are cucumbers in a hot 5% vinegar brine, water-bath processed by a tested recipe — dills, bread-and-butters, relish. Fermented pickles are the old way: cucumbers in a salt brine in a crock for three to four weeks at 21–24 °C (cooler takes five or six), turning sour on their own, then refrigerated or canned. Both start the same way — small, fresh, unwaxed pickling cucumbers, with a 1.5 mm (1/16 in) slice taken off the blossom end, because the blossom carries an enzyme that softens the whole jar. Use 5% vinegar and never dilute it, pickling salt, and the recipe’s exact ratios. What does not work is freezing: a frozen cucumber thaws limp, water-logged and off-flavoured. The one exception is ‘freezer pickles’, where slices are salted and sugared in vinegar first and the texture is part of the deal. Canning plain cucumbers in water is not a thing.

seeds.how: Cucumbers have separate male and female flowers and are pollinated by bees, so every cucumber variety in bee range crosses with every other (not with squash or melons — different species). Most modern slicers and many picklers are F1 hybrids and will not come true either, so start with an open-pollinated variety and only one of them, or isolate by 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), or hand-pollinate a few flowers and tape them shut. Seed is nowhere near ready at eating size: leave the chosen fruit on the vine until it is fat, yellow or orange and softening, then wait a few more weeks — roughly 45–60 days after the flower. Scoop the seeds and pulp into a jar with water, ferment 1–3 days at 21–27 °C, pour off the floaters, rinse the heavy seeds, and dry on a plate for a week or two.
seeds.viability: About 5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cucurbit family — keep cucumbers, squash, pumpkins and melons off the same bed for two or three years. Full sun, rich soil, steady water, and a trellis: trellised cucumbers are straighter, cleaner and easier for children to find. Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost once the soil at 2.5 cm (1 in) is 21 °C (70 °F); seed in cold soil rots. Sow 30 cm (12 in) apart along a trellis, or three to a hill 1 m (3 ft) apart. If you must start indoors, do it in pots no more than 3–4 weeks before planting out and move them without disturbing the roots. In zones 3–4 use black plastic or a dark mulch to warm the soil and pick a 50–55-day variety.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is 21 °C at 2.5 cm depth.

faqs.q: Why are my cucumbers bitter?
faqs.a: Bitterness is cucurbitacin, a compound the plant makes in its leaves and stems and pushes into the fruit when it is stressed — hot, dry spells are the usual cause. It concentrates at the stem end and just under the skin, so cut off the stem end and peel and most of it goes. Water deeply once a week in hot weather and look for ‘bitter-free’ varieties, which also attract fewer cucumber beetles.

faqs.q: Can you freeze cucumbers?
faqs.a: Not usefully. A frozen cucumber thaws limp and water-logged with an off flavour, which is why cucumbers appear on the official list of foods that do not freeze well. The exception is freezer pickles, where sliced cucumbers are salted, then packed in a sweet vinegar syrup and frozen; the texture changes but that is the point. For everything else, pickle them.

faqs.q: What is the difference between pickling and slicing cucumbers?
faqs.a: Pickling types are shorter, blockier, thinner-skinned and bumpier, bred to stay crisp in brine and to be picked small — 5–10 cm. Slicers are longer, smoother and thicker-skinned for eating fresh. You can pickle a slicer in a pinch, but it goes soft; you can eat a pickler fresh any day and many people prefer them.

faqs.q: Why do pickle recipes say to cut off the blossom end?
faqs.a: The blossom end carries enzymes that keep softening the cucumber after it is in the jar, and one soft cucumber turns into a jar of mush. Slice a thin 1.5 mm (1/16 in) piece off the end opposite the stem before brining. It is the single most useful pickle tip there is, along with using cucumbers within a day of picking.

faqs.q: How do I save cucumber seeds?
faqs.a: From an open-pollinated variety grown with no other cucumbers within 250 m, or from flowers you hand-pollinated and taped shut. Leave the fruit until it is fat, yellow-orange and soft, then a few weeks more. Scoop seeds and pulp into water, ferment 1–3 days, rinse the sinkers, dry for a week or two. Good for about five years.

faqs.q: Are cucumbers a good crop for kids?
faqs.a: One of the best: fast, nothing poisonous on the plant, and a trellis puts the fruit at eye level where a four-year-old can find the ones the grown-ups missed. Teach them to pick the small, dark ones and to snap the stem rather than pull the vine. A cucumber eaten warm off the plant, skin and all, is a different food from a fridge one.

temperate.name: Zucchini
temperate.tagline: Picked small every other day it is a delicacy; left a week it is a baseball bat, and the freezer is the only answer.
temperate.frostNote: Zucchini plants blacken and collapse at 0 °C, and any fruit touched by frost goes soft within a day or two. The evening before a frost, pick every fruit down to finger size and the open blossoms too. A sheet or two over the plant will carry it through one light frost — worth it in early September, not worth it in October when mildew has had the leaves anyway.
temperate.ready: 15–20 cm (6–8 in) long and 4–5 cm thick for the best texture, glossy, with the flower end still soft; 10 cm (4 in) if you want them sweetest. Marrows the size of your forearm are watery, seedy and hard-skinned — they still grate for the freezer but that is all. Check under the leaves: a fruit doubles in size in two hot days.
temperate.pick: Cut the stem with a knife, leaving 2–3 cm on the fruit — twisting tears the hollow stem and lets rot into the plant. Pick every second day in August, and pick the male flowers (the ones on long thin stems with no baby fruit behind them) for stuffing without costing you anything. Do not work in the plants when they are wet.

store.how: Unwashed, in a perforated bag. Longer than a week and the skin pits and the flesh goes water-soaked — cold damage.
Loose in a single layer. Big marrows with hardened skins last a few weeks on a cool floor; small ones do not.

temperate.preserveNote: Grate it and freeze it: young zucchini grated, steam-blanched 1–2 minutes until translucent, packed in measured 250 ml or 500 ml amounts and frozen, is the glut solved — each bag is a loaf of bread or a batch of fritters in winter, once you pour off the water that comes out on thawing. Slices blanched 3 minutes freeze too, but they come back soft and are for soup. Relish and pickles are the other answer: summer squash relish and bread-and-butter zucchini pickles are tested water-bath recipes with 5% vinegar. What does not work — and this surprises people every year — is canning plain zucchini or summer squash, in cubes or slices, in water or broth. The canning authorities withdrew those instructions decades ago because the squash packs down and heats unpredictably, and ‘canning summer squash without pickling is not recommended’ is the current rule. The only ways zucchini goes in a jar are a tested pickle or relish, or as a minor ingredient in a tested pressure-canned mixed-vegetable or tomato recipe.

seeds.how: Zucchini is Cucurbita pepo, the same species as acorn, delicata, spaghetti and patty-pan squash, most pie and jack-o’-lantern pumpkins, and ornamental gourds — and it crosses freely with all of them through bees. The fruit you eat this year is unaffected; the seed inside it is the problem. To save seed, grow one pepo variety, or isolate by 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), or hand-pollinate a female flower with a male from the same variety the morning they open and tape it shut. Then let that fruit grow into a full marrow and sit until the rind is too hard to dent with a thumbnail and the stem is dry, pick it, and leave it indoors another three weeks. Scoop, rinse, and dry the seeds on a plate for two or three weeks. A crossed seedling can give bitter fruit — if a zucchini tastes strongly bitter, spit it out and compost the plant.
seeds.viability: About 6 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cucurbit rotation — not where squash, pumpkins, cucumbers or melons grew in the last two or three years. Full sun and the richest soil you have; a shovel of compost under each hill. One plant per square metre feeds a family; two feeds the street. Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost once the soil at 5 cm is 21 °C (70 °F) — cold soil rots the seed and a transplant set out cold just sits. Squash resents transplanting, so if you must start indoors in a short season, use large pots, no more than three weeks ahead, and move them without touching the roots. Water at the base, not over the leaves, and in zones 3–4 cover the first month with a row cover to keep heat in and cucumber beetles off.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is 21 °C at 5 cm depth.

faqs.q: Can you freeze zucchini?
faqs.a: Yes — grated is the way. Grate young zucchini, steam-blanch 1–2 minutes until it looks translucent, pack in measured amounts (a 500 ml bag is a loaf of zucchini bread) and freeze. Drain the water off when it thaws. Slices can be blanched 3 minutes and frozen too, but they come back soft, so use them in soup and sauce.

faqs.q: Can you can zucchini?
faqs.a: Not plain. Canning summer squash on its own, in any liquid, is not recommended — the tested times were withdrawn because the squash does not heat reliably in the jar. Zucchini can only be canned as a tested pickle or relish (summer squash relish, bread-and-butter zucchini pickles) or as a small part of a tested pressure-canned mixed recipe. For plain zucchini, freeze it.

faqs.q: How big should zucchini be when you pick them?
faqs.a: Around 15–20 cm (6–8 in) and still glossy, with a soft flower end; 10 cm if you like them sweetest. Check under the leaves every other day in August because they double in two warm days. A big marrow is not wasted — grate it for the freezer — but it is watery and seedy, and leaving it on the plant slows the next fruit.

faqs.q: Why is my zucchini bitter?
faqs.a: Occasionally a plant carries high levels of cucurbitacin, the bitter compound in the squash family, either from stress or because the seed was a stray cross with an ornamental gourd. A faintly bitter one is a sign to water better; a strongly bitter one you should spit out, because a few grams can give a sharp stomach upset. Pull that plant and do not save its seed.

faqs.q: How do I save zucchini seeds?
faqs.a: Grow only one Cucurbita pepo variety (no acorn, delicata, spaghetti, patty-pan or pumpkin nearby) or hand-pollinate and tape a flower. Let the fruit grow to a full marrow with a rind you cannot dent, store it three weeks, then scoop, rinse and dry the seeds for two or three weeks. Good for about six years.

faqs.q: What can kids do with zucchini?
faqs.a: Send them on the marrow hunt: the giant one hiding under the leaves is the best find in the August garden and makes a good scale for weighing other things against. They can pick the big male flowers for stuffing without harming the crop, and grating for the freezer is a safe kitchen job with a box grater and supervision. The leaves and flowers are safe; the one warning is a fruit that tastes strongly bitter — spit it out and don’t eat any more from that plant. The stems and leaves are prickly enough that long sleeves help.

temperate.name: Winter squash
temperate.latin: Cucurbita maxima / C. moschata / C. pepo
temperate.tagline: Cured for ten days and kept on a cool shelf, the September harvest feeds you until March.
temperate.frostNote: The vines die at the first touch of 0 °C, but the fruit underneath usually comes through a light frost unmarked. A hard freeze is different: the flesh under the rind is damaged and the squash will rot in storage instead of keeping. So on a light-frost night leave them; on a hard-freeze forecast, or any frost after the vines are already dead and no longer sheltering the fruit, bring everything in or throw blankets and tarps over the patch. Fruit that is nearly mature finishes ripening indoors; a green, thin-skinned one does not.
temperate.ready: The rind is hard enough that a thumbnail cannot dent it, the skin has gone dull rather than glossy, the colour is full for the type (deep tan butternut with no green stripes, dark green buttercup, orange-flecked acorn), and the stem has started to dry and cork. Most types want 50–60 days from flowering, and a vine that is dying back on its own is telling you it is done.
temperate.pick: Cut, never pull: use secateurs or a knife and leave 5–10 cm (2–4 in) of stem on the fruit. A squash without its stem has an open wound and rots first. Do not carry them by the stem either. Handle like eggs — every bruise and scratch is where the rot starts — and keep the ones with any damage for eating first.
temperate.cure: Curing hardens the rind, heals small cuts and converts starch to sugar. Leave the squash somewhere warm and airy — 27–29 °C (80–85 °F) is the figure the extension services give — for 10 to 14 days: a sunny porch or a warm room with a fan, or in the field for a week or two if the weather is dry and sunny. Acorn and delicata types are the exception: do not cure them, it shortens their life; eat them within a couple of months.

store.where: Cool, dry room: cold room, insulated garage, basement corner
store.keeps: Acorn 1–2 months; butternut 2–3 months; buttercup, kabocha, hubbard 3–6 months
store.how: One layer on a shelf or slatted boards, not touching, not on a concrete floor, with air moving. Relative humidity 50–70%. Not near apples or pears, whose ethylene shortens the life. Never below 10 °C — chilled squash rots from the inside.

store.where: Spare bedroom closet, under the stairs, top of a basement stairwell
store.keeps: Roughly half as long as the ideal
store.how: Same rules: single layer, air space, check weekly and cook anything with a soft spot the same day. Warmer than 20 °C the flesh goes stringy and dry.

temperate.preserveNote: A cured squash on a cool shelf is already preserved, which is the whole point of the crop; the pantry work comes in January when they start to turn. Then the best method is to roast or steam the flesh, mash it, cool it, and freeze the purée in 500 ml tubs with 1 cm of headspace — it keeps a year and is pie, soup and baby food on demand. What does not work, and this is the one squash rule to carry in your head, is canning purée: mashed or puréed squash or pumpkin cannot be safely canned at home by any method, because the mass is too dense for heat to reach the centre of the jar in a predictable time, and neither can squash butter. The only way squash goes in a jar is as 2.5 cm (1 in) cubes, boiled two minutes and pressure-canned — 55 minutes for 500 ml jars, 90 minutes for litre jars, at 10 psi (weighted gauge) near sea level — and mashed after opening. There is no water-bath method for any squash. Dried squash chips and leather are a good use of a dehydrator, and the seeds roast.

seeds.how: Squash crosses within its species but not across species, and that is the key. Cucurbita pepo covers acorn, delicata, spaghetti squash, zucchini and most pumpkins; C. maxima covers buttercup, kabocha, hubbard and the giant pumpkins; C. moschata is butternut and its relatives. So a butternut will save true beside a buttercup and an acorn, but not beside another moschata, and your acorn is crossing with the zucchini three beds over. Grow one variety per species, isolate by 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), or hand-pollinate a female flower and tape it shut. Pick the seed fruit fully mature and let it sit at least three weeks — the seeds keep maturing inside — then scoop, rinse off the strings, pick out the fat seeds and dry on a plate for two to three weeks until one snaps instead of bending. Most garden varieties are open-pollinated, but check the packet for F1.
seeds.viability: About 6 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cucurbit rotation — two or three years away from squash, pumpkins, cucumbers and melons. Full sun, deep rich soil, and room: vining types want 1.5–1.8 m (5–6 ft) between rows and 60–90 cm (2–3 ft) between plants, or a sturdy trellis for the small-fruited kinds. Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost when the soil at 5 cm is 18 °C (65 °F); seed rots in cold soil. In zones 3–4, where 100 frost-free days is a good year, start seed indoors in large pots three weeks before planting out, transplant without disturbing the roots, and choose 85–95-day varieties — buttercup, early butternuts, delicata and most acorns ripen; a 110-day hubbard is a gamble. Row cover for the first month keeps the heat in and the beetles out.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is 18 °C at 5 cm depth; in zones 3–4 start indoors in pots 3 weeks before planting out.

faqs.q: When is winter squash ready to harvest?
faqs.a: When a thumbnail cannot dent the rind, the skin has gone dull, the colour is full for the type — butternut with no green left — and the stem is drying and corky. In most of southern Canada that is mid-September into October. Cut with 5–10 cm of stem and bring them in before a hard freeze; a light frost that kills the vines does not hurt the fruit.

faqs.q: How do you cure and store winter squash?
faqs.a: Cure 10–14 days somewhere warm and airy, around 27–29 °C, to harden the rind and heal nicks — except acorn and delicata, which are not cured. Then store at 10–15 °C in a dry room, single layer, not on concrete, not near apples. Butternut keeps 2–3 months, buttercup and hubbard 3–6, acorn 1–2. Check weekly and cook the soft ones first.

faqs.q: Can you can squash purée at home?
faqs.a: No, not by any method. Puréed or mashed squash and pumpkin cannot be safely home canned — the purée is too dense for heat to reach the centre of the jar reliably, and the same goes for squash butter. The only canned form is 2.5 cm cubes, pressure-canned 55 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litres at 10 psi near sea level. For purée, freeze it.

faqs.q: Can you freeze winter squash?
faqs.a: Yes, cooked. Roast or steam until soft, scoop, mash, cool quickly, and pack in 500 ml tubs or bags with 1 cm headspace; it keeps a year. Raw cubes can be blanched 3 minutes and frozen but come back soft, so purée is the better use of freezer space. A frozen 500 ml tub is one pie or one pot of soup.

faqs.q: Is winter squash frost hardy?
faqs.a: The plant is not — vines die at 0 °C — but the fruit takes a light frost without harm, especially while the leaves still shelter it. A hard freeze damages the flesh and the squash will not store. Bring them in or cover them when a hard freeze is forecast, or any time after the vines are dead.

faqs.q: How do I save squash seeds?
faqs.a: Only one variety per species — pepo (acorn, delicata, zucchini, most pumpkins), maxima (buttercup, kabocha, hubbard) and moschata (butternut) do not cross with each other but cross freely within each group. Let the seed fruit sit three weeks after harvest, scoop, rinse, keep the fat seeds, dry two to three weeks. Good for about six years.

faqs.q: What can kids do with winter squash?
faqs.a: Harvest day is theirs: they can thumbnail-test every fruit, carry the small ones in a wagon (by the body, never the stem), and line them up by kind to cure. In the kitchen, scooping and sorting seeds is a good counting job, and roasted seeds are the reward. A hubbard needs a grown-up and a heavy knife; a delicata a six-year-old can cut with help.

temperate.name: Pumpkins
temperate.tagline: One kind is for the porch and one is for the pie — and the seeds from both are for the oven.
temperate.frostNote: Pumpkin vines die at 0 °C; the fruit shrugs off a light frost but a hard freeze damages the flesh and a frozen pumpkin will not keep — it goes soft within weeks. If the vines are still alive and only a light frost is coming, leave them. If a hard freeze is forecast, or the vines are already dead and the fruit is lying exposed, cut them all and bring them in, or cover the patch with blankets. A pumpkin that is fully orange is ready to come in regardless.
temperate.ready: Deep, even colour for the variety — orange for most — with a rind a thumbnail cannot dent, a hollow sound when you knock on it, and a stem that is going hard and corky. Pie or sugar pumpkins are the small ones, 1–3 kg, with dense, sweet, smooth flesh; carving pumpkins are big, thin-walled and stringy. Both are ready on the same signs.
temperate.pick: Cut with secateurs or a knife and leave a handle of 8–10 cm (3–4 in) of stem — a pumpkin that loses its stem rots from that spot. Never carry one by the stem; it snaps and takes the top of the fruit with it. Avoid scratching the skin with fingernails or on the wheelbarrow edge, and eat any damaged ones first.
temperate.cure: Cure 10–14 days somewhere warm and airy, ideally 27–29 °C (80–85 °F), to harden the rind and heal small cuts: a sunny step, a porch, or a warm room with a fan. In a dry, sunny autumn they cure in the field for a week or two; in a wet one bring them under cover. Cured pumpkins keep roughly twice as long as uncured.

store.where: Cool, dry room: cold room, insulated garage, basement shelf
store.keeps: 2–3 months; a sound pie pumpkin up to 6
store.how: Single layer on boards or cardboard, not touching, not on concrete, relative humidity 50–70%, air moving. Not next to apples or pears. Never below 10 °C.

store.where: Front step or unheated porch (October only)
store.how: Fine for decoration through October, but once a pumpkin has sat through a freeze it is for the compost or the chickens, not the pie. Bring eating pumpkins indoors before the nights go below 0 °C.

temperate.preserveNote: The best thing to do with a pie pumpkin is leave it whole on a cool shelf until you want it, then roast it and freeze the purée in 500 ml tubs with 1 cm of headspace — one tub is one pie. The seeds are the second crop: rinse the strings off, dry them for a few hours, toss with oil and salt, and roast at 150 °C (300 °F) for 10–15 minutes, stirring. What does not work is canning purée, pumpkin butter or pumpkin pie filling: no tested home process exists for any of them, because a dense purée does not heat through to the centre of the jar in any predictable time, and this is a botulism question, not a texture one. The only jar form is 2.5 cm (1 in) cubes, boiled two minutes and pressure-canned 55 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litre jars at 10 psi (weighted gauge) near sea level, to be mashed after opening. There is no water-bath method. A carving pumpkin can be cooked, but the flesh is watery and stringy; use it for soup or feed it to the compost and grow a pie pumpkin for the kitchen.

seeds.how: Most pie and jack-o’-lantern pumpkins are Cucurbita pepo — the same species as zucchini, acorn, delicata, spaghetti squash and ornamental gourds — and they cross with all of those through bees; giant and some French pumpkins are C. maxima and cross with buttercup, kabocha and hubbard instead. Species do not cross with each other. The fruit this year is unaffected; it is next year’s plants from saved seed that come up as something odd, and a cross with a gourd can be bitter. To save seed grow one pepo variety, or isolate by 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), or hand-pollinate a female flower and tape it shut. Let the pumpkin cure and sit three weeks or more, then scoop, rinse, pick the plump seeds and dry them on a plate for two to three weeks. Most pumpkin varieties are open-pollinated; the packet will say if it is an F1.
seeds.viability: About 6 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cucurbit rotation — two or three years off beds that grew squash, pumpkins, cucumbers or melons. Full sun, a shovel of compost or manure under each hill, and space: vining pumpkins want 1.5–1.8 m (5–6 ft) between hills and 3 m (10 ft) between rows; bush types half that. Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost when the soil at 5 cm is 18 °C (65 °F), late May to early June in most of southern Canada. Pumpkins for Halloween need 90–110 days, so in zones 3–4 start seed indoors in large pots three weeks before planting out, transplant carefully, pick a 90–100-day pie or small carving variety, and use row cover for the first month. One plant per child is plenty.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is 18 °C at 5 cm depth; in zones 3–4 start indoors in pots 3 weeks before planting out.

faqs.q: When do you harvest pumpkins?
faqs.a: When the colour is deep and even, the rind resists a thumbnail, and the stem has gone hard — mid-September into October in most of southern Canada. Cut with 8–10 cm of stem and never carry by it. Bring them in before a hard freeze; a light frost that kills the vines does not hurt a mature pumpkin.

faqs.q: How do you store pumpkins so they last?
faqs.a: Cure them 10–14 days somewhere warm and airy, then keep them at 10–15 °C in a dry room — single layer, off the concrete, away from apples. A cured pie pumpkin keeps two to three months and often longer; a carving pumpkin a month or two. Below 10 °C they chill and rot from inside, and anything that has frozen on the porch is done.

faqs.q: Can you can pumpkin purée or pie filling?
faqs.a: No. There is no safe home method for canning puréed pumpkin, pumpkin butter or pie filling — the purée is too dense for heat to reach the centre of the jar reliably, and that is a botulism risk, not a quality issue. The only canned form is 2.5 cm cubes, pressure-canned 55 minutes for 500 ml jars at 10 psi near sea level, mashed when you open them. Freeze your purée instead.

faqs.q: How do you freeze pumpkin?
faqs.a: Cook it first: halve, seed, roast or steam until soft, scoop the flesh, mash or blend, cool quickly in a bowl set in cold water, and pack in 500 ml tubs or bags with 1 cm headspace. It keeps about a year; thaw in the fridge and pour off any water before baking. One 500 ml tub is a standard pie.

faqs.q: Can you eat a carving pumpkin?
faqs.a: You can, but the flesh is thin, watery and stringy compared with a pie pumpkin; it makes a passable soup and a poor pie. The seeds are just as good roasted. A jack-o’-lantern that has been cut open and sat on the step for days is not food — scoop and roast the seeds the day you carve, and compost the rest.

faqs.q: How do you roast pumpkin seeds?
faqs.a: Pull the seeds out of the strings in a bowl of water — they float free — rinse, and pat or air-dry them for a few hours. Toss with a little oil and salt and roast at 150 °C (300 °F) for 10–15 minutes, stirring once or twice, until they are golden and crack when you bite one. Cool completely and keep in a jar for a week or two, or the freezer for longer.

faqs.q: What should kids know about pumpkins?
faqs.a: Carrying, thumbnail-testing and seed-sorting are theirs; the knife is not. Teach them to lift a pumpkin from underneath, never by the stem. Counting seeds from one pumpkin into tens is a real maths lesson (expect 300–500), and roasting them is the payoff. A child who grows one pie pumpkin and eats the pie from it in November learns more about where food comes from than from any book.

temperate.name: Eggplant
temperate.tagline: One of the most cold-shy plants in the garden, and the one that has to be cooked before it goes in the freezer.
temperate.frostNote: Eggplant is less cold-hardy than tomatoes: 0 °C kills the plant, and fruit left out on nights near 5 °C gets chilling damage — pitting and brown seeds — even without a frost. Once September nights drop under 10 °C regularly, pick everything glossy and of usable size, small included. A sheet over the plants buys one cool night; it is not worth fighting for more than that. There is no ripening indoors.
temperate.ready: Full size for the variety, skin glossy and taut, and the flesh springs back when you press it with a thumb. A fruit that has gone dull, bronze or soft, or whose seeds have turned brown inside, is overripe and bitter. Pick young — a half-sized glossy eggplant eats better than a full-sized dull one — and picking keeps the plant setting.
temperate.pick: Cut with secateurs, leaving 2–3 cm of the stem and the green cap on; pulling tears the woody stem and often the branch. Wear gloves or watch your fingers — many varieties carry small spines on the cap. Handle like fruit, not a vegetable: a bruise turns brown in a day.

store.how: In a perforated bag or an open box with a damp towel. Eggplant wants 10–12 °C and high humidity — colder is damage, warmer is quick decay.
In a perforated bag, and use it fast: below 10 °C the skin pits and bronzes and the seeds brown within about a week. Not with apples — ethylene makes it worse.

temperate.preserveNote: Eggplant does not store and does not freeze raw — it discolours and turns to sponge — so it is preserved cooked. Roasted whole or in halves until collapsed, the flesh scooped and frozen in 250 ml tubs, is the best form: baba ghanoush, pasta sauce and curry all winter. Breaded and fried or baked slices freeze well with freezer paper between them, ready for parmigiana. The tested freezing method for plain slices is 8 mm (⅓ in) rounds blanched 4 minutes in boiling water with 125 ml (½ cup) lemon juice per 4 L to stop the browning, cooled, drained and packed. What does not work is canning eggplant on its own in any form — it is low-acid and there is no tested process — or pickling it by a family recipe or an internet one: eggplant goes in a jar only by a tested pickle such as Bernardin’s aubergine pickles, which pre-boils eggplant sticks in a measured vinegar-and-water brine, water-bath processed. Marinated eggplant in oil is a refrigerator food to eat within days, never a pantry one.

seeds.how: Eggplant flowers self-pollinate, so an open-pollinated variety comes true — but check the packet, because many of the glossy black supermarket-type varieties are F1 hybrids. Bees do move pollen between plants, so keep varieties 90–500 m (300–1,600 ft) apart, or bag a few flowers in organza. Seed is not ripe at eating stage: leave the chosen fruit on the plant until it goes dull, yellowish or brownish, soft, and comes off with a tug — weeks past when you would eat it. Cube it and blend with water in a food processor on a gentle setting or mash it in a bucket; good seed sinks, pulp floats and pours off. Rinse in a sieve and dry on a plate or coffee filter for two weeks.
seeds.viability: 4–6 years.

temperate.nextYear: Nightshade rotation — not where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant or tomatillos grew in the last three years. Full sun, the warmest, best-drained bed you have, steady water (drought makes it bitter), 45–60 cm (18–24 in) apart. Eggplant is the slowest of the nightshades: start indoors 9–10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat at 24–29 °C, and plant out two weeks after the last frost once nights hold above 10 °C — a seedling chilled in May can sulk all summer and set nothing. In zones 3–5 grow small-fruited, early varieties (Asian long types, baby and 60–65-day kinds) in black pots or through black plastic, under row cover until flowering.

sow.outdoors: Transplant about 2 weeks after the last frost, once nights hold above 10 °C.

faqs.q: When is eggplant ready to pick?
faqs.a: When it is glossy, taut and firm, at or a little under full size for the variety, and the flesh springs back from a thumb press. Dull skin, a bronze cast or softness mean it is overripe, with brown seeds and a bitter edge. Cut it with 2–3 cm of stem — do not pull — and pick small and often to keep the plant setting.

faqs.q: How do you store eggplant?
faqs.a: Briefly, and not too cold: 10–12 °C and humid is ideal, which usually means a cool basement or garage in a perforated bag, for up to a week. The fridge works for three to five days, but below 10 °C the skin pits and bronzes and the seeds brown within about a week, so plan to cook it soon after picking.

faqs.q: Can you freeze eggplant?
faqs.a: Only cooked or blanched. The easiest is to roast whole eggplants until they collapse, scoop the flesh and freeze it in 250 ml tubs. Breaded and baked slices freeze well with paper between them. Plain slices can be blanched 4 minutes in water with 125 ml lemon juice per 4 L, cooled and frozen. Raw eggplant frozen as-is browns and turns spongy.

faqs.q: Can you can or pickle eggplant?
faqs.a: Not plain — eggplant is low-acid and there is no tested home canning process for it on its own. It can be pickled by a tested recipe only, such as Bernardin’s aubergine pickles, which pre-boils eggplant sticks in a measured vinegar-and-water brine with a 15-minute water bath for 500 ml jars. Marinated eggplant in oil is a fridge food to eat within days, never a pantry jar.

faqs.q: Is eggplant frost tolerant?
faqs.a: No — it is the least cold-tolerant plant in the vegetable garden, less hardy than tomatoes. The plant dies at 0 °C, and the fruit is damaged by chilling on nights near 5 °C even without frost. Once September nights are regularly under 10 °C, pick what you have and cook it; covering buys one night at most.

faqs.q: How do I save eggplant seeds?
faqs.a: From an open-pollinated variety — many are F1 hybrids. Leave a fruit on the plant until it is dull, yellow-brown and soft, weeks past eating stage. Cube it and mash or blend gently with water; good seed sinks and pulp floats off. Rinse and dry for two weeks. Keep varieties 90 m apart or bag a few flowers. Good for four to six years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about eggplant?
faqs.a: It is a nightshade like tomato and potato: the fruit is food once cooked, and the leaves and stems are not. The caps and stems often carry small prickles, so picking is a gloves-on job for a six-year-old or a watch-and-carry job for a three-year-old. A purple eggplant is one of the few vegetables children will carry in from the garden just because it is beautiful, and that is a fair reason to grow one.

temperate.name: Carrots
temperate.tagline: The root that gets sweeter the longer autumn goes on — and keeps until spring if you treat it right.
temperate.frostNote: Leave them. Carrot tops take −4 to −6 °C with nothing worse than a scorched leaf, the roots below ground are untouched, and a few frosts turn starch to sugar so the carrots taste better for it. What hurts them is the soil freezing solid around the root. Once nights below −7 °C are forecast to run for days, either dig the lot or pile 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves over the row and keep digging under it.
temperate.ready: Shoulders 2–3 cm (¾–1¼ in) across at the soil line — brush the soil back to look rather than pulling to check. The days-to-maturity on the packet (55–75) is a guide; the real test is size, and a carrot left long past full size goes woody at the core. A July sowing dug in October after a couple of frosts is the best carrot of the year.
temperate.pick: Loosen the row with a fork first or the tops snap off and the carrot stays put. Pull on a dry day if they are for storage. Twist or cut the tops to 1 cm (½ in) straight away — leaves left on pull water out of the root and it goes limp within a day. Don’t wash carrots that are going into store; rub the loose soil off and leave the rest.

store.keeps: Until the ground freezes hard — into December in zones 5–6
store.how: 30 cm (12 in) of straw or dry leaves over the row, held down with boards or a tarp; dig from one end as you need them. Mark the row — it vanishes under snow.
Tops off, unwashed, in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a bin, or in perforated plastic bags in a crate. Look through them monthly and pull anything going soft.

store.where: Fridge crisper or a cooler in an unheated garage
store.how: Tops off in a perforated bag in the crisper; or packed in damp sand in a cooler in the garage, brought indoors if the garage is going to sit below −5 °C for long.

temperate.preserveNote: Carrots are best not put up at all: a cold room or a mulched row keeps them crisp into spring with no work. For jars, carrots are a low-acid vegetable and must be pressure-canned — 25 minutes for 500 ml jars and 30 for litres at 10 lb on a weighted gauge at sea level — never water-bathed, because boiling water does not reach the temperature that kills botulism spores. Pickled carrots are a different thing: the tested NCHFP and Bernardin recipes carry enough 5% vinegar to go in a boiling-water canner, so follow one exactly and don’t water the brine down. Freezing is good for cooking carrots if you blanch first (2 minutes for slices and sticks, 5 for small whole roots); unblanched carrots turn rubbery and lose flavour within weeks. Dried carrot shreds are fine for soup.

seeds.how: Carrots flower in their second year, so you keep the best roots over winter (in the ground under mulch where winters are mild, or in damp sand at 0–4 °C), replant them 45 cm (18 in) apart in spring, and cut the umbels when they turn brown and dry in late summer. The catch is Queen Anne’s lace: it is the same species, it grows along every roadside in eastern Canada, and garden carrots cross with it freely, giving thin, pale, bitter roots. Seed Savers Exchange wants 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) from wild carrot and other varieties, which most gardens cannot manage; bagging a few umbels and hand-pollinating is the realistic route. Save from at least five plants. For most families, carrot seed is one to buy.
seeds.viability: 3–6 years in a cool, dry, airtight jar — the low end if the jar is opened often.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with the umbel family (parsnip, celery, dill, parsley) and give carrots a bed where none grew last year, which keeps carrot rust fly down. Deep, loose, stone-free soil — a raised bed or one forked 30 cm (12 in) deep — grows straight roots; fresh manure forks them. Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost once the soil is above 7 °C, 5 mm (¼ in) deep, and keep the surface damp for the 1–3 weeks germination takes (a board over the row until they show helps). Thin to 5–8 cm (2–3 in). Sow again in early July for storage carrots that size up in cool weather. In zones 3–4 use a 60–65-day Nantes type and a floating row cover against rust fly.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost, when the soil is above 7 °C, and again in early July for storage roots.

faqs.q: When should I harvest carrots?
faqs.a: When the shoulder is 2–3 cm (¾–1¼ in) across at the soil line — brush the soil back to check. Spring-sown carrots are ready from July; the storage crop from a July sowing is dug in October or November, and it is sweeter after a few frosts. Dig before the ground freezes solid unless the row is under a thick mulch.

faqs.q: How do I store carrots for the winter without a cold room?
faqs.a: Tops off, unwashed, in perforated bags in the fridge crisper for one to three months, or packed in damp sand in a cooler in an unheated garage. Easier still, leave them in the bed under 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves and dig as needed until the ground freezes hard. A proper cold room at 0–2 °C with high humidity keeps them four to six months.

faqs.q: Can you freeze carrots?
faqs.a: Yes, blanched: 2 minutes for slices and sticks, 5 minutes for small whole carrots, then cool, drain and bag. They are soft when thawed, so use them in soups, stews and purée. Carrots frozen raw go rubbery and taste off within a few weeks.

faqs.q: Can carrots stay in the ground over winter?
faqs.a: Into early winter, yes, under a heavy mulch; the roots are fine at −4 to −6 °C and sweeter for it. What damages them is the soil freezing hard around them, so in zones 3–5 most gardeners dig the last of the crop in November or December. In zone 6–7 a mulched row can be dug through much of the winter.

faqs.q: Can I water-bath can carrots?
faqs.a: Plain carrots, no — they are low-acid and must be pressure-canned (25 minutes for 500 ml jars, 30 for litres at 10 lb weighted gauge at sea level). Pickled carrots from a tested recipe with 5% vinegar are water-bath canned, because the vinegar makes the jar acidic enough. Never swap one method for the other.

faqs.q: How do I save carrot seeds?
faqs.a: Overwinter a few of the best roots and replant them in spring; they flower and set seed in late summer of the second year. The problem is that carrots cross with Queen Anne’s lace, which is the same species and grows wild across southern Canada, so saved seed often gives thin, bitter roots unless you isolate or hand-pollinate. Seed keeps three to six years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about carrots?
faqs.a: Pulling carrots is a great job for small hands once an adult has loosened the row with a fork, and a garden carrot rinsed under the tap is safe to eat on the spot. The rule to teach is that carrots come from the garden only: the wild ‘carrot’ (Queen Anne’s lace) has deadly look-alikes, poison hemlock and water hemlock, so nobody pulls a white-flowered plant from the ditch to eat.

temperate.name: Beets
temperate.tagline: Two crops in one bed — the roots for the cold room, the greens for tonight.
temperate.frostNote: A light frost to about −3 °C does nothing but nip the leaves, and the roots are sweeter after it. But a beet sits half out of the ground, so a hard freeze (−5 °C and below) damages the exposed shoulder and that beet rots in storage. The night a hard frost is forecast, either dig them or pull soil and mulch up over the shoulders. Beets do not overwinter in the ground in zones 3–5: dig before the soil freezes.
temperate.ready: Roots 4–7 cm (1½–3 in) across — the shoulder shows above the soil, which is how you check without pulling. Small beets are tender; anything over 8 cm (3 in) tends to be woody unless the variety is bred for size. Greens are ready from the thinnings onward; take a leaf or two per plant and the root keeps growing.
temperate.pick: Pull by the base of the leaves on a dry day, loosening with a fork in heavy soil. Twist the tops off leaving 2–3 cm (1 in) of stem — cutting into the crown or trimming the tap root makes the beet bleed its colour and shortens its life in store. Don’t wash. Cook the greens the same day; they wilt fast.

store.how: Tops twisted off, in damp sand or sawdust in a bin, or in perforated bags. Beets shrivel faster than carrots, so keep the sand moist.

store.keeps: 1–2 months for roots; 3–5 days for greens
store.how: Roots in a perforated bag; greens separately in a bag with a damp towel.

store.where: Cooler in an unheated garage or porch
store.how: A cooler or insulated box of damp sand; bring it in if the garage is going to sit below −3 °C for long.

temperate.preserveNote: Pickled beets are what most people want from a beet glut, and they are safely water-bath canned because the tested recipes (NCHFP, Bernardin) carry enough 5% vinegar to bring the jar well under pH 4.6 — 30 minutes in a boiling-water canner for 500 ml jars. Plain beets are another matter: they are low-acid and must be pressure-canned, 30 minutes for 500 ml and 35 for litres at 10 lb weighted gauge, with the jars filled with fresh boiling water rather than the red cooking liquid. Never water-bath plain beets. Cooked beets freeze well sliced or cubed; raw beets do not. Beet greens are treated like spinach — blanch 2 minutes, squeeze, freeze.

seeds.how: Beets flower in their second year after a cold spell. Keep the best roots in damp sand at 0–4 °C over winter (or in the ground under heavy mulch where the soil stays above about −9 °C), replant them 45 cm (18 in) apart in spring, and let the 1–2 m seed stalks ripen in late summer; strip the dry seed clusters by hand. Beets are wind-pollinated and the pollen travels — Seed Savers Exchange asks for 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) between varieties — and they cross with Swiss chard, which is the same species, so a bolting chard plant in the bed ruins your beet seed. Save from at least five plants. Each ‘seed’ is a cluster of two to four, which is why beets always need thinning.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with chard and spinach (the same family) and follow a legume or a well-composted bed; beets want neutral to slightly alkaline soil, and a boron shortage shows up as black corky spots inside the root. Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost when the soil is 7–10 °C, 2 cm (¾ in) deep and 2–3 cm apart in rows 30 cm (12 in) apart, and thin to 8–10 cm (3–4 in) — eat the thinnings. Sow again every three weeks until early July; the July sowing gives the best storage roots. In zones 3–4 pick a 50–55-day variety and soak the seed overnight to speed germination.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, soil 7–10 °C; repeat every three weeks until early July.

faqs.q: When should I harvest beets?
faqs.a: At 4–7 cm (1½–3 in) across, about 50–65 days from sowing — you can see the shoulder above the soil. Spring sowings are ready from July; the storage crop comes out in October after a frost or two but before a hard freeze. Greens can be picked a leaf at a time all season.

faqs.q: How do I store beets for the winter?
faqs.a: Twist the tops off leaving 2–3 cm of stem, don’t wash, and pack them in damp sand or perforated bags at 0–2 °C with high humidity, where they keep three to five months. Without a cold room, the fridge crisper holds them one to two months and a cooler of damp sand in an unheated garage two to three. Keep the sand moist — beets shrivel faster than carrots.

faqs.q: Can you freeze beets?
faqs.a: Cooked, yes: boil whole until tender, slip the skins, slice or cube, cool and bag. They hold their colour and texture well for soups, salads and roasting. Raw beets freeze badly. Beet greens freeze like spinach, blanched 2 minutes.

faqs.q: Can I water-bath can beets?
faqs.a: Pickled beets from a tested recipe, yes — the 5% vinegar makes the jar acidic enough, and they process 30 minutes for 500 ml jars. Plain beets, no: they are low-acid and must be pressure-canned, 30 minutes for 500 ml and 35 for litres at 10 lb weighted gauge. Fill plain-beet jars with fresh boiling water, not the cooking liquid.

faqs.q: How do I save beet seeds?
faqs.a: Overwinter the best roots in damp sand at 0–4 °C and replant them in spring; they flower and set seed in their second summer. Beets are wind-pollinated and cross with Swiss chard and other beet varieties up to 800 m away, so only one Beta vulgaris can flower at a time. Seed keeps four to five years.

faqs.q: Are beets frost hardy?
faqs.a: Hardy to light frost: the leaves shrug off −2 to −3 °C and the roots are sweeter after it. The shoulder sits above the soil, though, so a hard freeze below −5 °C damages it and the beet will not store. Dig or mulch over the shoulders before a hard frost, and dig everything before the ground freezes.

faqs.q: What should kids know about beets?
faqs.a: Beets are safe to pull, rinse and eat raw in thin slices, and the greens are fine too. The juice dyes hands, aprons and chopping boards for a day, which children generally consider a feature. Pulling beets by their leafy handles and sorting them by size is a good job for a four-year-old.

temperate.name: Potatoes
temperate.tagline: The crop children remember digging — and the one that needs two weeks in the dark before it goes anywhere.
temperate.frostNote: The tops are tender: −1 to −2 °C blackens the leaves, which is harmless to the crop — it just ends the season, and the plants were dying back anyway. The tubers are safe under 10–15 cm (4–6 in) of soil through light frosts. Dig everything before a hard freeze or before the ground freezes, because a frozen tuber turns watery and rots in store. If a hard frost has already caught a hilled row, use anything that was near the surface first.
temperate.ready: New potatoes any time after the plants flower, 7–8 weeks from planting — dig gently at the side of a hill with your hands and take a few. Storage potatoes wait until the tops have yellowed and died back, then another two weeks in the ground so the skins set; a mature skin does not rub off under your thumb.
temperate.pick: Dig on a dry day with a fork, starting 30 cm (12 in) out from the stem and lifting toward it so you spear as few as possible. Let them sit on the soil for an hour to dry, then brush — don’t wash. Anything cut or speared goes to the kitchen this week, not the cellar. Keep every tuber out of sunlight from the moment it is up: light greens the skin within a day.
temperate.cure: Cure 1–2 weeks at 10–15 °C in high humidity and total darkness — a basement floor or a cool shed with a blanket over the crate. The skins thicken and small cuts heal, which is the difference between a crop that keeps until April and one that rots by Christmas.

store.how: Slatted crates, baskets or paper sacks — never sealed plastic — in the dark with some air movement. Not with onions, and not near apples: the ethylene starts them sprouting. Check monthly and rub off sprouts.

store.where: Cool basement corner or under the stairs
store.how: A covered crate or paper sack in the dark. Warmer than ideal, so they sprout sooner; use them up by late winter.
Paper bag, dark. The fridge is worse than the cupboard: below 4 °C the starch turns to sugar, so the potatoes taste sweet and brown too fast and unevenly when fried.

temperate.preserveNote: A potato is its own preserve: cured, then kept cold and dark, it lasts most of the winter. If you do can, potatoes are low-acid and must be pressure-canned — peeled, cubed, boiled 2 minutes, covered with fresh boiling water (the cooking water carries too much starch) and processed 35 minutes for 500 ml and 40 for litres at 10 lb weighted gauge; never water-bath. Raw potatoes do not freeze — they go black and spongy — but blanched new potatoes (3–5 minutes), mashed potato, and par-cooked chips and hash browns freeze well. Dried potato slices need blanching first.

seeds.how: Potatoes are grown from tubers, not seed, and every extension service says the same thing: buy certified seed potatoes each spring. A tuber carries the viruses and scab of the plant it grew on, and saved seed goes downhill over a few years — smaller crop, more disease. If you save your own anyway, mark the healthiest, most productive plants in summer, keep egg-sized tubers from only those plants, store them cold and dark, and set them in light for two weeks before planting so they green and sprout. Grocery potatoes are often treated to stop sprouting and may carry disease, so they are a poor bet. The small green ‘true seed’ balls that sometimes form after flowering are not worth growing — the plants do not come true.
seeds.viability: Seed tubers keep one winter at 4–7 °C in the dark and are planted the following spring.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with the nightshade family: not where potatoes, tomatoes, peppers or eggplant grew in the last three years, to keep blight and scab down. Loose, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0) grows cleaner skins — no lime, no fresh manure. Plant seed pieces with at least one eye each 2–3 weeks before the last frost once the soil is 7–10 °C, 10 cm (4 in) deep and 30 cm (12 in) apart in rows 75–90 cm (30–36 in) apart, and hill soil up around the stems twice as they grow to keep the tubers dark and increase the crop. In zones 3–4 choose an early or mid-season variety (65–85 days) and chit the seed indoors in light for two weeks for a head start.

sow.outdoors: Plant seed pieces 2–3 weeks before the last frost, when the soil is 7–10 °C.

faqs.q: When should I harvest potatoes?
faqs.a: New potatoes from about 7–8 weeks after planting, once the plants flower — take a few from the side of the hill and leave the plant growing. Storage potatoes come out two weeks after the tops have died back, when the skin no longer rubs off with your thumb, usually September into October. Dig before a hard freeze and before the ground freezes.

faqs.q: How do I store potatoes for the winter?
faqs.a: Cure them first: 1–2 weeks at 10–15 °C, high humidity, total darkness. Then keep them at 4–7 °C in the dark in slatted crates or paper sacks, with air movement, away from onions and apples; a cold room holds them five to seven months. Without one, a cool basement corner or under the stairs at 7–12 °C gives two to four months. Not the fridge.

faqs.q: Can you freeze potatoes?
faqs.a: Not raw — they turn black and spongy. Blanched new potatoes (3–5 minutes), mashed potato, par-cooked chips and hash browns, and cooked potato dishes all freeze well. Potatoes in frozen soups and stews go mealy, so add them fresh when you reheat.

faqs.q: Are green potatoes safe to eat?
faqs.a: The green is chlorophyll from light exposure, and it comes with solanine, which tastes bitter and can upset the stomach. Cut away small green patches and any sprouts generously; a potato that is green through or tastes bitter goes in the compost. Keep tubers hilled in the garden and in the dark in store and it does not happen.

faqs.q: Can I save my own seed potatoes?
faqs.a: You can, but certified seed is the safe bet: saved tubers carry viruses and scab forward, and yields fall over a few seasons. If you do save, choose egg-sized tubers from your healthiest plants, store them cold and dark, and set them in light for two weeks before planting to sprout. Never plant supermarket potatoes.

faqs.q: Are potatoes frost hardy?
faqs.a: The plants are not: −1 to −2 °C blackens the leaves, and in spring a frosted shoot has to regrow (hill soil over emerging shoots if a frost is forecast). The tubers underground are fine through light frosts in autumn, and the dead tops do not matter. Dig the crop before a hard freeze reaches into the soil.

faqs.q: What should kids know about potatoes?
faqs.a: The potato dig is the best day of the garden year for a child: hands in the loosened soil, treasure coming up by the handful, and counting and sorting by size at the end. The rules are that the leaves, stems and the little green fruits are not food (they hold the same solanine-type alkaloids as the tomato plant), green potatoes get cut away or composted, and the harvest goes straight into a box out of the sun.
