temperate.name: Parsnips
temperate.tagline: The one root that wants a hard frost before it is worth eating — and the last crop you can dig in spring.
temperate.frostNote: Do nothing — this is what you were waiting for. Parsnips need two to four weeks near 0 °C to turn their starch to sugar, and the roots stand −10 °C and far below under snow. Gardeners in zone 3 leave them in all winter. The one thing worth doing before the ground freezes is a thick mulch of straw or leaves over the row, so you can still get a fork in through December and again at the first thaw.
temperate.ready: Not before the first hard frosts — an early-dug parsnip is starchy and flat. The roots are full-sized (3–5 cm / 1–2 in at the shoulder, 20–30 cm / 8–12 in long) by late September in most gardens, so size is not the question; cold is. Anything left in the ground must come out in spring before the leaves regrow, usually by mid-April, because the root goes woody and hollow as the second-year flower stalk forms.
temperate.pick: Dig, don’t pull: the roots go deep and snap. Work a fork in alongside, lever, and lift. Trim the tops to 1 cm (½ in). Wear gloves and long sleeves when you handle the foliage on a sunny day — the sap makes skin react to sunlight, and the burn and blisters show up a day or two later and can leave a mark for months. It is the same reaction as wild parsnip, just milder in the garden plant. Overcast days and evenings are the safe time to weed and harvest.

store.keeps: All winter — dig into December and again March–April
store.how: 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves over the row before the ground freezes, with a stake to mark it. Dig in thaws; the roots do not mind being frozen in the soil.
Tops off, unwashed, in damp sand or perforated bags, like carrots. Dig for storage only after they have had their frosts; they sweeten further in the first two weeks at 0 °C.
Perforated bag, tops off. They shrivel faster than carrots, so this is the short-term spot.

temperate.preserveNote: Parsnips do not need preserving in a climate where the ground is their cold room. If you want some in the freezer, cube and blanch 2 minutes (NCHFP) — they go into soups and mash well, though the texture softens; roasting first and freezing the roasted chunks gives a better result. There is no tested home-canning process for plain parsnips: the NCHFP and USDA guides give pressure-canning times for carrots, beets and potatoes but none for parsnips, so don’t borrow the carrot time and hope. There is no tested pickled parsnip either. Dig, store cold, and eat them fresh from November to April.

seeds.how: Parsnips flower in their second summer, and they are the easiest biennial there is to save in the north: leave two or three good roots in the ground over winter and they throw 1.5 m (5 ft) stalks of yellow umbels in June. Let the flat, papery seeds turn brown and start to drop, cut the heads into a paper bag and rub the seed free. They are insect-pollinated and cross with wild parsnip — the same species, common along Ontario and Quebec roadsides — so look around first; Seed Savers Exchange asks for 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) isolation. The real reason to save your own is that bought parsnip seed is often already too old to germinate well.
seeds.viability: 1–2 years at most — the shortest of the common garden seeds. Buy or save fresh every year and sow thickly.

temperate.nextYear: Same family as carrots, so rotate them together, away from where either grew last year. Deep, loose soil without fresh manure or stones. Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost when the soil is 10 °C or more; parsnip seed is slow (2–4 weeks) and germinates poorly once it is a year old, so sow fresh seed thickly, 1 cm (½ in) deep, with a few radish seeds to mark the row, and thin to 8–10 cm (3–4 in). They need the whole season — 100–120 days — and will not size up from a July sowing. In zones 3–4 that spring sowing is the only one; a floating row cover keeps carrot rust fly off.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost, soil 10 °C or more, fresh seed only.

faqs.q: When should I harvest parsnips?
faqs.a: After the first hard frosts — late October into November in most of southern Canada — because the cold is what converts the starch to sugar; the roots are full size well before that. Dig through the winter under mulch whenever the ground is workable, and finish by mid-April before the leaves regrow and the root turns woody.

faqs.q: Can parsnips stay in the ground all winter?
faqs.a: Yes, that is the normal way to keep them. The roots take −10 °C and colder under snow without harm. Mulch the row with 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves before the ground freezes so you can still dig in December and again at the March thaw. Anything still in by late April goes hollow as the plant bolts.

faqs.q: Why did my arms burn after weeding the parsnips?
faqs.a: Parsnip leaves and stems carry a sap that makes skin react to sunlight — the same thing wild parsnip does, in a milder form. Sap on bare skin in bright sun leaves a red, sometimes blistered patch a day or two later that can mark the skin for months. Weed and harvest in gloves and long sleeves, or on cloudy days and evenings, and wash sap off straight away.

faqs.q: Can you freeze parsnips?
faqs.a: Yes: peel, cut into 1 cm (½ in) cubes, blanch 2 minutes, cool, drain and bag. They soften when thawed, so they are for soup, mash and roasting rather than anything crisp. Roasted parsnip chunks frozen on a tray reheat better than blanched ones.

faqs.q: How do I save parsnip seeds?
faqs.a: Leave a few roots in the ground over winter; they flower in June of the second year and the seed is dry by August. Cut the heads into a paper bag and rub the seed out. They cross with wild parsnip within 800 m, so check the roadsides nearby. Use the seed within a year — parsnip seed dies faster than any other common vegetable.

faqs.q: Are parsnips frost hardy?
faqs.a: The hardiest root in the garden. Frost does not just leave them alone, it improves them: two to four weeks near freezing turns starch to sugar. The roots survive −10 °C and below in the ground, and under snow and mulch they come through a zone 3 winter. Nothing needs covering on a frost night.

faqs.q: What should kids know about parsnips?
faqs.a: A frosted parsnip is one of the sweetest things in the garden and children who refuse them in June eat them roasted in December. The rule is that only grown-ups handle the leaves on sunny days, because the sap can burn skin in sunlight; kids can do the digging once the tops are cut off, and the roots themselves are safe to handle, wash and eat.

temperate.name: Turnips
temperate.tagline: The fastest root in the garden — six weeks from seed, with greens thrown in.
temperate.frostNote: Leave them. Turnip roots take −4 to −6 °C and taste milder and sweeter after a frost or two; the greens scorch at about −3 °C but recover from a light nip. They are less hardy than rutabagas or carrots, though: once nights head toward −7 °C and lower, dig the roots or mulch them heavily. Salad turnips (‘Hakurei’ types) are the least hardy and come in first.
temperate.ready: Spring-sown roots are at their best at 5–8 cm (2–3 in) across, about five to six weeks from sowing — bigger than that in warm weather and they turn hot, pithy and woody. Fall turnips can go a little larger in the cool. Greens are good any time; take the outer leaves and leave the centre growing.
temperate.pick: Pull by the tops, loosening with a trowel if the soil is dry and hard. For storage, twist the tops off leaving 1 cm (½ in), don’t wash, and don’t trim the root. Cook the greens that day. Dig the fall crop before the ground freezes.

store.how: Tops off, in damp sand or perforated bags. Turnips give off a cabbage smell in store — keep them away from the apples and out of the living room.

store.keeps: 2–4 weeks for roots; 3–4 days for greens
store.how: Perforated bag; greens separately wrapped in a damp towel.

store.keeps: A few extra weeks in late fall
store.how: 20–30 cm (8–12 in) of straw over the row and dig as needed. A late-autumn extension, not a whole-winter method for turnips in zones 3–5.

temperate.preserveNote: Turnips are a fresh-eating root first; the cold room is the main preserve and a couple of months is plenty for most families. For the freezer, cube and blanch 2 minutes (NCHFP) — the texture softens, so they are for soups, stews and mash. There is no tested process for canning plain turnips, so leave the pressure canner alone. Where turnips shine is grated and salted into sauerrüben (made exactly like sauerkraut and kept in the fridge once sour) and in quick fridge pickles with 5% vinegar, which take the peppery edge and keep it. The greens freeze like any other green, blanched 2 minutes.

seeds.how: Turnips are biennials — overwinter the roots in sand at 0–4 °C, or in the ground where the soil stays above about −10 °C, and replant them in spring — but the harder problem is crossing. Brassica rapa includes Chinese cabbage, bok choy, mizuna, tatsoi, broccoli raab and some mustards, and any of them flowering within 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) will cross with your turnips; a bolting bok choy in June is the usual culprit. Rutabagas are a different species and will not cross. Turnips are self-incompatible, so grow at least five plants and let them flower together. Collect the pods when they turn tan and shatter them in a bag.
seeds.viability: 4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cabbage family: not where turnips, rutabagas, radishes, cabbage, broccoli, kale or mustard grew in the last three years, which is the only real defence against root maggot and clubroot. Light, fertile soil and steady water. Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, 1 cm (½ in) deep, thinned to 8–10 cm (3–4 in), and again 6–8 weeks before the first fall frost for the storage crop — the fall crop is the better one, sweeter and with fewer pests. A floating row cover from sowing stops both flea beetle and root maggot. In zones 3–4 both sowings work; turnips are one of the few roots that make a crop from a late-July sowing.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, and again 6–8 weeks before the first fall frost.

faqs.q: When should I harvest turnips?
faqs.a: At 5–8 cm (2–3 in) across, about five to six weeks after sowing — pull one to check. Left bigger in warm weather they turn hot and woody. Spring sowings come out in June and July; the fall crop from an August sowing is dug in October and November, and it is sweeter after a frost.

faqs.q: How do I store turnips?
faqs.a: Twist off the tops, don’t wash, and keep them in damp sand or perforated bags at 0–2 °C with high humidity, where they last two to four months. In the fridge crisper they keep two to four weeks. They smell of cabbage in store, so give them their own corner.

faqs.q: Can you freeze turnips?
faqs.a: Yes, cubed and blanched 2 minutes, then cooled and bagged. They go soft when thawed, so use them in soups, stews and mash rather than roasted. Turnip greens freeze like spinach, blanched 2 minutes and squeezed dry.

faqs.q: Are turnips frost hardy?
faqs.a: Yes, to about −6 °C, and a frost or two sweetens them. The leaves scorch below −3 °C but the root is fine. They are less hardy than rutabagas and carrots, so dig or mulch heavily once nights go below −7 °C, and dig the crop before the ground freezes.

faqs.q: Can I can turnips?
faqs.a: Not plain — there is no tested home-canning process for turnips, so no safe time exists. Preserve them in the cold room, the freezer, as a quick fridge pickle, or fermented like sauerkraut and kept cold.

faqs.q: How do I save turnip seeds?
faqs.a: Overwinter the best roots and replant them in spring; they flower and set pods in early summer of the second year. The problem is crossing: turnips are Brassica rapa, the same species as Chinese cabbage, bok choy and mizuna, so none of those can be flowering within 800 m. Grow at least five plants. Seed keeps four years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about turnips?
faqs.a: A small salad turnip pulled, rinsed and eaten raw is crisp and mild, and children who like radishes usually like it. They are one of the quickest things a child can sow and harvest — six weeks from seed in a short row they own. Both root and leaves are safe to eat; the hot taste of an old turnip is a reason to pull them small, not a danger.

temperate.name: Rutabagas
temperate.tagline: The winter root of the north — a sack of them in the cold room is December sorted.
temperate.frostNote: Leave them in. Rutabagas improve after frost — most gardeners wait for at least one hard frost before digging — and the roots stand around −6 °C without harm; the tops look terrible after that but the root underneath is fine. Dig the crop before the ground starts to freeze solid, because a root frozen hard in the soil goes soft and splits in store. In zones 4–5 that is usually early to mid-November.
temperate.ready: 90–100 days from sowing: roots 10–13 cm (4–5 in) across with a purple shoulder standing out of the soil. Smaller is fine; much bigger and the centre can go pithy. They put on most of their size in September’s cool weather, so don’t dig them in August because they look big enough.
temperate.pick: Lift with a fork — the tap root goes down — and cut the tops to 2–3 cm (1 in). Trim the thin side roots. Don’t wash; let them dry on the surface for an hour and brush off the soil. Handle them like eggs if they are going into store: bruises rot.

store.how: Loose in crates, in damp sand, or in perforated bags. The shop ones are dipped in wax to stop them shrivelling; at home, high humidity does the same job. They smell of cabbage, so give them their own corner.

store.where: Cooler in an unheated garage or porch
store.how: An insulated box or cooler with damp sand or newspaper; bring it in when the garage is going well below −5 °C for days.
Perforated bag. One rutabaga is several meals, so the fridge is realistic for a small crop.

temperate.preserveNote: Rutabaga is a storage crop, full stop — the cold room does it better than any jar. For the freezer, cube, blanch 3 minutes (NCHFP), cool and bag; or cook and mash with butter and freeze the mash, which is the better product. There is no tested home-canning process for rutabaga, and its flavour gets stronger and more sulphurous in a canner, so don’t try. Grated rutabaga goes well into fermented kraut mixes with cabbage, kept in the fridge once sour.

seeds.how: Rutabagas are biennials: keep a few of the best roots in damp sand at 0–4 °C over winter (they rarely survive in the ground in zones 3–5), replant them in April with the crown at soil level, and the 1.5 m (5 ft) stalks of yellow flowers set long pods by July. Pick the pods when they go tan and thresh them in a bag. Brassica napus also includes canola and Siberian kale, which will cross with a flowering rutabaga; turnips, cabbage and broccoli are different species and will not. Seed Savers Exchange asks for 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) between varieties. Grow at least five plants together — they are poor self-pollinators.
seeds.viability: 4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cabbage family, so not where any brassica (cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, radish) grew in the last three or four years. Fertile, moisture-holding soil and even water; drought makes them woody. Direct sow in early summer — 90–100 days before your first fall frost, late May to mid-June in zones 4–5 — 1 cm (½ in) deep, thinned to 15–20 cm (6–8 in) in rows 45 cm (18 in) apart. Don’t sow in April: a spring rutabaga matures in summer heat and tastes of it. A floating row cover beats flea beetle and root maggot. In zone 3 sow by the first week of June; rutabagas are one of the most reliable storage crops there.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 90–100 days before the first fall frost — late May to mid-June in zones 4–5.

faqs.q: When should I harvest rutabagas?
faqs.a: In October or November, after at least one hard frost and before the ground starts to freeze solid. They are 90–100 days from sowing and 10–13 cm (4–5 in) across when ready, but they size up and sweeten in September’s cool weather, so there is nothing to gain by digging early.

faqs.q: How do I store rutabagas for the winter?
faqs.a: Cut the tops to 2–3 cm, don’t wash, and keep them at 0–4 °C with high humidity — loose in crates, in damp sand or in perforated bags — where they last four to six months. Without a cold room, a cooler of damp sand in an unheated garage gives two to four months and the fridge crisper one to two.

faqs.q: Can you freeze rutabaga?
faqs.a: Yes. Cube and blanch 3 minutes, then cool and bag; or boil until tender, mash with butter, cool and freeze, which reheats better. Raw rutabaga does not freeze. There is no tested recipe for canning it.

faqs.q: Are rutabagas frost hardy?
faqs.a: Yes. They take around −6 °C without damage and are sweeter for it — the usual advice is to wait for a hard frost before digging. The tops blacken but the root is fine. What they do not take is being frozen solid in the ground, so dig before the soil freezes hard, usually early to mid-November in zones 4–5.

faqs.q: Why are shop rutabagas waxed?
faqs.a: The paraffin coating stops the root losing moisture and shrivelling in a dry shop. At home you don’t need it: high humidity in the cold room (damp sand, perforated bags) does the same job. Peel a waxed one before cooking; a home-grown one just needs peeling as normal.

faqs.q: How do I save rutabaga seeds?
faqs.a: Store the best roots in damp sand over winter and replant them in April; they flower in June and the pods dry by late July of the second year. They are Brassica napus, so they will cross with canola and Siberian kale but not with turnips or cabbage. Grow at least five plants together. Seed keeps four years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about rutabagas?
faqs.a: Rutabaga is safe to eat raw in thin sticks — sweet and a bit peppery — and cut into oven chips it wins over most children. A big one hollowed out makes the original Halloween lantern: turnip and rutabaga lanterns came before pumpkins, and carving one is a fine wet-October job with an adult on the knife.

temperate.name: Radishes
temperate.tagline: Three weeks from seed to plate in spring — and a different vegetable altogether in autumn.
temperate.frostNote: Spring radishes take frost in the ground down to about −4 °C in their stride, and the fall crop tastes better for one. Winter types — daikon, black Spanish, watermelon — are hardier still and sit in the ground through −5 °C, but dig them before the ground freezes; a frozen daikon is mush. Nothing needs covering unless a hard freeze is coming and the winter radishes are not dug yet.
temperate.ready: Spring radishes three to five weeks after sowing, when the shoulder is 2–3 cm (¾–1¼ in) across and pushing up out of the soil — pull a test one. A week late and they are pithy, hot and cracked, so pull the row over a few days rather than waiting for all of them. Winter radishes need 50–70 days and come out in October–November: daikon at 3–5 cm (1–2 in) thick and 20 cm (8 in) or more long, black Spanish at 8–10 cm (3–4 in) across.
temperate.pick: Pull by the tops; dig daikon with a fork or it snaps. Twist off the leaves at once and rinse. Spring radishes are a same-week vegetable. For winter radishes going into store, cut the tops to 1 cm (½ in), don’t wash, and brush off the soil.

store.keeps: 1–2 weeks for spring types; 1–2 months for winter types
store.how: Tops off, in a perforated bag or a container with a damp towel; left with their leaves on they shrivel in days.

store.where: Cold room or root cellar (winter radishes only)
store.how: Daikon and black radish in damp sand or perforated bags, tops off, exactly like carrots.

store.where: Jar of water in the fridge
store.how: Trimmed spring radishes standing in cold water stay crisp — the trick for the ones the kids pulled too many of.

temperate.preserveNote: Radishes mostly don’t preserve, and it is better to know that than to fill a freezer with them: frozen radishes thaw limp, water-logged and off-smelling (the NCHFP lists them among the foods that do not freeze well), and there is no tested recipe for canning plain radishes. What works is a quick pickle — sliced radishes in 5% vinegar, salt and a little sugar, kept in the fridge and eaten within a month — the Bernardin Vietnamese carrot-and-daikon pickle for a tested canned version, and lacto-fermented daikon kept cold once it is sour. Winter radishes are the exception to ‘don’t store’: in a cold room they keep as well as a turnip. Sow fewer spring radishes, more often, rather than trying to put them up.

seeds.how: Spring radishes are annuals, which makes them one of the easiest seed crops there is: leave a few of the best roots unpulled, they bolt to 1 m (3 ft) of white-pink flowers within weeks, and the fat green pods that follow are a crop in themselves — crisp and peppery raw, and the rat-tail types are grown just for them. Let the rest of the pods dry tan on the plant, pull the whole plant and finish it under cover, then crush the pods and winnow. Radishes are insect-pollinated and self-incompatible, so grow at least five plants together, and they cross with other radish varieties and with wild radish within 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) — flower one variety at a time. Winter radishes are biennials and need overwintering first.
seeds.viability: 5–6 years.

temperate.nextYear: Cabbage family for rotation — not after turnips, rutabagas or brassicas — because root maggot is the main pest, and a floating row cover from sowing is the answer. Any decent soil, steady water. Direct sow spring radishes 3–4 weeks before the last frost, 1 cm (½ in) deep and 2–3 cm apart, and keep sowing a short row every 10 days until late May; stop for the heat of July, when they bolt and turn hot, and start again in mid-August. Sow winter radishes in late July to early August, about 70 days before the first frost, thinned to 10–15 cm (4–6 in). In zones 3–4 spring radishes are often the first harvest of the year, three weeks ahead of anything else.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 3–4 weeks before the last frost and every 10 days until late May; winter types about 70 days before the first fall frost.

faqs.q: When should I harvest radishes?
faqs.a: Spring radishes three to five weeks after sowing, as soon as the shoulder is 2–3 cm across — a few days late and they crack and go hot and pithy. Winter radishes (daikon, black Spanish) take 50–70 days and are dug in October and November before the ground freezes.

faqs.q: How do I store radishes?
faqs.a: Twist the tops off at once and keep them in a perforated bag or a container of water in the fridge; spring types last one to two weeks. Winter radishes keep one to two months in the crisper and two to three in a cold room packed in damp sand, like carrots.

faqs.q: Can you freeze radishes?
faqs.a: No. They thaw limp, water-logged and with an off smell — the NCHFP lists them among the foods that do not freeze well. Pickle them, ferment them, or eat them fresh. Winter radishes store in the cold instead.

faqs.q: Can you pickle radishes?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best thing to do with a surplus: sliced radishes or daikon sticks in 5% vinegar with salt and a little sugar, kept in the fridge and eaten within a month. For a shelf-stable jar, use a tested recipe such as Bernardin’s carrot-and-daikon pickle and process as written. Daikon also ferments well, kept cold once sour.

faqs.q: Are radishes frost hardy?
faqs.a: Spring radishes take −2 to −3 °C without trouble and the fall crop is milder after a frost. Winter types stand −5 °C in the ground. Dig the winter radishes before the soil freezes; nothing else needs doing on a frost night.

faqs.q: How do I save radish seeds?
faqs.a: Leave a few spring radishes to bolt; they flower within weeks and set pods, which you harvest when they dry tan in late summer. Grow at least five plants of one variety and keep other radishes (and wild radish) from flowering within 800 m. The green pods are edible too. Seed keeps five to six years.

faqs.q: What should kids know about radishes?
faqs.a: Radishes are the classic first crop for a child: big enough seed to handle, up in three days, ready in three weeks, and a short row is theirs from start to finish. Pull, rinse, eat — the only surprise is that some are hot, so taste a small bite first. The green seed pods on a bolted plant are safe and fun to eat straight off the stalk.

temperate.name: Onions
temperate.tagline: The crop whose storage life is decided in the three weeks after you pull it.
temperate.frostNote: Onion plants are hardy — spring seedlings take −4 °C — but by frost time the crop should be out of the ground and curing, and a cured bulb must not freeze: a frozen onion goes glassy and rots. The evening a frost is forecast, bring in any onions still drying outside on racks or on the soil, and lift any bulbs left in the bed. Green onions can stay out.
temperate.ready: When the tops yellow and fall over on their own — wait until about half the row has flopped, then bend the rest. The bulb has stopped growing at that point and the neck is softening. Don’t leave them to die back completely in a wet August; that is when neck rot gets in. Bulb size is set by day length, not by how long you leave them.
temperate.pick: Lift on a dry day with a fork, a week or so after the tops fall, once the outer skins have started to colour. Leave the tops on. Lay them out one layer deep in the sun for a day or two if the weather is dry, then move them under cover. Handle gently — a bruised onion is the first to rot — and don’t knock the soil off against anything hard.
temperate.cure: Cure 2–3 weeks somewhere warm (20–30 °C), dry and airy — a covered porch, a garage with the door open, a shed with a fan — spread one layer deep on racks or screens, or hung in small bunches by the tops. They are done when the necks are tight and papery, the outer skins rustle and the roots are dry and wiry. Then cut the tops to 2–3 cm (1 in), or braid them while the leaves are still pliable, trim the roots and sort: any thick-necked or soft bulb goes to the kitchen first, because it will not keep.

store.where: Cold room, unheated basement or enclosed porch
store.keeps: 4–6 months for storage types; longer for the hardest yellow keepers
store.how: Mesh bags, slatted crates or old tights hung up — never sealed plastic — with air all round. Dry is the point: onions want 60–70% humidity, the opposite of carrots and potatoes, so not in the root cellar with the damp sand and not next to the potatoes. Above about 5 °C they start to sprout.

store.where: Cool dark cupboard, pantry or under the stairs
store.how: Mesh bag or basket. Use the sweet and red onions first — they keep weeks, not months. Not the fridge: the humidity softens them and they sprout.

store.where: Fridge — cut or peeled onions only
store.how: In a closed container. Whole onions do not belong in the fridge.

temperate.preserveNote: A cured yellow storage onion in a cold, dry spot is the preserve; everything else is for the sweet onions and the ones that will not keep. Chopped onions freeze with no blanching — spread on a tray, then bag — and are good for cooking for a few months, though soft when thawed. Sliced onions dry well in a dehydrator and keep for a year as flakes or powder. What you cannot do is can onions plain: the only tested plain-onion process is for whole onions 2.5 cm (1 in) across or smaller — pressure canner, 40 minutes for 500 ml or litre jars at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m) — and larger or chopped plain onions have no tested process, so they go into jars only inside tested pickle, relish, salsa and sauce recipes, measured as written. Pickled pearl onions by the Bernardin recipe are water-bathed. And onions in oil are the same botulism risk as garlic in oil: refrigerate and use within four days, or freeze.

seeds.how: Onions flower in their second year, so you choose the best cured bulbs in autumn, keep them at 0–4 °C over winter, plant them in April 15 cm (6 in) apart, and let the 1 m (3 ft) globe heads set black seed by August; cut the heads as they dry, finish them in a paper bag and rub the seed out. They are insect-pollinated and cross with any other Allium cepa in flower — other onion varieties, shallots, multiplier onions — within 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), so flower one variety at a time. Save from at least five bulbs, more if you can. Only open-pollinated varieties come true (‘Ailsa Craig’, ‘Stuttgarter’, ‘Red Wethersfield’); many storage onions sold as transplants are F1 hybrids.
seeds.viability: 1–2 years — onion seed is the quickest to die. Buy or save fresh each year and test old packets on a damp paper towel in February.

temperate.nextYear: Allium family: not where onions, garlic, leeks or shallots grew in the last three years, because onion maggot and white rot persist in soil. Full sun, rich, well-drained soil, and no weed competition — onions have no canopy to shade weeds out. Northern gardens need long-day storage varieties (14 or more hours of daylight to bulb); the short-day sweet onions sold in spring never size up here. Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and set out 2–4 weeks before it, or plant sets as soon as the soil can be worked; transplants from seed store longer than sets. 10–15 cm (4–6 in) apart, 2 cm deep, rows 30 cm (12 in) apart. In zones 3–4 transplants or sets only — direct sowing does not have time.

sow.outdoors: Transplant or plant sets 2–4 weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked.

faqs.q: When should I harvest onions?
faqs.a: When about half the tops have yellowed and fallen over on their own — usually August in southern Canada — bend the rest, wait a week, and lift on a dry day with the tops still on. The bulbs do not grow once the tops go down, and leaving them in wet soil invites neck rot.

faqs.q: How do I cure onions?
faqs.a: Spread them one layer deep on racks or screens, or hang them in bunches, somewhere warm (20–30 °C), dry and airy, out of rain, for two to three weeks. They are cured when the necks are tight and papery, the skins rustle and the roots are dry. Then trim tops to 2–3 cm, sort out any thick-necked or soft bulbs for eating now, and store the rest.

faqs.q: How do I store onions for the winter?
faqs.a: Cold and dry — the opposite of root vegetables: 0–4 °C with 60–70% humidity, in mesh bags or slatted crates with air around them, which keeps a yellow storage onion four to six months. An unheated basement or enclosed porch works; the root cellar with the damp sand and the fridge do not. Sweet and red onions keep weeks, so eat those first.

faqs.q: Can you freeze onions?
faqs.a: Yes, chopped, with no blanching: spread on a tray, freeze, then bag. They are soft when thawed and for cooking only, and best used within a few months. Whole onions do not freeze well. Drying sliced onions in a dehydrator is the other good option for a surplus.

faqs.q: Can I can onions?
faqs.a: Not plain — there is no tested process for jars of plain onions at home. Onions go into jars only inside tested recipes: pickled pearl onions, relishes, salsas and sauces, with the quantities as written. Onions in oil are a botulism risk like garlic in oil: fridge for four days or the freezer.

faqs.q: How do I save onion seeds?
faqs.a: Overwinter the best cured bulbs at 0–4 °C, replant them in April, and harvest the seed heads when they dry in August. Only one variety of Allium cepa can flower within 800 m, and only open-pollinated varieties come true. Onion seed lasts just one to two years, so save or buy fresh every season.

faqs.q: What should kids know about onions?
faqs.a: Pulling onions and laying them out in rows to cure is a safe, satisfying job, and braiding the cured tops is good for older children. Cutting an onion makes eyes sting because the cells release a gas that reacts with the water in your eyes — chilling the onion first and using a sharp knife helps. Onion tops and bulbs are food; the flower heads in a seed bed are left alone until the seed is ripe.

temperate.name: Garlic
temperate.tagline: The one crop you plant in October — and the textbook case of what not to put in a jar of oil.
temperate.frostNote: Nothing to do — garlic is the hardiest thing in the garden. Cloves planted this month root through October, sit frozen under the mulch at −30 °C, and come up green in April; a few leaves showing before snow is normal and not a problem. The only garlic frost matters to is garlic still curing outside in July–August, which should be under cover anyway, and cured bulbs left in a shed that freezes hard, which crack. Stored garlic stays above 0 °C.
temperate.ready: Scapes (hardneck only) in late June, when the curling flower stalk has made one full loop — snap it off at the top leaf and eat it; left on, it costs you up to a third of the bulb. Bulbs in mid-July to early August, when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned and the top four or five are still green. Each green leaf is a wrapper on the bulb: wait too long and the wrappers rot away, the cloves burst apart, and the bulb will not store. Dig one and look — the cloves should fill the skin and be easy to tell apart.
temperate.pick: Loosen with a fork well out from the stem and lift the whole plant; never pull by the stalk, and never let the bulbs lie in the sun. Leave the soil on, the roots on and the tops on. Handle gently. Hardneck tops are stiff and come straight out; softneck tops will braid.
temperate.cure: Cure 2–4 weeks whole — leaves, roots and all — in the shade with plenty of moving air: hung in bunches of 5–10 from a rafter, or laid one deep on screens in a garage or covered porch, out of rain and sun. It is done when the outer wrappers are papery, the roots are dry and the cut stem is hard right through. Then brush off the soil (don’t wash), cut the roots to 1 cm (½ in) and the stem to 2–3 cm (1 in), and take off one dirty wrapper layer at most. Set aside the biggest, best bulbs for planting before you start eating.

store.where: Cold room, unheated porch or basement
store.keeps: 5–7 months for hardneck; 8–9 months for softneck
store.how: Mesh bags or open baskets at 60–70% humidity. Cold storage keeps longest, but garlic taken out of it sprouts fast, so bring a month’s worth into the kitchen at a time.

store.keeps: 3–5 months at 15–18 °C (hardneck at the short end); 1–2 months in a warm kitchen
store.how: A basket or paper bag in the dark with airflow — not a sealed jar. This is the practical house option; hardneck bulbs start to soften from February.
Peeled cloves in a closed container, for the week. Whole bulbs do not go in the fridge: the 4–10 °C range is exactly what tells a clove it is spring, and it sprouts.

temperate.preserveNote: Cured garlic is the preserve; the jar is for the surplus and the softening bulbs of late winter. Peeled cloves freeze whole or chopped, loose in a bag, with no blanching — soft when thawed but full-flavoured. Sliced garlic dries well at 55–60 °C and grinds to powder. Pickled garlic is safe only from a tested recipe (Ball or Bernardin, 5% vinegar, water-bath processed) — the vinegar is what makes it safe, and some cloves turn blue or green in it, which is harmless. Plain garlic cannot be canned: no safe processing time exists, pressure canner or not. And garlic in oil is the classic home botulism case — a low-acid vegetable in an oxygen-free medium at room temperature — so any garlic-in-oil, garlic butter or garlic confit you make goes straight to the fridge and is used within four days, or into the freezer in small portions. Health Canada allows a week refrigerated at 4 °C; the NCHFP says four days; there is no way to tell by look, smell or taste when it has gone wrong.

seeds.how: Garlic is grown from cloves, and the clove you plant is a clone of the plant it came from, so a home crop improves year on year as you select it. Set aside the biggest, soundest bulbs at curing time — a tenth to a sixth of the crop — keep them whole, cool and dry, and break them into cloves only the day you plant; the biggest cloves grow the biggest bulbs. Hardneck varieties also make bulbils in the scape head: sown like seed they take two or three years to make a full bulb, but they are disease-free and the quickest way to multiply a variety. Don’t plant supermarket garlic — much of it is softneck from a warm climate, sometimes treated against sprouting, and it can bring nematodes and white rot into a clean bed.
seeds.viability: Cloves are planted the autumn they are harvested; a cured bulb kept dry at 15–18 °C is good for planting until about November.

temperate.nextYear: This is the October job: plant garlic 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes — a week or two after the first killing frost — which is early October in zones 3–4 and mid-to-late October in zones 5–6. Allium rotation: not where onions, leeks or garlic grew in the last three years. Full sun and rich, well-drained soil with compost dug in; wet feet rot the cloves over winter. Cloves pointed end up, 5 cm (2 in) deep to the base (7 cm / 3 in in zone 3), 15 cm (6 in) apart in rows 30 cm (12 in) apart, then 10 cm (4 in) of straw or shredded leaves over the bed. Pull the mulch back in April as shoots appear, feed with compost, snap the scapes in June, and stop watering two weeks before harvest. Hardneck is the type for Canada — hardier, bigger cloves, scapes — and ‘Music’, the Porcelains and the Rocamboles are the standards from Quebec to the Prairies.

sow.outdoors: Plant cloves in autumn, 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes — early to late October across zones 3–6.

faqs.q: When do you plant garlic in Canada?
faqs.a: In autumn, 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes — a week or two after the first killing frost. That is early October in zones 3–4 and mid-to-late October in zones 5–6; even early November works in southern Ontario if the soil is still open. Cloves 5 cm deep, 15 cm apart, pointed end up, under 10 cm of straw or leaves.

faqs.q: When should I harvest garlic?
faqs.a: Mid-July to early August, when the bottom third to half of the leaves have browned and four or five are still green. Dig a test bulb: the cloves should fill the skin and be easy to tell apart. Too early and the bulbs are small; too late and the wrappers rot and the cloves split, which means they will not store. Scapes come off in late June, once they have curled.

faqs.q: How do I cure and store garlic?
faqs.a: Hang the whole plants in the shade with good airflow for two to four weeks until the wrappers are papery and the stem is dry through, then trim and brush. Store either cold (0–4 °C) or at cool room temperature (15–18 °C), always dry and airy: at a cool 15–18 °C garlic keeps about three to five months (hardneck at the short end), and longer in the cold; in a warm 20–30 °C kitchen, only a month or two. Not the fridge — 4–10 °C makes it sprout.

faqs.q: Can I store garlic in oil?
faqs.a: Only in the fridge for four days, or in the freezer. Garlic is low-acid and oil keeps air out, which is exactly what Clostridium botulinum needs; a jar of garlic in oil on the counter can produce botulism toxin with no change in look, smell or taste. The NCHFP says four days refrigerated, Health Canada allows a week at 4 °C; freezing in small portions is the safe way to keep it longer.

faqs.q: Can you freeze garlic?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the easiest way to deal with a surplus: peel the cloves and freeze them whole or chopped, loose in a bag, no blanching. They are soft when thawed but the flavour is all there. Garlic in oil can also be frozen in small portions — it just cannot sit at room temperature or in the fridge for more than four days.

faqs.q: Should I grow hardneck or softneck garlic?
faqs.a: Hardneck in most of Canada: it is hardier, gives bigger, easier-to-peel cloves, and produces scapes in June. Softneck stores longer (six to nine months against hardneck’s three to seven) and braids, but needs a milder winter. Plant certified or locally grown seed garlic, not supermarket bulbs.

faqs.q: What should kids know about garlic?
faqs.a: Planting garlic is the best autumn job there is for a child: break the bulb into cloves, count them, push each one pointed end up into a hole, and tuck the bed in with straw for the winter. Nothing is poisonous — the cloves, scapes and leaves are all food — and in April the green spears coming up through the snow are the first thing alive in the garden.

temperate.name: Leeks
temperate.tagline: The allium that stands in the garden through December, waiting to be dug for soup.
temperate.frostNote: Leave them standing. Leeks take −7 °C without protection and the hardy blue-green winter varieties (‘Bandit’, ‘Bleu de Solaise’, ‘Siegfried’) go to −15 °C and below under snow; a frost sweetens them. The job before the ground freezes is to bank 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves around the stems so you can still get a fork in through December and into January. Summer leeks (‘King Richard’ types) are much less hardy — dig those before −5 °C.
temperate.ready: Any time from pencil-thick in August for baby leeks; full size is a shaft 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) thick, usually from mid-September on. The white part is what you are growing, and it is only as long as the stem was buried or hilled — it does not get longer in store, so if the white is short, hill more next year. Leeks do not go over; they just get bigger, and by their second spring they send up a flower stalk and a hard core.
temperate.pick: Dig, don’t pull — the roots hold hard and the shaft tears. Push a fork in alongside, lever, and lift. Trim the roots to 1 cm (½ in) and the leaves to a fan 10 cm (4 in) above the white, and shake out the soil. Slit lengthways and rinse under the tap in the kitchen: grit works its way between the layers while you hill.

store.keeps: Into January, or until the ground freezes solid
store.how: 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves banked around the stems and over the row, marked with a stake; dig in thaws. The method for anywhere the snow comes early and stays.

store.where: Cold room or root cellar, heeled in
store.how: Dig the leeks with their roots on before a hard freeze, stand them upright in a bucket or deep box of damp sand with the white buried, and keep the sand damp. They behave as if still planted.
Unwashed, trimmed, loosely wrapped in a bag; longer than that and they yellow and go slimy at the cut.

temperate.preserveNote: Leeks are kept, not preserved — in the ground or heeled into sand — and that is the better product by far. For the freezer, slice the white and pale green into rings, wash well, blanch 1–2 minutes, cool, drain and freeze flat in bags: they lose their crispness and are only for soup, stock, pies and braises, but potato-leek soup in February is reason enough. There is no tested home-canning process for leeks on their own, and leeks in oil carry the same botulism risk as garlic in oil — fridge for four days or the freezer. Dried leek flakes are fine for stock.

seeds.how: Leeks flower in their second year: the plants you leave in the ground over winter send up 1.5 m (5 ft) stalks with a drumstick head of mauve flowers in July, and black seed follows in September — the easiest biennial seed in the north, because the parent plant is hardy enough to stay put. Where winters are too hard for that, dig a few leeks in late fall, heel them into sand in the cold room and replant in April. They are insect-pollinated and cross with other leek varieties (and with elephant garlic, which is the same species) within 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile), so flower one variety at a time and save from at least five plants. Cut the heads as they dry, finish them in a paper bag, and rub out the seed.
seeds.viability: 2 years — leek seed, like onion, fades fast.

temperate.nextYear: Allium rotation: not after onions, garlic or leeks within three years. Rich, moisture-holding soil with compost, full sun. Leeks need the longest start of any garden vegetable: sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, 5 mm (¼ in) deep and thick in a tray, and keep the grass-like seedlings trimmed to 10 cm (4 in). Transplant 1–2 weeks before the last frost once the seedlings are pencil-thick, dropping each into a 15 cm (6 in) dibber hole 15 cm apart and watering it in without filling the hole — the soil washes in over the season and blanches the shaft; hill more soil up in August. In zones 3–4 sow the hardy winter types in February and set out under a row cover in late April; a summer leek sown in March still makes a crop by October.

sow.outdoors: Transplant 1–2 weeks before the last frost, when the seedlings are pencil-thick.

faqs.q: When should I harvest leeks?
faqs.a: Whenever they are thick enough — pencil-thin baby leeks from August, full-sized 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) shafts from mid-September through December and beyond. They do not spoil by staying in the ground; they get bigger and sweeter with frost, and only turn woody when they bolt the following spring.

faqs.q: Can leeks stay in the ground over winter?
faqs.a: Yes — that is where they keep best. Leeks take −7 °C unprotected and the blue-green winter varieties survive −15 °C and lower under snow. Bank 30 cm (12 in) of straw or leaves around the stems before the ground freezes and dig during thaws into January; in zone 6 and milder they can be dug all winter.

faqs.q: How do I store leeks?
faqs.a: Lifted leeks last only one to two weeks in the fridge, unwashed and loosely bagged. For longer, dig them roots-on before a hard freeze and heel them upright into a box of damp sand in a cold room at 0–2 °C, where they keep two to three months as if still planted. Easiest of all: leave them in the ground under mulch.

faqs.q: Can you freeze leeks?
faqs.a: Yes. Slice the white and pale green into rings, wash out the grit, blanch 1–2 minutes, cool, drain and freeze flat in bags. They go soft when thawed, so they are for soup, stock, pies and braises — which is most of what a leek is for in winter anyway.

faqs.q: How do I save leek seeds?
faqs.a: Leave a few leeks in the ground over winter; they flower in July of the second year and the black seed is ready in September. Dry the heads in a paper bag and rub the seed out. They cross with other leek varieties within 800 m, so flower one at a time, and the seed only lasts about two years.

faqs.q: Are leeks frost hardy?
faqs.a: Among the hardiest vegetables there are: −7 °C does nothing, and winter varieties stand −15 °C and below with snow or mulch over them. Frost sweetens them. The limit is the ground freezing solid so you cannot dig, which is what the mulch is for. Summer leeks are the exception and should come in before −5 °C.

faqs.q: What should kids know about leeks?
faqs.a: Digging leeks out of a snowy bed in December is a small adventure, and the whole plant — white, green, flower — is safe to handle and eat. Leeks are the mild member of the onion family, which is why children who refuse onions will eat leek-and-potato soup. The grit between the layers is a good lesson in why you wash vegetables.

temperate.name: Cabbage
temperate.tagline: The head that keeps all winter in a cold room — and turns into sauerkraut when it will not.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it. A firm head shrugs off −4 to −6 °C with nothing worse than a few blistered wrapper leaves, and storage cabbage is sweeter for a frost or two. Short dips to −10 °C are survivable, but after a night like that cut the heads within a day or two and peel off anything glassy or dark. Do not let a mature head sit through a run of hard freezes — the damage works inward.
temperate.ready: The head is firm when you press it with the heel of your hand — no give at all. Early cabbages are ready in July and August at the size of a softball; storage types in October at anything from 1 to 4 kg. A head that has stopped getting bigger but is still loose is not ready; a head that has split has gone past ready.
temperate.pick: Cut the stem just under the head with a stout knife, and for storage leave three or four wrapper leaves on, or pull the whole plant roots and all. If a head is firm but you are not ready for it, give the plant a quarter twist to break some roots — it stops the head taking up water and splitting after rain. Cut early heads promptly; the stump will often throw a few small heads later.

store.how: Heads with wrapper leaves on, roots on or wrapped loosely in newspaper, on slatted shelves or hung by the root, not touching. Peel the outer leaves at use. Cabbage smells in storage — keep it away from the apples and the living room.
Whole, unwashed, in a loose perforated bag. A cut head wrapped tightly lasts about a week.

store.where: Unheated garage or shed, before hard freeze
store.how: In a box lined with newspaper, lid loose. Move it to the fridge once nights fall below −5 °C out there.

temperate.preserveNote: Cabbage is the one crop in this group that mostly does not need preserving: a storage variety in a cold room at 0–2 °C is good into March. What will not keep as a head becomes sauerkraut — shredded and salted at 2–2.5 % by weight, which is the tested ratio of 3 tablespoons of canning salt per 2.3 kg (5 lb) of cabbage, pressed under its own brine for 3–4 weeks at 20–24 °C (5–6 weeks if the room is 15–18 °C). Finished kraut keeps several months in the fridge or can be water-bath canned, hot-packed, 10 minutes for 500 ml jars and 15 for litres at 0–300 m. Cabbage freezes only blanched — 1½ minutes for shreds or thin wedges — and comes out fit for soup and cabbage rolls, not slaw. There is no tested recipe for canning plain cabbage, and the National Center for Home Food Preservation does not recommend it.

seeds.how: Cabbage flowers in its second year, and it crosses with everything else in Brassica oleracea — kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kohlrabi, collards — so only one of the family may flower within 250 m (800 ft) that spring, and seed savers who want purity use 800 m. Choose at least five of your best heads (twenty is better), dig them before a hard freeze with roots on, trim the loose leaves, pack the roots in damp sand in a crate and keep them at 1–4 °C and high humidity all winter. Replant in April; cut an X in the top of the head so the flower stalk can push through. Yellow flowers in June, pods in July; cut whole branches when most pods are tan and dry them on a sheet, then rub the pods between your hands and winnow. A season spent on seed is a season with no cabbage from those plants, which is why most families buy cabbage seed and save bean seed.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: nothing from the cabbage family in that bed for three or four years, to keep clubroot and cabbage root maggot down. Rich, moist soil, full sun, pH 6.5 or above, and steady water right to harvest — uneven water is what splits heads. Space 45 cm (18 in) apart. Start spring cabbage indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant around the frost date under a row cover, which also stops the moth. For storage cabbage, sow in early June and transplant by early July so it heads up in cool October weather. In zones 3–4 pick storage varieties under 100 days.

sow.outdoors: Transplant around the last frost date; sow storage cabbage in early June for July transplanting.

faqs.q: When should I harvest cabbage?
faqs.a: When the head is firm all the way through under hand pressure — size matters less than firmness. Early types come in July and August; storage types are cut in October and early November after a frost or two, which sweetens them. If the head is firm and you are not ready, twist the plant a quarter turn to slow it and stop splitting.

faqs.q: How do I store cabbage for the winter?
faqs.a: Cut storage varieties with a few wrapper leaves on, or pull them with the root, and keep them at 0–2 °C and high humidity: a cold room, an insulated bin in an unheated porch, or the fridge crisper for one or two heads. Hang them by the root or set them on slatted shelves not touching. Peel the outer leaves at use. Three to five months is normal; a split or soft head will not store, so eat those first.

faqs.q: Can you freeze cabbage?
faqs.a: Yes, but only blanched and only for cooking. Shred or cut thin wedges, water-blanch 1½ minutes, cool in ice water, drain, bag and freeze. It comes out soft — right for soups, stews, colcannon and cabbage rolls, wrong for coleslaw. Sauerkraut is the better use of a glut.

faqs.q: How much salt goes in sauerkraut?
faqs.a: Two to two and a half percent of the cabbage by weight. The tested recipe is 3 tablespoons of canning or pickling salt for every 2.3 kg (5 lb) of shredded cabbage; weigh the cabbage and use a scale for the salt if you have one. Pack it hard, keep it under the brine with a weight, and let it ferment 3–4 weeks at 20–24 °C. Use canning salt, not iodised table salt, which clouds the brine.

faqs.q: Is cabbage frost hardy?
faqs.a: Yes. A mature head takes −4 to −6 °C without harm and tastes better for it; cabbage, kale and collards will even stand short spells near −10 °C. The limit is repeated hard freezes, which damage the head from the outside in — so after a night near −10 °C, cut what is left and get it into the cold room.

faqs.q: Can I save cabbage seed?
faqs.a: Only with patience. Cabbage is a biennial, so the plant must be kept alive through winter — dug and stored in damp sand at 1–4 °C in most of Canada — and replanted in spring to flower. It also crosses with kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower and kohlrabi, so nothing else in the family can flower within 250 m. Seed keeps 4–5 years once you have it.

faqs.q: What can kids do with the cabbage harvest?
faqs.a: Pounding shredded cabbage for sauerkraut is the best job in the preserving kitchen — wash hands, salt the shreds, and let them squeeze and punch until the brine runs; they can watch the bubbles in the crock every day for a month. Cabbage heads are heavy and the knife work is for an adult, but a six-year-old can peel wrapper leaves and sort heads into ‘eat now’ and ‘store’.

temperate.name: Kale
temperate.tagline: The last green standing — sweeter after frost and still pickable from under the snow.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it, and look forward to it. Frost turns kale’s starch to sugar, and the plants stand to −10 °C without protection; under a blanket of snow they go lower still and you can dig them out to pick in December. Young seedlings are tougher than they look (about −4 °C). What ends kale is not one cold night but weeks of −15 °C bare wind with no snow — a row cover or a few evergreen boughs over the plants carries them through that.
temperate.ready: Any leaf as long as your hand. Pick the lower, older leaves first and leave the growing tip and at least four young leaves at the top so the plant keeps producing. Leaves are at their best after the first frosts in October; the small ones in the crown are the tenderest at any time.
temperate.pick: Snap or cut each leaf stalk off close to the main stem, working from the bottom up. Never cut the top. One picking of ten plants fills a basket, and the plants will be ready again in a week. In winter, pick on a day above freezing, or let frozen leaves thaw on the plant before you touch them — frozen kale shatters.

store.keeps: Until deep winter, longer under snow or a row cover
store.how: Leave the plants standing and pick what you need. Mulch the base with straw once the ground freezes.
Unwashed, in a perforated bag. Wash just before use.
Loose in an open bag or crate, misted; it wilts fast in dry air.

temperate.preserveNote: Kale’s best preserve is the plant itself, left in the ground and picked through November and December. For what you cannot eat fresh, blanch stripped leaves 2 minutes, squeeze out the water, and freeze in flat packs or pucks for soup and smoothies — unblanched kale goes bitter and grey within weeks. Dried kale chips — leaves rubbed with a little oil and salt and baked at 110 °C (225 °F) for 40–60 minutes, or in a dehydrator until they shatter — are the one dried green children ask for, but they go limp in days unless jarred airtight. There is a tested pressure-canning recipe for greens (70 minutes for 500 ml jars at 10 lb), but the result is grey and soft and few people do it twice; freezing is better in every way.

seeds.how: Kale is a biennial and the easiest of the cabbage family to get seed from, because in zones 5 and up the plants usually live through winter in the ground (mulch the crowns; snow cover helps) and bolt to yellow flowers in May. In colder gardens dig a few plants in November, pot them, and hold them at 1–4 °C in a cold room or garage, then replant in April. It crosses with every other Brassica oleracea — cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, collards, kohlrabi — so only one of them may flower within 250 m (800 ft). Save from at least five plants, ideally twenty. Cut whole seed stalks when most of the pods are tan and brittle, dry them on a sheet for two weeks, then rub the pods between your hands and winnow in a breeze.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with the rest of the cabbage family: not where any brassica grew in the last three years. Kale is undemanding — any decent soil, full sun or light shade, steady water, and a handful of compost. Space 30 cm (12 in) apart in rows 60 cm apart. Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before and transplant 3–4 weeks before the frost date. The crop that matters is the fall one: sow again in early July for plants that are full-sized when the frosts come. In zones 3–4 that July sowing is the main sowing. A row cover from day one keeps off the cabbage moth and flea beetles.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, and again in early July for the fall and winter crop.

faqs.q: Is kale frost hardy?
faqs.a: Very. Kale stands to −10 °C with no cover and keeps going under snow; frost actually improves it, converting starch to sugar so the leaves taste sweeter in November than in August. What kills it is prolonged bare cold around −15 °C with drying wind, so in zones 3–4 throw a row cover or evergreen boughs over the row once the snow is unreliable.

faqs.q: When should I harvest kale?
faqs.a: From June onwards, whenever a lower leaf is hand-sized, and best of all from October after the first frosts. Pick from the bottom up and always leave the top cluster of young leaves; a plant picked that way produces from June to December. Winter leaves should be picked thawed, not frozen.

faqs.q: Can you freeze kale?
faqs.a: Yes, blanched. Strip the leaves from the ribs, water-blanch 2 minutes, plunge into ice water, squeeze out the water hard, and freeze in flattened bags or as pucks in a muffin tin. Frozen kale is for cooking and smoothies — it will not come back crisp. Skip the blanching and it turns grey and bitter in a month.

faqs.q: How do I make kale chips that last?
faqs.a: Dry leaves, a teaspoon of oil rubbed in, a pinch of salt, single layer, 110 °C (225 °F) for 40–60 minutes until they lift off the tray and shatter — or a dehydrator at 50–55 °C for a few hours. Cool completely and seal in a jar with a tight lid; in the open air they are limp by morning.

faqs.q: Can I save kale seed?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the easiest brassica to do it with, because the plants usually survive winter in the ground in zone 5 and warmer, then flower in May. Save from at least five plants and remember it crosses with cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower, so nothing else in the family can be flowering within 250 m. The seed keeps 4–5 years.

faqs.q: Can kids pick kale?
faqs.a: It is one of the best jobs for them: the leaves snap off with a downward tug and nothing is sharp. Teach them to take the big bottom leaves and leave the little ones at the top, and in winter to wait until the leaves have thawed in the sun. Baking kale chips is a four-year-old’s recipe from start to finish.

temperate.name: Swiss chard
temperate.tagline: A beet grown for its leaves — cut it and it comes again from May until a hard frost.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it for a light frost: chard takes −1 to −2 °C with nothing worse than a few limp outer leaves, and keeps growing through October until nights reach about −4 °C. If the forecast says −3 °C or colder, pick the big leaves that evening and cover the crowns with a sheet or row cover; the small leaves at the centre will usually survive and give you another cutting. A hard freeze finishes the tops, but a mulched crown often sends up new leaves in April.
temperate.ready: Outer leaves 20–30 cm (8–12 in) long with a glossy, crisp stalk; baby leaves at 8 cm for salad. There is no ‘mature’ date — a chard plant is ready from six weeks after sowing until frost. Leaves that have gone dull and leathery are past it; pull them off and compost them so the plant puts its effort into new growth.
temperate.pick: Cut or twist off the outer stalks at the base, 2–3 cm above the crown, and leave the inner four or five leaves standing. Pick a third of the plant at a time at most. For a fresh start on a tired plant, cut the whole thing 5 cm above the soil; it regrows in two or three weeks. Chard is in the same family as beets and spinach and tastes like both.

store.how: Unwashed, stalks on, in a perforated bag. It wilts within hours in dry air.

store.where: In the garden under a row cover
store.how: A hoop cover or old sheet over the row on cold nights; pick on mild days.
Stood in a jar of water like flowers, or loose in a damp cloth.

temperate.preserveNote: Chard freezes well if you treat the leaves and stalks as two vegetables: strip the leaves, blanch them 2 minutes, squeeze and freeze in pucks for soup, pies and pasta; chop the stalks and blanch them separately, since they take longer to soften. The stalks also make a good refrigerator pickle in a tested vinegar brine. What does not work is freezing it raw — it goes slimy and bitter — or drying it, which leaves you with dust. Greens can be pressure-canned by the NCHFP recipe (70 minutes for 500 ml jars at 10 lb), but the texture is poor and the freezer is better.

seeds.how: Chard is the same species as the beet and crosses freely with it: both are wind-pollinated and the pollen travels, so no beet or other chard may be flowering within 250 m (800 ft) in the seed year, and real purity wants 1.6 km. It is a biennial — no seed until the second summer. In zones 5–6 a heavily mulched plant often overwinters in place; elsewhere dig a few plants before a hard freeze, trim the leaves to 5 cm, store the roots in damp sand at 1–4 °C and replant in April. Save from at least five plants, better twenty. The seed stalk grows to 1.5 m; cut it when two-thirds of the seed clusters are brown, dry it on a sheet for two weeks, and strip the clusters by hand. Each ‘seed’ is a cluster of two to five true seeds, which is why chard always needs thinning.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with beets and spinach (the goosefoot family): not where any of them grew last year. Chard wants full sun to light shade, soil with compost worked in, and water through dry spells — it is tough but turns bitter when parched. Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, 1–2 cm deep, when the soil is 10 °C, and thin to 20–30 cm (8–12 in) apart, eating the thinnings. One sowing lasts the year; a second in mid-July gives tender leaves for the fall. In zones 3–4 start a few plants indoors 4 weeks before the frost date for an earlier first cutting. Six plants feed a family.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost, once the soil is 10 °C; sow again in mid-July.

faqs.q: Is Swiss chard frost hardy?
faqs.a: Partly. It takes light frosts of −1 to −2 °C and keeps growing through October until the nights reach about −4 °C; a hard freeze blackens the leaves. Cover the row with a sheet or row cover when −3 °C is forecast and you will get several more weeks. The crown often survives winter under mulch in zones 5 and up and regrows in spring, but it will bolt to seed by June.

faqs.q: How do I harvest chard so it keeps producing?
faqs.a: Take the outer leaves and leave the centre. Twist or cut each stalk off near the base, never more than a third of the plant at once, and leave at least four young leaves standing. Picked that way a plant produces from June to the first hard frost. If it gets tired or bolts, cut it off 5 cm above the soil and it will regrow.

faqs.q: Can you freeze Swiss chard?
faqs.a: Yes. Separate leaves from stalks. Blanch the leaves 2 minutes in boiling water, cool in ice water, squeeze dry and freeze in pucks or flat bags; blanch chopped stalks separately a little longer. Frozen chard is for cooked dishes. Raw-frozen chard turns slimy and bitter, so always blanch.

faqs.q: Why do chard seeds come up in clumps?
faqs.a: Because each ‘seed’ is really a dried fruit cluster holding two to five seeds, the same as beets. Sow them 5 cm apart, then thin the clumps to one plant at 20–30 cm spacing once they have two true leaves. The thinnings are good in salad.

faqs.q: Can I save chard seed?
faqs.a: Yes, but it takes two years and some space. Chard is a biennial and crosses with beets, so overwinter the plants (mulched in the ground in zone 5 and up, or dug and stored in damp sand at 1–4 °C) and let them flower the next summer with no beets or other chard flowering within 250 m. Cut the stalks when two-thirds of the seed is brown. The seed keeps 4–5 years.

faqs.q: Can kids eat chard straight from the garden?
faqs.a: Yes — rinsed, the young leaves are mild and the stalks are crunchy. Rainbow chard is the one to grow with children: red, yellow, orange and pink stems in one packet, and they can pick ‘a leaf of each colour’. Young leaves are good raw in a salad; the bigger leaves are better cooked.

temperate.name: Broccoli
temperate.tagline: One big head, then weeks of side shoots — if you cut it before the buds turn yellow.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it for anything down to −4 °C: broccoli grows on through the first frosts and the fall crop is the best of the year. Heads start to take damage somewhere around −5 to −6 °C — buds turn brown and soft — so if that is forecast, cut any head that is close to ready and throw a row cover over the rest. The plants themselves survive worse and keep producing side shoots until a hard freeze.
temperate.ready: A head that is tight and dark green with the individual buds the size of a match head, still closed. Size depends on variety and weather — 10 to 20 cm across in a home garden. When the buds swell and begin to loosen, or you see one yellow petal, cut it that day; broccoli goes from ready to flowering in two or three warm days.
temperate.pick: Cut the main stem on a slant 12–15 cm (5–6 in) below the head with a sharp knife, in the cool of the morning. Leave the plant: within two weeks it throws side shoots from the leaf joints, smaller heads you can pick for a month or more. Soak heads for 30 minutes in salted water (4 teaspoons salt to 4 litres) before cooking or freezing to float out cabbage worms.

store.how: Unwashed, in a perforated bag or loosely wrapped. Wash and salt-soak just before use. Heads yellow and go limp fast in a warm fridge.
Stems in a shallow pan of water, heads covered loosely with a damp cloth. Away from apples and ripening fruit.

temperate.preserveNote: Broccoli is a freezer crop and nothing else. Cut into florets no more than 4 cm across, split the stalks, salt-soak if worms are about, water-blanch 3 minutes (or steam 5), cool in ice water, drain well and freeze on a tray before bagging. It comes out fit for stir-fries, soups and casseroles. The peeled stalks are worth freezing too. There is no tested recipe for canning plain broccoli — pressure canning ruins the texture and the smell — and drying it gives a product nobody wants. Pickled broccoli stems appear in some tested mixed-vegetable pickle recipes; follow those exactly rather than swapping broccoli into a cucumber recipe.

seeds.how: Most broccoli sold to gardeners is an F1 hybrid (the packet will say so), and its saved seed grows into a muddle of loose, uneven plants. Seed is worth saving only from an open-pollinated variety — ‘De Cicco’, ‘Calabrese’ and ‘Waltham 29’ are the common ones. Broccoli is unusual in the family in that it flowers the same year if you let a head bolt, so it needs no overwintering: leave the best three to five heads from at least five plants to open into yellow flowers, keep every other Brassica oleracea (cabbage, kale, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi) from flowering within 250 m (800 ft), and let the pods dry on the plant. Rub the brittle pods out between your hands and winnow. In zones 3–5 the pods often have not ripened before a hard freeze, which is the real obstacle.
seeds.viability: 3–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: no cabbage-family crop in that bed for three or four years. Broccoli wants rich, moist soil, steady nitrogen and full sun, and it hates heat — heads sown to mature in July are small and bolt; heads sown to mature in September and October are the big ones. Space 30–45 cm (12–18 in) apart; closer gives smaller heads but more side shoots. Start indoors 6–7 weeks before the last frost and transplant two weeks before it under a row cover for the moth. Sow the fall crop in early July and transplant in late July. In zones 3–4 the fall crop is the reliable one; pick a variety of 60 days or less.

sow.outdoors: Transplant 2 weeks before the last frost; sow again in early July for the fall crop.

faqs.q: When do I harvest broccoli?
faqs.a: When the head is tight, dark green and the buds are still closed and no bigger than match heads — before anything turns yellow. Once it is ready it will not wait: a couple of warm days and the buds open into flowers and the head goes bitter and loose. Cut in the morning, 12–15 cm down the stem, and leave the plant for side shoots.

faqs.q: Will broccoli keep producing after I cut the head?
faqs.a: Yes. Side shoots form at the leaf joints within two weeks of cutting the main head and keep coming for a month or more, especially on the fall crop and in cool weather. They are small — the size of a toddler’s fist — but they add up to more than the main head over a season. Keep the plants watered and fed.

faqs.q: Can you freeze broccoli?
faqs.a: Yes, blanched. Cut florets no more than 4 cm across, soak 30 minutes in salted water to bring out worms, water-blanch 3 minutes (steam 5), chill in ice water, drain, and freeze on a tray before bagging. Frozen broccoli is for cooking; it will not come back crunchy for dipping. Do not freeze it raw — it goes yellow and sulphurous.

faqs.q: Is broccoli frost hardy?
faqs.a: Yes, to about −4 °C, and the fall crop improves after a light frost. Heads begin to suffer around −5 to −6 °C — brown, soft buds — so cut what is near ready before a night like that and cover the rest. The plants survive harder cold and go on making side shoots into November in zones 5–6.

faqs.q: Can I save broccoli seed?
faqs.a: Only from an open-pollinated variety; most garden broccoli is an F1 hybrid that will not come true. Let a few heads flower and set pods the same season, keep other cabbage-family plants from flowering within 250 m, and dry the pods on the plant. In short-season gardens the pods often do not ripen in time. Seed keeps 3–5 years.

faqs.q: There are green worms in my broccoli — is it safe?
faqs.a: Yes. They are cabbage worms (the caterpillar of the white butterfly) and they are harmless; the trouble is purely that nobody wants one on the plate. Soak heads upside down in salted water (4 teaspoons salt to 4 litres) for 30 minutes and they float out. A row cover over the plants from transplanting stops the butterfly laying in the first place — a good job for kids to help pin down.

temperate.name: Cauliflower
temperate.tagline: The fussiest brassica: tie the leaves over the head, cut it while it is tight, and freeze what you cannot eat.
temperate.frostNote: The plant is tougher than the head. Leaves shrug off −2 °C, but a developing white curd is marked by frost at about −2 to −3 °C — brown spots that spread to rot — and ruined at −5 °C. If frost is forecast and a head is showing, tie the outer leaves over it (which you should have done anyway) or throw a row cover or a bucket over the plant; if the head is near full size, cut it that evening. Plants with no head yet can be left.
temperate.ready: A compact, firm, white (or purple or orange, by variety) head 15–20 cm across, with the curd sections still pressed tightly together. Check every day or two once the head is visible: in warm weather it goes from ready to ‘ricey’ — grainy, loosening, separating into florets — in under a week, and in spring crops faster. Smaller and tight beats bigger and loose every time.
temperate.pick: Cut the stem below the head with a knife, keeping a ring of leaves around it to protect the curd on the way to the kitchen. There are no side shoots worth waiting for — pull the plant and compost it. For a white head on a non-self-blanching variety, bring three or four big outer leaves up over the curd when it is about 5 cm (2 in) across and hold them with a rubber band or clothes peg; harvest comes 4–8 days later in summer, up to two weeks in cool fall weather.

store.how: Unwashed, stem down, in a perforated bag or loose wrap; moisture on the curd causes brown spots.
Head wrapped in its own leaves, on a shelf, not touching anything. Even in ideal conditions cauliflower does not keep more than three weeks.

temperate.preserveNote: Freezing is the main method: break into florets about 2.5 cm (1 in) across, soak 30 minutes in salted water if worms are about, blanch 3 minutes in water with 4 teaspoons of salt per 4 litres, chill, drain, and tray-freeze before bagging. It cooks up well in soups, curries and gratins; raw-frozen cauliflower turns to grey mush. The other good home is a jar: the NCHFP ‘Pickled cauliflower or Brussels sprouts’ recipe (5 % vinegar, sugar, onions, mustard and celery seed, blanch 3 minutes, process 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath) and the tested mixed-vegetable pickles that include cauliflower. Follow those ratios exactly — cauliflower is a low-acid vegetable and only the vinegar makes a water-bath jar safe. There is no tested recipe for canning plain cauliflower.

seeds.how: Nearly every cauliflower variety sold is an F1 hybrid and will not come true, and the open-pollinated ones are the hardest of the whole cabbage family to grow for seed: the plant must be healthy enough to carry a full head and then push a flower stalk through it, which in most of Canada means overwintering it at 1–4 °C in a cold room and replanting in spring. It crosses with cabbage, kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi, so none of them may flower within 250 m (800 ft). Seed savers who do it keep at least five plants, let the curd open into yellow flowers, and dry the pods on the plant before rubbing them out. For most families this is the crop to buy seed for every year and save the effort for beans.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with the cabbage family: nothing from it in that bed for three or four years. Cauliflower wants what cabbage wants, only more reliably — rich, moist, limed soil, full sun, no check in growth at any point, because a stressed plant ‘buttons’ into a head the size of a coin. Space 45 cm (18 in) apart. Start indoors 7–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant 2 weeks before it under a row cover, but in most Canadian gardens the fall crop is the one that works: sow in late June or early July, transplant in late July, and let it head up in cool September and October weather. In zones 3–4 pick a 55–65 day variety and grow it as the fall crop only.

sow.outdoors: Transplant 2 weeks before the last frost; for the more reliable fall crop, sow in early July and transplant in late July.

faqs.q: When is cauliflower ready to pick?
faqs.a: When the head is firm, compact and 15–20 cm across with the curd sections still pressed tightly together. Look every day or two once a head shows; in warm weather it separates into a loose, grainy ‘ricey’ head within a week, and it is better cut small and tight than large and loose. Cut below the head with a few leaves left on.

faqs.q: Why do I have to tie the leaves over cauliflower?
faqs.a: To keep the curd white. Sunlight turns a developing white head yellow-brown and gives it a stronger flavour. When the head is about 5 cm across, pull three or four big outer leaves up over it and fasten them with a rubber band or peg; cut the head 4–8 days later (up to two weeks in cool fall weather). Self-blanching varieties curl their own leaves over, and coloured varieties need no tying.

faqs.q: Can you freeze cauliflower?
faqs.a: Yes, blanched. Break into 2.5 cm florets, salt-soak if there are worms, blanch 3 minutes in salted water, chill in ice water, drain well, and freeze on a tray before bagging. It is good for soups, curries, cauliflower cheese and roasting from frozen. Never freeze it raw — it goes watery and grey.

faqs.q: Is cauliflower frost hardy?
faqs.a: Less than its relatives. The leaves take −2 °C, but a developing head is spotted by frost at about −2 to −3 °C and spoiled at −5 °C, so cover plants with heads, or cut heads that are close, when a frost is forecast. Plants without heads yet can stand a light frost without harm.

faqs.q: Can I pickle cauliflower?
faqs.a: Yes, with a tested recipe. The NCHFP ‘Pickled cauliflower or Brussels sprouts’ recipe uses 12 cups of florets, 4 cups of 5 % vinegar and 2 cups of sugar with onion and spices, blanched 3 minutes and processed 10 minutes in a boiling-water bath. Cauliflower is also in most tested mixed-pickle and giardiniera recipes. Do not cut the vinegar or add extra vegetables — the acid is what makes the jar safe.

faqs.q: How do kids help with cauliflower?
faqs.a: Checking the heads is their job: once a head shows, send them out every morning to see if it has grown, and let them put the rubber band on the leaves. Breaking a head into florets for the freezer is safe knife-free work. Growing a purple or orange variety next to a white one gets the most reluctant eater to try it.
