temperate.name: Brussels sprouts
temperate.tagline: Not worth picking until it has frozen a few times — then the sweetest thing left standing in November.
temperate.frostNote: Leave them — this is the crop frost is for. Sprouts are bland before the first frosts and sweet after several; the plants stand −7 °C (20 °F) without any damage and come through brief −10 °C nights, with the outer leaves of the sprouts taking the hit and peeling off clean. Pick on a day above freezing, or let frozen sprouts thaw on the stalk — a frozen sprout snapped off goes mushy. Before a long spell of −12 °C and below with no snow, cut the whole stalks and bring them into the cold room.
temperate.ready: Firm, tight sprouts 2.5–4 cm (1–1½ in) across, the lowest ones first; they ripen from the bottom of the stalk upward over six weeks or more. Squeeze one: ready is hard like a walnut, past it is soft and the outer leaves are flaring open and yellowing. Taste improves markedly after the first few frosts, so the real season in most of Canada starts in October.
temperate.pick: Snap off the leaf below a sprout, then twist the sprout off downward, working up the stalk a few rounds at a time and leaving the smaller ones above to size up. To bring the whole stalk on at once, ‘top’ the plant — pinch out the growing tip — in early September, when the bottom sprouts are 1–2 cm across and about a month before you want the main harvest; the plant stops making new leaves and fattens what it has. Topped stalks can be cut whole at soil level once cold weather settles in.

store.where: On the plant in the garden
store.how: Leave the stalk standing and pick upward as you need them; snow is a good insulator.

store.where: Cold room or unheated garage, whole stalk
store.how: Cut stalks at ground level, strip the leaves, stand them upright in a bucket with a little water or hang them. Pick sprouts off as needed.

store.keeps: Up to 2 weeks (best within a few days)
store.how: Unwashed, untrimmed, in a perforated bag. They go strong-smelling and yellow as they age.

temperate.preserveNote: A stalk of sprouts in a cold garage is its own preserve for a month or more, and a plant left in the garden under snow is better still. For the freezer, trim and wash, sort by size, and blanch 3 minutes for small sprouts, 4 for medium and 5 for large, then chill, drain and bag; frozen sprouts are for roasting and braising, not steaming whole. The tested NCHFP ‘Pickled cauliflower or Brussels sprouts’ recipe (small sprouts boiled 4 minutes in salted water, then packed in a 5 % vinegar brine with sugar and spices and water-bath processed 10 minutes) is the only way to can them: there is no tested recipe for plain canned sprouts, and raw-frozen or dried sprouts are bitter and grey.

seeds.how: Brussels sprouts are biennial, cross with every other Brassica oleracea, and are the hardest of the family to get seed from in a cold climate, because the plant has to live through winter and flower the next June. In zones 6–7 a mulched plant sometimes manages it in the ground; elsewhere dig the best five or more plants in November, pot them, hold them at 1–4 °C in a cold room, and replant in April. Keep cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower and kohlrabi from flowering within 250 m (800 ft). Cut the branches when most pods are tan, dry them on a sheet, and rub out the seed. Many good varieties are F1 hybrids in any case — check the packet — so this is a project for a seed-saver with space and a cold room, not a first-year job.
seeds.viability: 4–5 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: no cabbage-family crop in that bed for three or four years. Sprouts need the longest season of any brassica — 90 to 110 days from transplant plus a cold autumn — and firm, rich, limed soil with steady water; loose soil and drought give loose, bitter sprouts. Space 45–60 cm (18–24 in) apart and stake tall varieties. Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost (mid-April to early May in most of southern Canada) and transplant around the last frost date under a row cover; do not plant them late, as you might broccoli. Top the plants in early September. In zones 3–4 choose a variety under 100 days and start it indoors in early April.

sow.outdoors: Transplant around the last frost date; they need the whole season and a cold autumn.

faqs.q: When should I harvest Brussels sprouts?
faqs.a: After the first few frosts, from the bottom of the stalk up, when the sprouts are firm and 2.5–4 cm across. Frost converts starch to sugar and takes away the bitterness, so in most of southern Canada the season runs from October into December. Snap off the leaf under a sprout, then twist the sprout off downward, and leave the small ones above to grow.

faqs.q: Should I cut the top off my Brussels sprout plant?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want the whole stalk to finish together. Pinch out the growing tip in early September, when the lowest sprouts are 1–2 cm across and about a month before the main harvest: the plant stops making leaves and puts everything into sizing up the sprouts already there. If you would rather pick a few at a time into December, leave the top on.

faqs.q: How cold can Brussels sprouts take?
faqs.a: A lot. Plants are undamaged at −7 °C (20 °F) and come through short −10 °C nights, with snow helping rather than hurting; the outer sprout leaves may brown and peel off. Pick when thawed, not frozen. Before a long stretch below −12 °C with bare ground, cut the stalks and stand them in a cold garage, where they keep for weeks.

faqs.q: How do I store Brussels sprouts?
faqs.a: On the stalk. Cut whole stalks at ground level, strip the leaves and stand them in a bucket in a cold room or unheated garage at 0–4 °C, picking sprouts as you need them for three to six weeks. Picked sprouts keep up to two weeks in a bag in the fridge crisper, but they are at their best in the first few days.

faqs.q: Can you freeze Brussels sprouts?
faqs.a: Yes, blanched by size: 3 minutes for small, 4 for medium, 5 for large, then into ice water, drained and bagged. Frozen sprouts are soft when thawed, so halve and roast or braise them rather than steaming. Raw-frozen sprouts turn bitter and grey.

faqs.q: What can kids do with Brussels sprouts?
faqs.a: Picking is perfect for them: the sprouts twist off with a downward snap, the stalk is sturdy, and they can see the row of little cabbages. Have them taste one raw before the frost and one after — the difference is the best lesson in the garden about why we wait. A whole stalk carried into the house is a trophy.

temperate.name: Lettuce
temperate.tagline: Eat it the week it is ready — it is the one crop that cannot be put up for winter.
temperate.frostNote: Lettuce takes a light frost of −1 to −2 °C with a few translucent outer leaves and nothing worse, especially leaf and butterhead types; a sheet or row cover over the bed on those nights keeps it perfect. At −3 to −4 °C mature heads freeze through and collapse into slime when they thaw, so if that is forecast, cut every head that is near ready and eat or give away through the week. Small seedlings sown in September are tougher than full heads and will stand −5 °C under a cover.
temperate.ready: Leaf lettuce from 10–15 cm (4–6 in) tall; butterhead when the centre leaves cup inward into a loose heart; romaine when the head is 20–25 cm tall and firm; crisphead when the head is compact and firm to a squeeze. Pick in the cool of the morning, when the leaves are full of water. A plant that has stretched upward with a tall central stalk and leaves that taste bitter has bolted; pull it or let it go to seed.
temperate.pick: Three ways. Take the outer leaves from leaf and romaine types a few at a time and the plant keeps going for weeks. Cut a whole bed of leaf lettuce 2–3 cm above the crown with scissors — ‘cut and come again’ — and it regrows twice. Or cut a whole head at the base. Harvest in the morning and get it into cold water and the fridge within the hour; lettuce picked at noon never crisps up.

store.keeps: Leaf and butterhead about 1 week; crisphead up to 2 weeks
store.how: Whole heads unwashed in a perforated bag; washed leaves spun dry and rolled in a towel inside a bag. Away from apples and tomatoes, whose ethylene browns the ribs.

store.where: In the garden under a row cover
store.keeps: Into late October and November in zones 5–6
store.how: A hoop cover or cold frame over the fall sowing; pick on mild days.

temperate.preserveNote: Lettuce does not preserve, and no tested method pretends otherwise. Frozen, its thin cell walls burst and it thaws to green water; canned or pickled it is slime; dried it is dust. The honest answer to a glut is to eat it, give it away, and stop sowing a whole packet at once — sow a short row every two or three weeks instead. The only ‘preserving’ that works is stretching the season: a cold frame or row cover over September-sown lettuce gives salads into November, and a sowing of a hardy variety under cover in late September or October overwinters as small plants in zones 5 and up for the first salad of April. Bolted lettuce is good for one thing — seed.

seeds.how: Lettuce is self-pollinating and comes true from any open-pollinated variety (which is most of them), with 3–6 m (10–20 ft) between varieties enough to keep them pure. Let one or two of your best, slowest-to-bolt plants go: the stalk shoots up to a metre in July, opens dozens of small yellow flowers, and 2–3 weeks after each flower a tuft of white fluff appears — the seed is ripe under it. Shake or bend the plant into a paper bag every few days for a couple of weeks, or cut the whole top when most tufts show and dry it upside down in a bag indoors. Rub the fluff between your hands and blow the chaff away. One plant gives more seed than a family uses in five years.
seeds.viability: Up to 6 years stored cool and dry; count on 3.

temperate.nextYear: Lettuce has no serious rotation needs — just not the same spot three years running. It wants loose, fertile soil with compost, steady water, and shade from the afternoon sun in July. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked, 4–6 weeks before the last frost, and every 2–3 weeks after that until the heat of July; start the first batch indoors 5 weeks before the frost date to transplant for an early cutting. Seed will not germinate in soil above about 27 °C, so midsummer sowings go in the shade or in trays indoors. Sow again from mid-August for the fall, and a hardy variety under cover in late September to overwinter. Thin leaf types to 10–20 cm, heads to 30 cm (12 in).

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before the last frost as soon as the soil can be worked, then every 2–3 weeks; sow again from mid-August for fall.

faqs.q: Can you freeze lettuce?
faqs.a: No. Lettuce is mostly water held in thin cell walls; freezing bursts them and it thaws to limp green mush. It cannot be canned, pickled or dried to any purpose either. Eat it fresh, give it away, and sow smaller amounts more often so it never piles up.

faqs.q: How long does lettuce keep in the fridge?
faqs.a: Crisphead about two weeks; leaf and butterhead up to three or four weeks if the leaves are dry when you bag them. Pick in the morning, dunk in cold water, spin or towel dry, and store in a perforated bag in the crisper, away from apples and tomatoes. A head stored wet rots in days.

faqs.q: Is lettuce frost hardy?
faqs.a: Half. It takes −1 to −2 °C with a few glassy outer leaves, and a sheet or row cover gets it through those nights untouched; at −3 to −4 °C full heads freeze and collapse. Small fall seedlings are hardier than mature heads and will overwinter under a cold frame in zones 5 and up.

faqs.q: Why is my lettuce bitter and tall?
faqs.a: It has bolted — sent up a flower stalk in response to heat and long days — and once that starts the leaves turn bitter and milky. Nothing reverses it. Pull it, or leave one plant to flower and save the seed. Next year sow in cool weather, water steadily, give midsummer sowings afternoon shade, and choose slow-bolting varieties.

faqs.q: How do I save lettuce seed?
faqs.a: Let a good plant bolt and flower; 2–3 weeks after the yellow flowers, tufts of white fluff appear and the seed under them is ripe. Shake the head into a paper bag every few days, or cut the top and dry it upside down in a bag. Rub and winnow. Lettuce self-pollinates, so it comes true, and the seed keeps up to six years.

faqs.q: What lettuce should I grow with kids?
faqs.a: A row of cut-and-come-again leaf lettuce — they can snip it with scissors 2 cm above the crown, it regrows in two weeks, and nothing in it is sharp or bitter when young. Let them sow it too; the seed is tiny but forgiving. Picking salad for supper with a four-year-old is as close to a sure thing as the garden offers.

temperate.name: Spinach
temperate.tagline: The hardiest green there is: sown in September, picked in April, and the first thing in the freezer in June.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it. Spinach stands heavy frost — −6 to −8 °C does it no harm, and small plants under a row cover or snow survive −15 °C and worse and start growing again in March. Frost sweetens it. The only time to act is a sudden deep freeze on bare ground before the plants have hardened off, when a row cover or a layer of straw over the bed is worth five minutes. Pick thawed leaves, not frozen ones.
temperate.ready: Leaves 8–15 cm (3–6 in) long, dark green and thick; baby leaves at 5 cm for salad. Spring spinach is ready 5–6 weeks from sowing and must be picked before the plants stretch and bolt in June’s long days. Fall spinach grows slower and holds for weeks. A plant that has a thickening central stem and arrow-shaped leaves is bolting — cut the whole thing now.
temperate.pick: Take the outer leaves one by one, pinching the stems, and the plant keeps giving for several weeks; or cut the whole plant 2–3 cm above the crown and it regrows once or twice. Harvest in the morning, wash in two changes of cold water — spinach holds grit like nothing else — and chill at once. In spring pick hard; the first warm week brings bolting and no amount of water stops it.

store.how: Unwashed, in a perforated bag, loosely packed; crushing bruises it. Wash just before use.

store.where: In the garden under a row cover or snow
store.keeps: All winter as small plants, for picking in March and April
store.how: Sow a hardy variety in September, let it reach 4–6 leaves, cover with a hoop and row cover or straw once the ground freezes.
Loose in an open bag, misted.

temperate.preserveNote: Spinach is the easiest green to freeze and the one most worth it: a June glut becomes a winter of lasagne, pies and soups. Wash well, blanch 2 minutes, chill in ice water, squeeze out as much water as you can, and freeze in pucks or flat packs — a muffin tin gives handy portions. It does not freeze raw; unblanched leaves turn to a dark, bitter mass. The tested pressure-canning recipe for spinach and greens (steam-wilted, 70 minutes for 500 ml jars and 90 for litres at 10 lb) is safe but gives a soft grey product most people regret. Drying spinach produces flakes for soup and little else.

seeds.how: Spinach seed is harder than it looks. The plants are dioecious — separate male and female plants — and wind-pollinated with light pollen that travels far, so you need a block of at least 10 plants (20–50 is better) with roughly half of them male, and no other spinach flowering within 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile). Let a spring sowing bolt in June: the males throw pollen first and then die back; keep them until the females have set seed along their stems. Pull the female plants when two-thirds of the seed is tan, hang them to dry for 10 days, strip the seed by hand (wear gloves — some varieties are prickly) and winnow. Most families with one short row are better off buying spinach seed and saving their effort for lettuce and peas.
seeds.viability: Up to 6 years stored cool and dry; count on 3.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate with beets and chard, its relatives: not where they grew last year. Spinach wants rich, moist soil, a neutral pH (it sulks in acid soil), and cool weather above all — long June days and heat make it bolt whatever you do. Direct sow 4–6 weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil is thawed and about 7 °C, 1–2 cm deep, 7–8 cm (3 in) apart; sow again every two weeks until mid-May and stop. Sow the main fall crop in mid-August and a hardy variety (‘Bloomsdale’, ‘Giant Winter’) in mid-September to overwinter under cover for April. In zones 3–4 the fall sowing goes in early August and overwintering needs a cold frame.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before the last frost as soon as the ground thaws; again in mid-August for fall, and in mid-September to overwinter under cover.

faqs.q: Is spinach frost hardy?
faqs.a: Extremely. Established plants take −6 to −8 °C without damage and taste sweeter for it; small plants under a row cover or snow survive −15 °C and resume growth in March. It is the best crop for a fall sowing in Canada: sow in mid-September, cover once the ground freezes, and pick in April before anything else is up.

faqs.q: Can you freeze spinach?
faqs.a: Yes — it is the best thing to do with it. Wash, blanch 2 minutes, plunge into ice water, squeeze hard, and freeze in pucks or flat packs. One kilogram of leaves becomes a few handfuls, so a June glut fits in a drawer. Frozen spinach is for cooking; do not freeze it raw, which turns it dark and bitter.

faqs.q: Why does my spinach bolt in June?
faqs.a: Long days and heat tell spinach to flower, and no amount of water stops it once the days pass about 14 hours. Sow it early — 4–6 weeks before the last frost — pick hard through May, and stop sowing by mid-May. The fall crop sown in August grows into shortening days and holds for weeks without bolting.

faqs.q: How do I overwinter spinach?
faqs.a: Sow a hardy variety in mid-September so the plants reach 4–6 leaves before hard frost. Once the ground freezes, cover the bed with a hoop and row cover, or straw, and leave it; snow is the best cover of all. In March uncover on mild days, and you will be picking by mid-April in zones 5–6. Zone 3–4 gardens need a cold frame.

faqs.q: Can I save spinach seed?
faqs.a: Yes, but it is one of the harder ones. Spinach has separate male and female plants and is wind-pollinated, so it needs a block of at least 10 plants and no other spinach flowering within several hundred metres. Let a spring sowing bolt, keep the males until the females have set seed, then pull the females when two-thirds of the seed is tan and hang them to dry. Seed keeps up to 6 years.

faqs.q: Can kids eat spinach from the garden?
faqs.a: Yes, rinsed well — spinach hides grit, so the job is two sinks of cold water, which they will enjoy. Baby leaves are mild and good raw; big leaves are better cooked. It is the easiest spring sowing for a child, with big seeds that come up in a week.

temperate.name: Peas
temperate.tagline: The first sowing of the year and the first thing in the freezer — pick them every day or they turn to starch.
temperate.frostNote: It depends on the stage. Spring seedlings are tough — they shrug off −4 °C and a dusting of snow, which is why peas go in a month before the last frost. A plant in flower or pod is a different thing: flowers and young pods are damaged at −2 °C and killed at −4 °C. For a fall crop in September or October, pick every pod that is near ready the evening a frost is forecast and throw a row cover or sheet over the row; a light frost under cover does no harm. After a hard frost, pull the vines for the compost or leave them to dry for seed.
temperate.ready: Shelling peas: pods full and rounded but still bright green and shiny — open one; the peas should be sweet and just touching, not square-packed. Snap peas: pods plump, nearly full, crisp enough to snap. Snow peas: pods flat and 5–8 cm long, with the peas inside only just showing as bumps. Every type is ready about three weeks after flowering and goes starchy within days of being ready, so check the row daily once pods appear.
temperate.pick: With two hands: hold the vine with one and pull the pod with the other, or you will tear the plant out. Pick from the bottom up every day or two; a vine with mature pods left on it stops flowering. Pick in the cool of the morning and shell or chill within the hour — sugar turns to starch fast in a warm pod. Eat or freeze shelling peas the same day.

store.keeps: 3–5 days; shelled, up to a week, but sweetness fades daily
store.how: Unwashed pods in a perforated bag; shelled peas in a covered container. The freezer is the better place for anything you will not eat in two days.
In the pod, in a shallow crate, misted.

temperate.preserveNote: Peas are the freezer crop that started the home freezer: shell, blanch 1½ minutes, chill in ice water, drain, and freeze loose on a tray before bagging, within an hour or two of picking. Snap and snow peas blanch 1½ minutes for small pods and 2 for large, strings removed, and come out soft but good in stir-fries. Shelling peas left to dry on the vine, or spread on screens until they are hard enough to shatter under a hammer, keep for years in jars as soup peas — the old Québécois habitant soup is made from exactly these. Canning plain peas is pressure-canner only, 40 minutes for both 500 ml and litre jars at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m): peas are a low-acid vegetable and there is no safe water-bath time. Canned peas are olive-drab and soft; the freezer wins.

seeds.how: Peas are the classic beginner’s seed. The flowers pollinate themselves before they open, so almost any variety comes true, and 3–6 m (10–20 ft) between varieties is plenty. Mark your best plants early and leave their pods unpicked until they are brown, papery and rattle — about six weeks after the eating stage. If rain or frost threatens before that, pull the whole plants and hang them under cover until the pods are dry. Shell by hand (a good evening job for small fingers), spread the peas on a tray for two more weeks, and store them in a jar when a pea shatters rather than dents under a hammer. Four days in the deep freeze at −18 °C kills pea weevil larvae hiding inside the seed. Save from five to ten plants.
seeds.viability: 3–4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: peas and beans fix their own nitrogen, so they follow heavy feeders (corn, brassicas) and lead into leafy crops; do not put them where peas grew last year. They want well-drained soil, a neutral pH, cool weather and something to climb — even bush types stand better on a bit of netting. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked, 4–6 weeks before the last frost and once the soil is 10 °C, 2–3 cm deep and 5 cm (2 in) apart in a wide double row; peas sown into cold wet soil rot, and peas sown late in May hit summer heat and give one small picking. A fall crop sown in mid to late July in zones 5–6 crops in September. In zones 3–4 sow the moment the frost is out and choose 55–60 day varieties.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked and is above about 5 °C; a fall sowing in late July in zones 5–6.

faqs.q: When should I pick peas?
faqs.a: About three weeks after flowering, and then every day or two. Shelling peas are ready when the pods are rounded and shiny and the peas inside are sweet and just touching; snap peas when the pods are plump and crisp; snow peas when the pods are flat and 5–8 cm long. A day or two past ready they go starchy and the vine stops flowering, so pick everything that is close.

faqs.q: Can you freeze peas?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best way to keep them. Shell, blanch 1½ minutes in boiling water, plunge into ice water, drain, and freeze loose on a tray before bagging — within an hour or two of picking, because the sugar turns to starch fast. Snap and snow peas blanch 1½–2 minutes with strings removed. Frozen peas go straight into the pot from the freezer.

faqs.q: Can I can peas?
faqs.a: Only in a pressure canner. Peas are a low-acid vegetable, so a sealed jar can grow botulism unless it has been heated above boiling: the tested time is 40 minutes for both 500 ml and litre jars at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m). There is no water-bath time for plain peas. Canned peas are soft and khaki; freezing gives a far better result for less work.

faqs.q: Are peas frost hardy?
faqs.a: Seedlings are — they take −4 °C and light snow, which is why peas are sown a month before the last frost. Plants in flower or pod are not: blossoms and young pods are hurt at −2 °C and killed at −4 °C. For a fall crop, pick what is near ready and cover the row when frost is forecast.

faqs.q: How do I save pea seed?
faqs.a: Leave the pods on your best plants until they are brown and rattle, pull and hang the plants if wet weather comes first, then shell and dry the peas two more weeks until one shatters under a hammer. Peas self-pollinate, so they come true; 3–6 m from another variety is enough. Four days in the deep freeze kills pea weevil. Seed keeps 3–4 years.

faqs.q: Why are peas a good crop for kids?
faqs.a: Big seeds a toddler can push into the soil, a short wait, and a snack that grows at eye level — snap peas eaten off the vine are most children’s first garden food. Teach them the two-hand pick so the vine stays put. Shelling a bowl of peas on the step and sorting the dried seed by size for next year are both jobs a four-year-old takes seriously.

temperate.name: Green beans
temperate.tagline: Pick them young and pick them often — and never, ever water-bath a jar of plain beans.
temperate.frostNote: Bring them in. Beans are killed at 0 °C: the leaves blacken and the pods go water-soaked and limp by morning. The evening a frost is forecast, pick every pod of eating size and anything close, and throw a sheet or row cover over the plants — a light frost under cover often leaves them producing for two or three more weeks of September. A pod frosted on the plant is not worth saving.
temperate.ready: Pods the thickness of a pencil, smooth, crisp enough to snap cleanly in half, with the seeds inside still small — no bulges along the pod. Most varieties are ready 50–60 days from sowing and 10–14 days after the flowers. Once the seeds show as lumps, the pod is tough and stringy; let those go on to dry beans or compost them.
temperate.pick: With two hands, holding the stem with one and snapping the pod off with the other, or the plant comes out of the ground. Pick every two or three days — a plant with mature pods left on it stops flowering, and a bush bean planting picked clean gives three or four flushes. Never pick or handle beans when the leaves are wet; it spreads rust and bacterial blight down the row. Pole beans keep producing until frost if you keep up with them.

store.how: Unwashed, in a perforated bag; beans chill-damage below 4 °C, so the crisper, not the back of the fridge. Wash just before use.
Fresh-picked beans hold their quality only a few hours at room temperature; cook or chill them the same day.

temperate.preserveNote: Green beans are the home freezer’s second crop after peas: snap or cut into 5–10 cm lengths, blanch 3 minutes, chill in ice water, drain, and tray-freeze before bagging. They also make the best pickle in this group — dilly beans, raw-packed with dill and garlic into sterilized jars (boiled 10 minutes) in a tested brine of equal parts 5 % vinegar and water with canning salt, processed 5 minutes in a boiling-water bath at 0–300 m by the NCHFP recipe. Plain beans in water are another matter entirely: they are a low-acid vegetable and must be pressure-canned, 20 minutes for 500 ml jars and 25 for litres at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m). There is no safe boiling-water time for plain green beans, and no family recipe changes that — home-canned green beans top the historical list of foods behind botulism cases in North America, because for a century people water-bathed them. Drying green beans (‘leather britches’) works but gives a chewy, musty product; the freezer is better.

seeds.how: Beans self-pollinate before the flower opens, so any open-pollinated variety comes true and 3–6 m (10–20 ft) from another variety is enough (a few bumblebees will cross the odd flower; move to 30 m if purity really matters). Leave pods on your healthiest plants unpicked until they are tan, papery and rattle, which takes about six weeks past the eating stage; pull and hang the plants under cover if frost or a wet spell comes first. Shell by hand, spread the seed on a tray for another two weeks, and jar it when a bean shatters rather than dents under a hammer. Four days in the deep freeze at −18 °C kills any bean weevil eggs. Save from five to ten plants and never from a plant that showed mottled or yellowed leaves — several bean diseases ride on the seed.
seeds.viability: 3–4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: beans fix nitrogen, so follow corn or brassicas with them and put leafy crops after them; not where beans or peas grew last year, to keep root rot and blight down. Full sun, average soil, no extra nitrogen (it gives leaves instead of pods), and steady water once the flowers come. Direct sow a week after the last frost when the soil is 16 °C (60 °F) — beans sown into cold wet soil rot — 2–3 cm deep and 10 cm (4 in) apart in rows 60–90 cm apart, or 6–8 seeds around each pole. Sow bush beans again every three weeks until early July for a steady supply. In zones 3–4, one sowing of a 50–55 day bush variety in early June, under a row cover for the first weeks, is the dependable plan.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1 week after the last frost, once the soil is 16 °C; sow bush beans again every 3 weeks until early July.

faqs.q: When do I pick green beans?
faqs.a: When the pods are pencil-thick, smooth and snap cleanly, before the seeds inside show as bumps — usually 10–14 days after flowering. Pick every two or three days with two hands so you do not uproot the plant, and only when the leaves are dry. Pods left to swell turn tough and tell the plant to stop flowering.

faqs.q: Can you freeze green beans?
faqs.a: Yes: snap or cut into 5–10 cm pieces, blanch 3 minutes in boiling water, plunge into ice water, drain well, and freeze on a tray before bagging. They keep a year and go into soups, stews and casseroles without thawing. Unblanched beans toughen and lose flavour within a couple of months.

faqs.q: Can I water-bath can green beans?
faqs.a: Not plain ones, ever. Green beans are a low-acid vegetable: a sealed jar that has only reached boiling can grow Clostridium botulinum, and home-canned low-acid vegetables — green beans, corn, beets, asparagus — are the commonest cause of botulism in North America. Plain beans need a pressure canner — 20 minutes for 500 ml jars, 25 for litres, at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m). The water-bath exception is pickled dilly beans, where the tested vinegar brine supplies the acid.

faqs.q: How do I make dilly beans?
faqs.a: Follow the NCHFP recipe: 1.8 kg (4 lb) of young straight beans trimmed to fit 500 ml jars, packed raw with a head of dill and a clove of garlic each, covered with a boiling brine of 1 litre (4 cups) 5 % white vinegar, 1 litre water and 125 ml (½ cup) canning salt, 1 cm headspace, processed 5 minutes in a boiling-water bath at 0–300 m. Do not reduce the vinegar or add extra beans to the jars. Wait two weeks before opening.

faqs.q: Are green beans frost hardy?
faqs.a: No. They are killed at 0 °C — leaves black, pods water-soaked. Pick everything of size the evening a frost is forecast and cover the plants with a sheet; a light frost under cover often leaves them producing for another two or three weeks. Frosted pods are not worth saving.

faqs.q: How do I save green bean seed?
faqs.a: Leave pods on a few of your best plants until they are tan and rattle, about six weeks past the eating stage; pull and hang the plants indoors if rain or frost comes first. Shell, dry two more weeks, freeze the seed four days to kill weevils, and jar it. Beans self-pollinate, so they come true, and the seed keeps 3–4 years. Children can do every step.

temperate.name: Dry beans
temperate.tagline: The crop that stores itself: leave the pods to rattle, shell them on the step, and eat them in February.
temperate.frostNote: The plant is tender but the crop is not. Frost at 0 °C kills the leaves, and that does no harm to pods that are already yellow or tan and leathery — it just stops them getting any riper. If most pods are still green and plump when a hard frost is forecast, pull the whole plants roots and all that evening and hang them upside down in a dry garage or porch; the seed goes on maturing from the plant for two or three weeks. Do the same when a wet week is forecast in late September — pods that have dried and then been soaked rot or sprout in the pod.
temperate.ready: Pods dry, tan or yellow, papery, and the beans rattle when you shake them; a bitten bean dents but does not squash. Most varieties reach this 85–100 days from sowing, in September in zones 5–6. Pods on one plant ripen over two or three weeks, so pick the dry ones as they come, or wait until most of the plant has yellowed and pull it whole.
temperate.pick: Pick dry pods on a dry afternoon, or pull whole plants once nine in ten pods are dry and hang them in bunches under cover. Shell small amounts by hand; for a big crop, put the pods in a pillowcase or feed sack and tread on it, or beat it against the floor, then pour the lot slowly from one bucket to another in a breeze so the chaff blows away. Spread the beans on trays indoors for two more weeks until one shatters under a hammer rather than denting.

store.where: Kitchen cupboard or pantry, in jars
store.keeps: 2–3 years at full quality; several more edible but slower to cook
store.how: Fully dry beans in glass jars or tins with tight lids, labelled with the variety and year, out of the light. Freeze the jar four days first to kill bean weevil eggs.
In sealed jars; dry is what matters, not cold. Damp beans mould.

temperate.preserveNote: Dry beans are already preserved the day they come off the plant; the only jobs are getting them fully dry, killing the weevils — four days in a deep freeze at −18 °C (0 °F) in a sealed bag, or 30 minutes in a 54 °C (130 °F) oven — and keeping them in a tight jar. A jar of your own beans takes an overnight soak and an hour’s simmer, which is where pressure canning earns its place: soak, boil 30 minutes, fill jars with beans and cooking water, and process 75 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 for litres at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m) by the NCHFP recipe, for shelf-stable beans ready for a weeknight. Cooked beans also freeze well in their liquid. What does not work is water-bath canning beans in any form, or ‘dry canning’ raw beans in a sealed jar in the oven, which does nothing against botulism and can crack the jars.

seeds.how: Every dry bean you harvest is a seed, which makes this the easiest seed-saving there is and the one to start children on. Beans self-pollinate, so an open-pollinated variety comes true with 3–6 m (10–20 ft) from other varieties — and nearly all dry beans are open-pollinated heirlooms with names and stories (‘Jacob’s Cattle’, ‘Soldier’, ‘Vermont Cranberry’). Set aside the biggest, best-coloured beans from the healthiest plants, never from plants that showed yellow mottled leaves, since bean mosaic and blight travel on the seed. Dry them hard, freeze four days against weevils, and keep them in a labelled jar. Children can sort the saved seed by colour and size and cull the wrinkled ones; it is the kind of counting that sticks.
seeds.viability: 3–4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate as for green beans: after corn or brassicas, before leafy crops, and not where beans or peas grew last year. Full sun, average well-drained soil, no added nitrogen, and a dry September — which is why dry beans do better on light soil and in open, airy spots than in a damp corner. Direct sow a week after the last frost when the soil is 16 °C (60 °F), 2–3 cm deep and 10 cm (4 in) apart in rows 60–75 cm apart, and be done sowing by early June so the pods dry before the fall rains. Pole types yield more per square metre but need a trellis; bush types can be pulled whole and hung. In zones 3–4 choose a variety of 85 days or less and sow in the first week of June; a row cover for the first fortnight helps.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1 week after the last frost, once the soil is 16 °C, and finish sowing by early June so the pods dry before the fall rains.

faqs.q: When do I harvest dry beans?
faqs.a: When the pods are tan, papery and rattle, usually in September — 85–100 days from sowing. Pick dry pods as they come on dry afternoons, or wait until most of the plant has yellowed and pull it whole. If frost or a wet week is forecast first, pull the plants and hang them under cover; the beans finish ripening from the hanging plant.

faqs.q: How do I shell and store dry beans?
faqs.a: Shell small lots by hand; for more, put the pods in a sack and tread on it, then pour the beans between two buckets in a breeze to blow the chaff away. Dry them on trays indoors for two more weeks until one shatters under a hammer, freeze the jarred beans four days to kill weevils, and keep them sealed in a cupboard. They cook best within 2–3 years but keep edible much longer.

faqs.q: Why are there little holes in my stored beans?
faqs.a: Bean weevils. The eggs are laid on the pods in the garden and the larvae develop inside the dry bean, eating their way out in the jar. Four days in a deep freeze at −18 °C in a sealed bag, once the beans are fully dry, kills every stage; so does 30 minutes at 54 °C (130 °F) in the oven. Do it before the beans go into the cupboard, not after you find the holes.

faqs.q: Can I can my dried beans?
faqs.a: Yes, in a pressure canner, by the NCHFP recipe: soak 12–18 hours (or boil 2 minutes and stand an hour), drain, boil 30 minutes in fresh water, fill jars with beans and liquid leaving 2.5 cm headspace, and process 75 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 for litres at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m). Beans are low-acid: there is no water-bath method, and ‘dry canning’ raw beans in oven-sealed jars is unsafe.

faqs.q: Do frosted bean plants ruin the beans?
faqs.a: Not if the pods were already drying. Frost kills the leaves at 0 °C but does nothing to tan, leathery pods beyond stopping further ripening. Pods still green and plump will not finish on a dead plant, so if most are green when frost is forecast, pull the plants that evening and hang them upside down somewhere dry for two or three weeks.

faqs.q: Can kids save bean seed?
faqs.a: This is the seed for them. Shelling dry pods on the porch, picking out the biggest and brightest beans for next year, sorting by colour into egg cartons and counting them into labelled jars — a four-year-old can do all of it, and a six-year-old can plant them next June and see the same colours come back. Keep the seed from plants that were healthy, and keep it dry.

temperate.name: Sweet corn
temperate.tagline: Twenty minutes from stalk to pot is the rule — and the freezer is the only way to keep August.
temperate.frostNote: Bring it in. Corn is killed at 0 °C: the leaves go limp and straw-coloured and the ears stop filling that night. The evening a frost is forecast, pick every ear that passes the milk test and freeze or eat it within the day; ears that are not yet filled will not finish on a frosted plant and can go to the chickens or the compost. Nothing covers a corn patch, so a late sowing in a short-season garden is a bet on the weather.
temperate.ready: About 18–24 days after the silks first show, when the silks are brown and dry and the ear feels full and rounded to the tip through the husk. Then the milk test: peel back a strip of husk and press a thumbnail into a kernel near the top. Milky white juice means pick it; clear, watery juice means wait two days; thick and doughy means it is past and should be fed to the chickens or cut for soup. Check the ears every day once the silks brown.
temperate.pick: In the cool of the morning, if you can. Hold the stalk with one hand, grip the ear with the other, bend it down sharply and twist — it snaps off clean. Get it into the shade and the kitchen fast: in standard (‘su’) varieties the sugar starts turning to starch the moment the ear leaves the plant, and half of it is gone within a day at room temperature. Supersweet (‘sh2’) and sugary-enhanced (‘se’) types hold longer. Raccoons will know the night before you do — electric fence with two wires at 12 and 25 cm off the ground, or pick a day early.

store.keeps: 1–2 days for standard types; up to a week for supersweets
store.how: Husks on, in a bag, in the coldest part of the fridge, picked that morning. Every hour warm costs sweetness.
Only on the way to the pot. Standard sweet corn loses much of its sugar in a day at room temperature.

temperate.preserveNote: Freezing within hours of picking is the only way to keep sweet corn tasting like August. For kernels, husk and silk, blanch whole ears 4 minutes, chill in ice water, cut the kernels off at about two-thirds of their depth without scraping the cob, and bag flat — this is the cut corn that goes into every winter chowder. For corn on the cob, blanch by ear size — 7 minutes for small ears under 3 cm across, 9 for medium, 11 for large — and chill thoroughly, or the cob tastes woody; frozen cobs are good but never quite fresh. Canning corn is pressure-canner only, 55 minutes for 500 ml jars and 85 for litres of whole kernels at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m), and cream-style corn in 500 ml jars only for 85 minutes; corn is a low-acid vegetable and there is no safe water-bath time. Supersweet varieties can brown in the jar, so can a small test batch first. Blanched kernels also dry well for soup.

seeds.how: Nearly every sweet corn sold is an F1 hybrid, and seed saved from it grows a ragged, uneven patch — so for most gardens the answer is simply to buy sweet corn seed every year. Corn is wind-pollinated and crosses with any corn within hundreds of metres, including the neighbour’s field; seed savers keep at least 250 m (800 ft) between varieties and prefer 800 m, or stagger sowings so that two patches silk at least two weeks apart. Even a supersweet eaten fresh goes starchy if a field-corn patch pollinates it, so 100 m (300 ft) or two weeks of separation matters for the table too. Where saving corn seed does make sense is with an open-pollinated flour, flint or dent corn — the old ‘Gaspé’ flint, the ‘Painted Mountain’ flours, the eight-row flints — or an open-pollinated sweet corn like ‘Golden Bantam’: leave the best ears on the stalks until the husks are dry and brown, pick, pull back the husks and hang the ears to finish drying for a month, then shell by hand. Save from dozens of plants at least — corn inbreeds badly from a handful — and from the whole patch rather than one favourite.
seeds.viability: 1–3 years; sow fresh seed when you can.

temperate.nextYear: Rotate: corn is a heavy feeder, so follow it with beans or peas and put it where last year’s legumes or a manured bed were; not after corn two years running, to break corn borer and rootworm. Full sun, rich soil with compost or manure, and water when the tassels and silks come. Sow in a block of at least four short rows, never one long row — the pollen falls from the tassels onto the silks and a single row sets half-filled ears — 25–30 cm (10–12 in) apart in the row, rows 75 cm apart. Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost when the soil is 16 °C (60 °F), 3–4 cm deep; supersweets want 18 °C and rot in cold soil. In zones 3–4 pick a 65–70 day variety, warm the soil under black plastic, and start a few in pots indoors three weeks before planting out if you must.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once the soil is 16 °C (18 °C for supersweets), in a block of at least four rows.

faqs.q: How do I know when sweet corn is ready?
faqs.a: The silks have turned brown and dry, about three weeks after they first showed, and the ear feels full to the tip. Then peel back a strip of husk and press a kernel with your thumbnail: milky juice means pick it now, clear juice means wait two days, and thick doughy juice means it is past. Check every day once the silks brown — the window is only a few days.

faqs.q: How long does sweet corn keep after picking?
faqs.a: Standard varieties lose much of their sugar within a day, so eat them the day they are picked — the old rule is to have the water boiling before you go out to the patch. Supersweet and sugary-enhanced types hold several days in the husk in a cold fridge. For anything you will not eat in two days, freeze it the day it is picked.

faqs.q: Can you freeze corn on the cob?
faqs.a: Yes. Husk and silk, blanch by ear size — 7 minutes for small ears, 9 for medium, 11 for large — chill thoroughly in ice water so the cob does not go woody, dry, and bag. For better quality and less freezer space, blanch whole ears 4 minutes, chill, cut the kernels off at two-thirds depth without scraping the cob, and freeze them flat.

faqs.q: Can I can sweet corn?
faqs.a: Only in a pressure canner. Corn is a low-acid vegetable, so sealed jars must be heated above boiling: whole kernels process 55 minutes for 500 ml jars and 85 for litres at 10 lb (weighted gauge, 0–300 m); cream-style corn goes in 500 ml jars only, for 85 minutes. There is no water-bath method. Some supersweet varieties brown in the jar, so test a small batch.

faqs.q: Can I save seed from my sweet corn?
faqs.a: Almost certainly not usefully — nearly all sweet corn is an F1 hybrid and the saved seed grows an uneven patch. If you want to save corn seed, grow an open-pollinated flint, flour or dent corn, or an old open-pollinated sweet corn, with 250 m or two weeks of silking between it and any other corn, let the ears dry on the stalk, and shell them after a month hanging indoors. Save from the whole patch; the seed keeps only 1–3 years.

faqs.q: How do I keep raccoons out of the corn?
faqs.a: An electric fence is the only thing that reliably works: two wires, at about 12 and 25 cm off the ground, switched on from the day the silks show. Raccoons arrive the night the corn is ready, which is a good reason to walk the patch with the children each evening doing the milk test and picking anything close. A radio in the patch buys a night or two at most.

temperate.name: Apples
temperate.tagline: The one harvest that can feed a family until March — if you know which apples keep and which don’t.
temperate.frostNote: The tree does not care about frost; the fruit does. Apples on the branch start to freeze at about −2 °C (28 °F). One short dip to there only shortens their storage life; several nights below it soften skin and flesh, and at −5 °C (22 °F) the fruit freezes solid and turns to mush when it thaws. If a hard freeze is forecast, pick everything that is ripe or close to it that afternoon. If you miss it and wake to frozen apples, leave them alone until midday — picking a frozen apple bruises it — and use any that are still firm soon, because they will not keep.
temperate.ready: Cut one open: the seeds have gone from white to brown (on late varieties this happens weeks early, so it is a necessary sign, not a sufficient one). The ground colour — the skin in the stem dimple and on the shaded side — has shifted from leaf-green to yellow or cream. The flesh is white or cream, not greenish. Cup the apple, lift it and give it a quarter turn: a ripe apple comes away with its stem; one you have to yank is not ready. A few sound apples on the ground under the tree means the rest are days away. The keen can buy tincture of iodine, cut an apple across and paint the cut face: starch stains blue-black, so an unripe apple goes dark all over and a ripe one stains only a thin ring under the skin. Iodine is poisonous — the tested apple goes in the compost, not a mouth.
temperate.pick: Lift and twist upward with the stem on; never pull straight down, which tears out the spur that carries next year’s fruit, and never pull the stem out of the apple, because that hole is where rot starts. Handle them like eggs and set them, not drop them, into a padded basket — a bruise you cannot see today is a rotten apple in November. Pick on a dry day. Sort as you go: perfect fruit for storage, anything marked for the kitchen this week. Storage varieties can be picked a touch early and firm; apples for eating now want full ripeness.

store.keeps: 2–6 months by variety; late keepers (Northern Spy, Haralson, Golden Russet types) longest, early apples weeks only
store.how: One layer deep in crates lined with newspaper, or in plastic bags with a few holes punched in them to hold humidity. Keep them in their own space: apples give off ethylene that ages everything stored near them, and they take up the smell of onions and potatoes. Hold McIntosh and Honeycrisp at about 3 °C rather than 0 — they suffer chilling injury at the coldest setting.
In a bag with holes, away from the vegetables. Apples ripen roughly four times faster at 10 °C than at 0 °C, so the fridge is worth a lot more than the counter.

store.keeps: 4–10 weeks, less in a warm fall
store.how: Boxes with newspaper between layers, off the concrete, checked every week. Pull anything soft or spotted at once — one rotting apple really does spoil the box, because the ethylene it gives off ripens its neighbours.

temperate.preserveNote: Apples are high-acid, so everything you make from them water-baths without added acid: applesauce (sugar optional, hot pack, 15 minutes for 500 ml jars and 20 for litres at 0–300 m), apple butter (the tested recipe cooks apples down with cider, vinegar and sugar until a spoonful mounds without weeping, then 5 minutes for 500 ml jars), and sliced apples in very light syrup, juice or water (hot pack, 20 minutes). Slices freeze well for pies if you hold them in water with ascorbic acid first or steam-blanch them 2 minutes, then tray-freeze; the texture is for cooking, not eating. Dried rings are the children’s favourite: dip 5 mm slices in ascorbic-acid water, dry at 60 °C (140 °F) for about six hours until leathery with no damp centre, and condition them in a loose jar for a week before sealing. Fresh-pressed cider is unpasteurized: bring it to a boil before giving it to children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system — freezing keeps the flavour but does not make it safe. What does not work: canning pie filling thickened with flour or cornstarch (only Clear Jel, in a tested recipe, is safe — thickeners stop the heat reaching the centre of the jar), raw-packing apple slices (they float and brown), and putting windfalls in jars or juice — extension food-safety services say drops have been in contact with soil and animals, are often bruised enough for moulds to start inside, and are less acidic than picked fruit, and the mould toxin patulin survives cooking. Windfalls that are sound go in a pie this week; the rest go to the compost.

seeds.how: An apple seed does not grow into its parent. Every seed is a cross with whatever tree the bees visited, so the seedling is a new and almost always sour apple; named varieties exist only because someone grafted a bud of the original onto a rootstock, and every McIntosh in the world is a piece of the first one. If a child wants to try, the honest version is an experiment: push a few seeds into a pot of soil outdoors in October (they need a cold winter before they will sprout), and see what comes up in May. It will be a tree; it will not be the apple they ate. To make more of a variety you like, learn to graft in late winter — a cleft or whip graft onto a hardy rootstock is a good Saturday with a ten-year-old.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — the variety lives in the grafted wood, not the seed. Seeds sown outdoors in autumn come up the following spring, as wild cards.

temperate.nextYear: There is no rotation; there is housekeeping. Pick up and compost every drop as it falls through September and October — apple maggot and codling moth overwinter in dropped fruit — and rake the leaves out from under the tree in November to break the scab cycle. Put a plastic spiral or hardware-cloth guard on the trunk before snow so mice and rabbits cannot girdle it. Do not feed after midsummer; prune in late winter while the tree is bare. Plant new trees bare-root in early spring as soon as the ground thaws, in full sun with drainage, and plant two different varieties (or one near a flowering crab) — most apples will not set fruit on their own pollen. In zones 3–4 choose trees on hardy rootstock and varieties bred for the cold, Honeycrisp and Haralson among the known ones; late keepers are the ones most likely to still be on the tree when the first hard freeze comes, so plan to pick them before, not after.

sow.outdoors: Plant bare-root trees in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; potted trees any time until early September.

faqs.q: When are apples ready to pick?
faqs.a: When the seeds inside have turned brown, the skin colour in the stem dimple has gone from green to yellow, and the apple lifts off with a twist instead of a tug. A few sound apples dropping on their own is the tree telling you the rest are close. Early varieties ripen in August and do not keep; the storage apples come in late September and October, and in most of southern Canada the whole crop is in before the end of October.

faqs.q: How do I store apples for the winter?
faqs.a: Cold and damp: 0–4 °C with high humidity, which in a house means a cold room, a second fridge or a crisper drawer, with the apples in bags with a few holes punched in them. Keep them away from the vegetables — apples give off ethylene that ages everything near them and they pick up the smell of onions and potatoes. Late varieties keep 3–6 months this way; an early apple keeps a few weeks whatever you do. Check every week and pull anything soft.

faqs.q: Can you freeze apples?
faqs.a: Yes, as slices for pies and sauce, not for eating out of hand. Peel and slice, hold the slices in water with a half-teaspoon of ascorbic acid per litre (or steam-blanch them 2 minutes) so they do not brown, then freeze on a tray and bag them. Applesauce freezes perfectly as it is and is the fastest way through a glut on a weeknight.

faqs.q: Can I grow an apple tree from a seed?
faqs.a: You can grow a tree; you cannot grow that apple. Apple seeds are crosses with whichever tree pollinated the flower, so the seedling is a new variety and almost always a sour one. It is still a good experiment for a child — plant a few seeds in a pot outside in autumn, since they need a cold winter to sprout, and watch for them in May. Named apples are made by grafting a bud onto a rootstock, which is a skill worth learning in late winter.

faqs.q: Will frost hurt apples still on the tree?
faqs.a: A light frost, no — apples do not start to freeze until about −2 °C (28 °F), and a brief dip to there only shortens how long they keep. Several nights below that soften the flesh, and at around −5 °C (22 °F) the fruit freezes hard and is ruined. If a hard freeze is forecast, pick what is ripe that afternoon. If the apples do freeze, wait until they have thawed at midday before touching them, and use the firm ones soon.

faqs.q: Are windfall apples safe to use?
faqs.a: For the kitchen this week, a windfall that fell today, is firm and unbroken, cut open and cooked, is a judgement call most gardeners make in favour of pie. For jars and juice, no: extension food-safety services say not to can or juice from dropped fruit, because drops have touched soil and animal droppings, are usually bruised enough for moulds to start in the core where you cannot see them, are less acidic than picked fruit, and the mould toxin patulin is not destroyed by heat. The useful children’s job is picking up drops every day into a bucket for the compost, which also keeps the wasps down. Teach them to look before they lift: a wasp feeding inside the hollow of a dropped apple is the commonest sting in an orchard, and no one bites into a windfall.

faqs.q: Do apples need added lemon juice when canning?
faqs.a: No. Apples are a high-acid fruit, well below the pH 4.6 line, so applesauce, apple butter and sliced apples are safely water-bath canned by their tested recipes without extra acid. The ascorbic acid or lemon juice you see in sliced-apple recipes is there to stop browning, not for safety. Where it does matter is anything mixed with low-acid ingredients — apple pie filling is only safe by a tested recipe with Clear Jel, and apple-and-vegetable chutneys need their vinegar measured, not tasted.

temperate.name: Pears
temperate.tagline: The fruit you must pick before it is ripe — a pear left to soften on the tree is mush outside and grit at the core.
temperate.frostNote: Pears are normally off the tree before the first hard frost, which is one more reason to pick them mature-green in September rather than waiting for them to soften. The fruit itself behaves like an apple: a light frost on the branch does no harm, but around −2 °C the flesh starts to freeze and a few such nights ruin it. If a hard freeze is forecast and the pears are full size and lift off when tilted, pick them all that afternoon and ripen them indoors. Frozen fruit must thaw on the tree before you touch it.
temperate.ready: This is the crop people get wrong, because the sign of readiness is not softness. A European pear is picked mature but hard and ripened off the tree; left on, it ripens from the inside out, the core goes brown and the flesh turns gritty. Ready to pick means: full size for the variety; the skin has lightened from deep green to a paler green or yellow-green; the lenticels (the little dots) have gone from white to brown; the seeds are turning brown; and when you cup the pear and tilt it to horizontal it snaps cleanly off the spur. If you have to twist and pull, wait a few days. It is better to pick a little early than a little late. Bartlett comes in mid-August to early September in zones 5–6; Bosc, Anjou and the other winter pears in late September and October.
temperate.pick: Lift the pear to horizontal and let it snap off; keep the stem on. Handle gently — hard pears bruise invisibly and the bruise shows up as a brown patch when they ripen. Into shallow boxes, one or two layers, and straight to a cold place. Separate the two kinds: summer pears (Bartlett, Clapp’s, Flemish Beauty) to ripen soon, winter pears (Bosc, Anjou, Comice) to the cold room for their chilling first.

store.where: Fridge or cold room, for storage pears
store.keeps: Bartlett 4–6 weeks; Bosc 7–10 weeks; Anjou 3–4 months
store.how: In perforated bags or a lined crate, away from vegetables. Winter pears need this cold spell before they will ripen properly: Bosc and Comice want 2–4 weeks, Anjou 4–8 weeks; Bartlett needs only a day or two. Pull a few at a time to ripen on the counter.

store.keeps: 3–10 days to ripe, then 2–3 days in the fridge
store.how: In a bowl or a paper bag out of the sun; a ripe banana or apple in the bag speeds it up. Bartlett takes about 5 days, Bosc and Comice about 7, Anjou up to 9. Check the neck daily — press gently just below the stem — and refrigerate the ones that yield.
Boxes with newspaper between layers, checked weekly. Warmer than a fridge, so it ripens them slowly rather than holding them; fine for a month of Bartletts, not for keeping Anjou until February.

temperate.preserveNote: Pears are the home canner’s best fruit after peaches: ripened-but-still-firm halves, held in ascorbic-acid water while you work, boiled 5 minutes in very light or light syrup, apple juice or plain water, hot-packed with 1 cm (½ in) headspace and processed 20 minutes for 500 ml jars and 25 for litres at 0–300 m. Use fruit that has had its chilling and a few days on the counter — a rock-hard pear cans woody, a soft one cans to mush. Pear butter and pear sauce follow the tested apple recipes. Dried pear slices (5 mm, dipped in ascorbic acid, 60 °C/140 °F for 6–10 hours until suede-like with no moist pockets) are excellent and keep a year. Freezing is the weak option: pears go brown and soft when thawed, so freeze them only as purée, or in syrup with ascorbic acid for smoothies and sauce. What does not work: canning pears raw-packed (the tested method is hot pack only), canning unripe fruit, and waiting for tree-ripe pears to make anything — by then the core has gone.

seeds.how: Like apples, pears do not come true from seed: every seedling is a cross and a gamble, and the named varieties are grafted onto rootstock. Pear seeds sown outdoors in autumn will sprout in spring if a child wants to grow a tree, but it will be a new pear of its own and may take ten years to show you what. To propagate a variety, graft a dormant scion onto a pear or quince rootstock in late winter; pears graft easily.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — the variety lives in the grafted wood.

temperate.nextYear: Pears need a partner: plant two different varieties that bloom together, within sight of each other, or you will get flowers and no fruit. Full sun, deep soil, and go easy on nitrogen — soft lush growth is what fire blight attacks, and that disease is the reason to prune out any blackened, hooked shoot tips the moment you see them, cutting 30 cm below the damage into clean wood and wiping the blade. Prune lightly in late winter; pears fruit on spurs that last for years. Pick up drops, mouse-guard the trunk before snow, and plant bare-root trees in early spring. In zones 3–4 choose prairie-bred varieties and a sheltered spot; standard Bartlett is a zone 5 tree.

sow.outdoors: Plant bare-root trees in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked.

faqs.q: When do you pick pears?
faqs.a: Before they are ripe. Pick when the pear is full size, the skin has lightened a shade, the little dots on the skin have gone brown, and the fruit snaps off cleanly when you tilt it to horizontal — but while it is still hard. Bartlett comes in late August to early September in southern Ontario and Quebec; Bosc and Anjou in late September and October. If you wait for softness on the tree, the core goes brown and the flesh gritty.

faqs.q: Do pears ripen off the tree?
faqs.a: Yes — that is how European pears are meant to be ripened. Pick them mature and hard, give winter varieties their cold spell, then bring them to room temperature (18–24 °C) for 3–10 days. Bartlett needs only a day or two in the fridge first; Bosc and Comice want 2–4 weeks at 0–2 °C and Anjou 4–8, or they ripen unevenly or not at all. A banana or apple in the bag speeds things up.

faqs.q: How do you tell when a pear is ripe to eat?
faqs.a: Check the neck: press gently with a thumb just below the stem. When that spot gives slightly, the pear is ripe all the way through; by the time the fat end is soft, the middle is past it. Colour helps with Bartlett, which goes from green to yellow, but Bosc and Anjou barely change colour at all. This is a good daily job for a child — one pear, one thumb, no squeezing the rest.

faqs.q: How do you store pears for the winter?
faqs.a: Pick them hard and put them straight into the coldest place you have, ideally 0–2 °C with high humidity — a fridge, a cold room or a crisper drawer in perforated bags. Bartlett keeps 4–6 weeks that way, Bosc 2 months, Anjou up to 4 months. Bring out a few at a time to ripen on the counter. An unheated garage at 5–8 °C ripens them slowly rather than holding them, so it buys weeks, not months.

faqs.q: Can you freeze pears?
faqs.a: You can, but they come out brown and soft, so freeze them only in the forms where that does not matter: puréed as pear sauce, or sliced into syrup with a half-teaspoon of ascorbic acid per litre for smoothies and baking. For eating quality, can them in light syrup or dry them instead.

faqs.q: Are pears frost hardy?
faqs.a: The trees are hardy to zone 5 for most varieties (prairie-bred pears to zone 3), and the fruit on the branch takes a light frost without harm. Around −2 °C the flesh begins to freeze, and a few nights like that ruin it — but since pears are picked hard in September, they should be in the cold room before that happens. If a hard freeze is forecast and the fruit lifts off when tilted, pick it all that afternoon.

temperate.name: Rhubarb
temperate.tagline: The first harvest of the Canadian year and the toughest plant in the garden — eat the stalks, never the leaves.
temperate.frostNote: Autumn frost needs nothing from you. The leaves collapse after a few degrees of frost, the crown is already shutting down, and that is exactly what it wants; rhubarb survives winters across the prairies with nothing but snow on it. In spring it is the reverse question: new stalks take light frosts in stride, and a stalk that is still firm and upright after a frost is fine to eat. A stalk that has frozen hard and gone soft and limp is not — a severe freeze can move oxalic acid from the leaf into the stalk — so after a bad spring night, pull the mushy ones and compost them and wait for the next flush.
temperate.ready: Stalks 25–40 cm (10–15 in) long and as thick as a thumb, from late April in zone 6 to mid-May in zone 3. Colour tells you the variety, not the ripeness — a green-stalked rhubarb is ready when it is green. Take nothing the year you plant, a light picking the second year, and a full 8–10 weeks from the third year on. When the new stalks come up thin and spindly, the crown is telling you it has given enough.
temperate.pick: Grasp the stalk at its base, pull and twist it to one side; it comes away cleanly. Do not cut with a knife — the stub left behind is where crown rot gets in. Take no more than a third to half of the stalks at any one pass and stop by the end of June or the first days of July, so the plant keeps a full head of leaves to rebuild the crown for next year. Cut the leaves off straight away (they draw water out of the stalk) and compost them. Snap out any flower stalk the day you see it — it drains the crown and the stalks go stringy.

store.keeps: Through June — pull as you need it
store.how: Rhubarb keeps best where it grows; harvest the morning you cook.
Leaves off, unwashed, in a plastic bag. Limp stalks firm up again in a jug of cold water for an hour.

temperate.preserveNote: The freezer is the method, and rhubarb is the easiest thing in the garden to freeze: wash, trim, cut into 2 cm pieces, spread on a tray, freeze, bag. No blanching is needed; a one-minute blanch holds the colour a little better if you care, and you can pack raw pieces in syrup for a dessert fruit. Stewed rhubarb water-baths safely because it is strongly acid: the tested recipe heats 1 litre of cut rhubarb with 125 ml (½ cup) sugar until the juice runs and it boils, hot-packs it with 1 cm headspace, and processes 500 ml and litre jars 15 minutes at 0–300 m. The sugar is for quality, not safety. Strawberry-rhubarb jam is the classic — use a tested pectin recipe, since rhubarb on its own is short of pectin. What does not work: drying (leathery, sour, pointless), canning stalks that have frozen soft in the garden, and anything at all made from the leaves.

seeds.how: Rhubarb is grown from crowns, not seed: seedlings are variable, slow (three years to the first picking) and rarely as good as the parent. Divide an established crown when it is 5–10 years old and the stalks have gone thin and crowded. Extension services prefer early spring, as soon as the ground can be worked and before the buds open; many gardeners do it in fall once the leaves have died back, and that works too. Dig the whole crown, cut it with a sharp spade into pieces that each have two or three fat pink buds and a good chunk of root, and replant them 1 m apart with the buds 5 cm (2 in) below the surface. A healthy crown gives five to ten new plants. Water them weekly through dry weather in their first season and take nothing from them that year.
seeds.viability: Not grown from seed in practice. Divisions give a light picking in their second spring and a full crop in the third.

temperate.nextYear: Rhubarb is a permanent resident, so it goes at the edge of the garden where the roots will never be dug over, in full sun and rich, well-drained soil — it rots in a wet spot. After the leaves die back, spread 5 cm of compost or rotted manure around (not on top of) the crown; that is the whole fertiliser program. Keep flower stalks cut, keep it watered in a July drought, and leave every leaf on after the harvest ends. Plant crowns 1 m apart in early spring. Hardiness is not the question in Canada: it is grown from zone 2 up, and the prairies are full of fifty-year-old plants. In hot zone 7 summers it needs afternoon shade more than anything.

sow.outdoors: Plant crowns or divisions as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, buds 5 cm (2 in) below the surface and 1 m apart.

faqs.q: When should you stop harvesting rhubarb?
faqs.a: By the end of June or the first week of July in most of Canada, and sooner if the new stalks are coming up thin. The leaves left standing through summer feed the crown for next year’s crop; keep pulling into August and the plant comes back weak. A stalk or two for a pie in July will not hurt an old crown, but the main harvest is April to June.

faqs.q: Are rhubarb leaves poisonous?
faqs.a: Yes. The leaves contain high levels of oxalic acid and are not food for people or animals; the rule in a family garden is that the leaf comes off before the stalk goes in the basket, and nothing from a rhubarb leaf goes in a mouth. They are fine in the compost — the oxalic acid breaks down quickly there and does not harm the pile or the garden it goes on.

faqs.q: Can you freeze rhubarb without blanching?
faqs.a: Yes. Cut the stalks into 2 cm pieces, freeze them on a tray and bag them; they keep a year and go straight from the freezer into a crumble or a pot of sauce. A one-minute blanch keeps the colour slightly brighter, which matters for a pink variety and not at all for a green one.

faqs.q: Is rhubarb safe to eat after a frost?
faqs.a: If the stalk is still firm and standing, yes — light frosts do not hurt it and the first stalks of the year usually come through several. If a hard freeze has left stalks soft, limp and mushy, pull and compost those; a severe freeze can move oxalic acid from the leaf down into a damaged stalk. New stalks will replace them within a couple of weeks.

faqs.q: When and how do you divide rhubarb?
faqs.a: When a crown is 5–10 years old and the stalks have become thin and crowded. Early spring, before the buds open, is the time extension services recommend; fall after the leaves die down also works. Dig the crown, chop it into pieces with two or three buds and plenty of root each, and replant with the buds 5 cm below the surface and 1 m apart. Take nothing from the divisions their first year.

faqs.q: Can kids pick rhubarb?
faqs.a: It is one of the best first harvests: the stalk comes off with a pull and a twist that a four-year-old can manage, and nothing needs a knife. Two rules — only the stalks, and the leaf comes off and goes to the compost before anything else happens. A raw stalk dipped in a saucer of sugar is the traditional reward, and it is safe.

temperate.name: Strawberries
temperate.tagline: Three weeks of June glory from a June-bearer, or a trickle until frost from a day-neutral — either way, the freezer is the answer.
temperate.frostNote: The plants shrug off autumn frost; it is the flowers and fruit that do not. If you grow day-neutral or everbearing plants that are still fruiting in September and October, throw a row cover or old sheet over them on a frost night: open blossoms die at −1 °C, white-bud flowers and green fruit at about −2 °C, and anything already coloured should be picked that evening. June-bearers need nothing until the mulch goes on. Do not mulch at the first frost — wait until the plants have hardened through two or three frosts and the soil is cold, usually late October or November, then cover the rows with 10–15 cm (4–6 in) of clean straw. An unmulched crown dies at about −9 °C (15 °F), and in a snowless January that is an ordinary night. Pull the straw into the paths when growth starts in April.
temperate.ready: Red to the very tip and up under the cap with no white shoulder — a strawberry ripens from the tip toward the stem and does not ripen one bit after picking. Fully coloured, glossy, and giving slightly to a thumb. Check every day once the first ones colour; a berry goes from perfect to overripe in two warm days. June-bearers crop for about three weeks from mid-June; day-neutrals from June until frost with a lull in the July heat; everbearers in early summer and again in early fall.
temperate.pick: Pinch the stem with a thumbnail just above the cap so the berry comes away with its cap on; pulling the berry off the cap bruises it and it will not keep. Pick in the cool of the morning, into shallow containers no more than two berries deep, and get them out of the sun. Do not wash them until you use them. Pick off and bin any mouldy or bird-pecked fruit as you go, so grey mould does not spread down the row.

store.keeps: 3–5 days, 7 at most for firm varieties
store.how: In a shallow, covered container or a perforated bag, caps on, unwashed, one or two layers. Sort out any soft one the day you pick.
For eating now only. A strawberry at room temperature is a strawberry in decline.

temperate.preserveNote: Freeze them. Hull, rinse, dry on a towel, spread on a tray, freeze, bag: whole berries that pour out loose all winter for smoothies, sauce and muffins. Sliced or crushed berries freeze well with 180 ml (¾ cup) sugar per litre of fruit for pie and shortcake. Strawberry jam is the other great use — a tested powdered- or liquid-pectin recipe, water-bathed 5–10 minutes depending on the recipe and your altitude — and uncooked freezer jam, which tastes more like the fruit than any cooked jam, keeps three weeks in the fridge and a year in the freezer. What does not work: canning strawberries whole. They are not on the tested list for canned berries because they collapse, float, bleach pale and lose their flavour in the jar; the way to keep strawberries in a jar is as jam. Dried strawberry slices and fruit leather are good but a lot of fruit for a little result.

seeds.how: Strawberries make their own plants: after the June crop every plant sends out runners with daughter plants along them. Choose the first daughter on each runner (the one nearest the mother, the strongest), set it onto bare soil or into a sunk pot of potting mix while it is still attached, pin it down with a bent wire or a stone, and keep it watered. It roots in three to four weeks; cut the cord and, by early September at the latest, move it to its new bed — plants rooted later than that will not fruit well next June. Take runners only from healthy, vigorous mothers. Seed is pointless: garden strawberries are hybrids and their seedlings do not come true. Note that many modern varieties are protected by plant breeders’ rights, which forbid propagating them for sale; your own garden is your own business.
seeds.viability: Not from seed. A daughter plant rooted by early September fruits the following June, and a bed renews itself from its own runners every 3–4 years.

temperate.nextYear: Next year’s crop is made this summer. Right after the last June picking — before the first of August — renovate June-bearing beds: mow or shear the leaves off 2–3 cm above the crowns, rake them away, narrow the rows back to 30 cm, pull the weakest plants, feed, and water the stubble back to life. Skip the mowing for day-neutrals; just thin them. Beds wear out after three or four years, so start a new one every second spring from your own runners, and put it where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or raspberries have not grown for several years — they share verticillium wilt. Full sun, well-drained soil, 45 cm between plants; pinch every flower off June-bearers in their planting year and off day-neutrals for the first six weeks. In zones 3–4 choose hardy June-bearers such as Kent, Honeoye and Cavendish, and treat the straw mulch as non-negotiable.

sow.outdoors: Plant dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, 2–4 weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked.

faqs.q: When are strawberries ready to pick?
faqs.a: When they are red to the tip and up under the cap, with no white shoulder, glossy, and just yielding to a thumb. They ripen from the tip up and stop ripening the second they are picked, so a half-white berry stays half-white. June-bearers crop for about three weeks from mid-June in southern Ontario and Quebec, a week or two later in zone 3–4; day-neutrals keep going until frost.

faqs.q: Can you freeze strawberries?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best way to keep them. Hull, rinse, dry well, freeze whole on a tray and bag them; they keep a year. For pies and shortcake, slice or crush them with ¾ cup of sugar per litre of fruit before freezing. Thawed strawberries are soft, so they are for sauce, smoothies and baking rather than a bowl.

faqs.q: How do you store fresh strawberries?
faqs.a: Unwashed, caps on, in a shallow covered container in the fridge at 0–4 °C, and eat them within three to five days. Washing before storage starts the rot; wash just before eating. Sort out anything soft the day you pick, because one mouldy berry takes the container with it.

faqs.q: Can you can strawberries?
faqs.a: Not whole — strawberries are left off the tested list for canned berries because they collapse, float and lose colour and flavour in the jar. Strawberry jam is how they go in a jar: a tested pectin recipe, water-bathed. Uncooked freezer jam tastes even more like June, keeps three weeks in the fridge or a year frozen, and is a fine first canning project for a child because there is no hot jar to handle.

faqs.q: Do strawberries need to be covered for winter?
faqs.a: Yes, in most of Canada. The crowns can die at around −9 °C without snow cover, so after the plants have hardened through two or three frosts and the soil has gone cold — late October or November — cover the rows with 10–15 cm of clean straw. Not earlier, or the plants rot under warm mulch. Rake it into the paths when growth starts in April, and pull it back over the rows on a frosty night during bloom, since open flowers die at −1 °C.

faqs.q: What is strawberry renovation?
faqs.a: The after-harvest haircut that keeps a June-bearing bed productive. Within a week or two of the last picking, mow or shear the leaves off just above the crowns, rake them away, narrow each row to about 30 cm wide, thin out the weakest plants, fertilise, and water well. It feels brutal and the bed looks like a stubble field for a fortnight; by September it is dense with new leaves and the fruit buds for next June are being set. Do it before August 1.

faqs.q: What should kids know about picking strawberries?
faqs.a: Pinch the stem above the green cap rather than pulling the berry, and put it in the box, not drop it. Only the all-red ones — a strawberry does not ripen after picking, so a white-tipped berry is a wasted berry. Picking into a shallow box two deep keeps them from crushing, and the picker gets to eat the ones the slugs started.
