temperate.name: Raspberries
temperate.tagline: Pick every second day or lose them — and tray-freeze the surplus the same afternoon.
temperate.frostNote: The canes are among the hardiest things in the garden — Boyne, Nova and Latham overwinter in zone 3 — so autumn frost asks nothing of the plants. It does end the fall crop: on primocane (fall-bearing) varieties the open flowers are damaged by any frost at all and the ripe fruit turns to mush after a hard one around −2 °C, so the evening before a hard frost pick every berry with colour on it. Ripe fruit comes through a light frost of −1 °C fine. Do not prune anything until the canes are fully dormant and bare.
temperate.ready: Full colour for the variety, plump, slightly soft, and — the real test — it slides off its core with the gentlest pull, leaving the white plug on the plant. If you have to tug, it needs another day. Summer-bearing (floricane) types crop for three to four weeks from early July; fall-bearing (primocane) types from mid-August until frost. Berries ripen a few at a time along a cane, so there is no single picking day.
temperate.pick: Every two days, daily in a heat wave, in the morning once the dew has dried. Lift each berry with two fingers; a ripe one needs no force. Shallow containers, no more than two deep, into the shade as you fill them and into the fridge within the hour. Do not wash them before storing or freezing — wet raspberries mould within a day. Pick off and bin any mouldy fruit so it does not spread along the row.

store.how: Spread in a shallow covered container, unwashed, straight from the garden. If you cannot eat them in two days, freeze them today.
For the bowl on the table. Raspberries at room temperature are a same-day fruit.

temperate.preserveNote: Rinse them gently in cold water, drain and dry on a towel, then spread them on a tray, freeze and bag. They hold their shape and flavour better than any other berry. For jam, raspberries have enough natural pectin to set with sugar alone by a tested long-boil recipe, or quickly with added pectin; for seedless jam press half or all of the fruit through a food mill or sieve before measuring, then follow the recipe’s weights. Whole raspberries are on the tested list for canning (raw pack in syrup, 15 minutes for 500 ml jars at 0–300 m) but come out soft and pale — jam, syrup and the freezer suit them better. Raspberry vinegar is a safe and good use for a surplus. What does not work: washing before storage (mould in a day), and drying — a dried raspberry is a hard seedy pebble; make leather from the purée instead.

seeds.how: Red raspberries spread by suckers from the roots, and that is how you make more of them. In early spring before the buds break (or in late fall after the leaves drop), dig a sucker that came up a hand’s width or more from the row with a good piece of root attached, cut the top back to 15–20 cm, and replant it 60–90 cm apart in the new row. Take suckers only from a healthy, productive patch: viruses build up in raspberries over the years and travel with the plant, so when an old patch starts to decline, buy certified stock and start again somewhere else rather than moving its suckers. Seeds do not come true and take years.
seeds.viability: Not from seed. A sucker moved in early spring fruits the next summer (summer types) or that same autumn (fall types).

temperate.nextYear: Pruning is the whole art. Summer-bearing: as soon as the harvest ends, cut every cane that fruited (brown, woody, peeling) right to the ground, and in early spring thin the new canes to four or five strong ones per 30 cm of row and tip them back to about 1.2–1.5 m. Fall-bearing, the simple way: mow every cane to the ground in late fall once the leaves have dropped or in early spring before growth, and take one big crop from August to frost on the new canes. Full sun, well-drained soil, a wire on posts at 1 m to lean on, and 60–90 cm between plants in rows 2 m apart with the paths kept mown so suckers cannot wander. Never plant where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or strawberries grew in the last few years — they share verticillium wilt. In zones 3–4 stick with hardy summer-bearers (Boyne, Nova, Latham); a fall-bearer that ripens in September may lose most of its crop to frost there.

sow.outdoors: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, 60–90 cm (2–3 ft) apart, and cut them back to 15 cm after planting.

faqs.q: When are raspberries ready to pick?
faqs.a: When the berry is fully coloured, slightly soft, and slips off its white core with a gentle pull — if it resists, come back tomorrow. Summer varieties crop for three or four weeks from early July in southern Ontario and Quebec; fall varieties from mid-August until the first hard frost. Pick every second day, every day in hot weather.

faqs.q: Can you freeze raspberries without washing them?
faqs.a: Yes — that is the right way. Spread the berries straight from the patch on a tray, freeze them, and bag them; rinse them as you use them if you want to. Washed raspberries hold water and mould in the fridge or clump and ice up in the freezer. Frozen on a tray they stay loose and whole for a year.

faqs.q: How long do raspberries keep in the fridge?
faqs.a: Two or three days at most, unwashed, in a shallow covered container at 0–4 °C. They are the shortest-lived fruit in the garden, which is why anything you cannot eat in two days should be frozen the day it is picked.

faqs.q: How do you prune raspberries in the fall?
faqs.a: It depends which kind you have. Summer-bearing canes that fruited in July are dead wood: cut them to the ground any time after harvest, and leave the green new canes to fruit next year. Fall-bearing varieties are simplest of all: once the leaves drop (or in early spring before growth) mow every cane to the ground, and the new canes carry the whole crop next August. Cutting a summer-bearer to the ground in fall means no raspberries next year, so know which you have.

faqs.q: How do you make seedless raspberry jam?
faqs.a: Press the raw crushed fruit through a food mill or a fine sieve to take out the seeds — all of it for truly seedless, half of it for a jam with some texture — and then measure the purée exactly as the tested recipe measures crushed fruit. The proportions of fruit, sugar and pectin are what make the jam set and keep, so sieve first and measure second.

faqs.q: Are raspberries frost hardy?
faqs.a: The plants, very: standard varieties overwinter to zone 3 (Boyne, Nova and Latham) or zone 4 (Killarney, Prelude) with no protection. The fall crop is not — open flowers are damaged by any frost and ripe fruit goes mushy after a hard one around −2 °C, though a light −1 °C frost leaves ripe berries fine. Pick everything coloured the evening before a hard frost, and leave the pruning until the canes are dormant.

faqs.q: What should kids know about picking raspberries?
faqs.a: Two fingers, a gentle pull, and if it does not come, leave it. The white core stays on the plant; if the core came too, the berry was not ripe. Pick into a shallow box held under the branch, not a deep bucket, and watch the thorns — long sleeves on the first few trips. Eating as you go is part of the job.

temperate.name: Haskap (honeyberry)
temperate.tagline: The Canadian berry: hardy to zone 2, ripe before the strawberries, and the first jam of the year.
temperate.frostNote: Frost is not haskap’s problem in either direction. The dormant bush has come through −45 °C in Saskatoon without damage, and the open flowers in early May survive −6 to −7 °C, which is why it fruits reliably where strawberry blossoms are lost. There is nothing to do on an autumn frost night; the crop was in by July. The one thing to leave alone is the leaves, which often look tired and brown-edged by late August — that is normal for the species, not a problem to fix.
temperate.ready: The skin turns deep blue 5–10 days before the fruit is ripe, and that is the trap. Bite one in half: if the inside is green, or greenish and tastes grassy, wait a week; when it is purple-red right to the centre and sweet-tart, pick. Ripe berries drop into your hand at a touch, and the earliest ones start to fall on their own. The first fruit colours around the first week of June in Saskatoon and mid-June in southern Ontario and Quebec, with the main picking in the second half of June and into July for later varieties.
temperate.pick: Hand-pick into a shallow container — the fruit is soft and the skin is thin — or lay a tarp under the bush and shake the branches, which drops the ripe ones and leaves the green. Net the bushes the day the fruit turns blue: cedar waxwings and robins strip an unnetted haskap in a morning, and the mesh must be no bigger than 1.25 cm (½ in) or birds get their heads stuck in it. Pick every few days over two or three weeks; a mature bush gives 3–4.5 kg (6–10 lb).

store.how: Shallow covered container, unwashed. They are softer than blueberries and bruise if piled.
Tray-freeze, bag. This is where most of the crop should go.

temperate.preserveNote: Haskap is the easiest berry to freeze and the one that comes out best: rinse, dry, tray-freeze, bag. The skin dissolves and the seeds go unnoticed when the thawed fruit is cooked, so frozen haskap makes sauce, pie, muffins and smoothies all winter with nothing lost. It is tart and high in acid, and it makes a deep purple jam, jelly and syrup that water-bath by a tested berry-jam recipe with pectin; juice and wine are the commercial uses. The University of Saskatchewan lists freezing, drying, fermenting and canning as its routes, but there is no tested recipe specific to whole haskap in syrup — so jam, syrup and the freezer are the home options, and whole canned haskap is not. Dried haskap works in a dehydrator like a blueberry, slowly.

seeds.how: Haskap varieties are clones and will not come from seed: a seedling is a new, unpredictable plant that takes years to show you what it is, and the Canadian cultivars are protected varieties that only licensed nurseries may propagate for sale. Buy plants, and buy at least two different, compatible varieties, because haskap cannot pollinate itself. For your own garden, softwood cuttings taken in June root under a plastic bag and are the way to fill out a hedge. Named pairs that work: Aurora with Borealis, Tundra or the Indigo series (Indigo Gem, Indigo Treat, Indigo Yum); the older Russian types pollinate most University of Saskatchewan varieties. Plant them close together in the same row — bees work along a row, not across the garden — with roughly one pollinator for every eight bushes if you are planting many.
seeds.viability: Not from seed. A rooted cutting takes about three years to fruit; a nursery plant gives its first real crop in year three.

temperate.nextYear: Full sun is best, though it tolerates part shade; any reasonable soil from pH 5.5 to 8, well drained. Space bushes 1 m apart for a hedge or 1.3 m to keep them separate, mulch them, and keep two or more compatible varieties within a few metres of each other. No pruning for the first three or four years; after that, in late fall or winter when the shape is easy to see, take out the oldest and the crossing branches, and an overgrown bush can be cut to 15 cm (6 in) above the ground and will regrow. The breeding programme at the University of Saskatchewan bred these for zone 2, so in zones 3–5 the only planning is bird netting and a spring reminder that the flowers do not need covering. Plant in spring in the coldest zones so the roots settle before winter.

sow.outdoors: Plant potted bushes any time from early spring to September; spring is best in zones 2–3.

faqs.q: How do you know when haskap is ripe?
faqs.a: Not by the outside. The skin turns blue a week or more before the berry is ripe, so cut or bite one open: green or pale inside means wait 5–7 days; purple-red all the way through and sweet-tart means pick. Ripe berries fall into your hand at a touch. In southern Ontario and Quebec that is the second half of June — before the strawberries — and the second and third weeks of June on the prairies.

faqs.q: Do you need two haskap plants?
faqs.a: Yes, two different varieties that bloom at the same time; a haskap cannot set fruit with its own pollen, and two plants of the same variety are the same clone. Both bushes fruit — there is no sterile ‘male’. Aurora was bred as the partner for Borealis and also pollinates Tundra and the Indigo series, which makes it the easy second plant. Put them in the same row, a metre or two apart.

faqs.q: Can you freeze haskap?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best thing to do with them: rinse, dry, freeze on a tray, bag, and they keep a year. Thawed haskap is soft, but the skins dissolve and the seeds are unnoticeable in cooking, so frozen fruit goes straight into muffins, sauce, pie and smoothies. Most growers freeze the bulk of the crop the day it is picked.

faqs.q: Which haskap varieties grow in Canada?
faqs.a: The University of Saskatchewan varieties were bred for it: Borealis and Tundra (2007), the Indigo series (Gem, Treat, Yum), Honey Bee, Aurora (the large, sweet mid-season one), and the later Boreal Beauty, Boreal Blizzard and Boreal Beast. All are hardy to zone 2. Pick two that are listed as compatible — Aurora with almost any of the others is the simplest pair.

faqs.q: Is haskap frost hardy?
faqs.a: About as hardy as a fruit gets. The dormant bush takes −45 °C, and the open flowers survive −6 to −7 °C in May, so a late spring frost that kills strawberry blossom leaves a haskap crop untouched. There is nothing to cover and nothing to bring in.

faqs.q: Is haskap a good berry for kids to pick?
faqs.a: One of the best: a bush at child height, no thorns, soft fruit that falls off when it is ready, and it is the first fruit of the year, before anything else. Two rules — only berries that are purple all the way through (open one together to show the difference), and leave the bird netting pinned down behind you. A tarp under the bush and a good shake is a job a five-year-old will ask to do again.

temperate.name: Basil
temperate.tagline: The most tender thing in the garden and the worst herb to dry — pesto in the freezer is the whole plan.
temperate.frostNote: Basil is finished by the first frost and damaged well before it. Below about 10 °C it stops growing, and a single night near 5 °C blackens the leaves — the same cold injury a fridge does to it. When the forecast shows a night in the low single digits, do not cover it: cut every plant at the base that afternoon and spend the evening making pesto. There is nothing to save by waiting.
temperate.ready: From the time a plant is 15–20 cm tall with six or more pairs of leaves, and continuously from then on. Flavour is highest just as the flower buds form and before they open, and falls off once it flowers and sets seed, so the moment you see a flower spike, pinch it out. Pick mid-morning after the dew has dried.
temperate.pick: Cut whole stems back to just above a pair of leaves rather than plucking single leaves; each cut stem branches into two and the plant gets bushier all summer. Never take more than a third at once in midseason. The final harvest, when cold is coming, is the whole plant.

store.how: Like a bunch of flowers: stems in a glass of water, out of direct sun, a loose plastic bag over the top. Change the water daily. Not the fridge.
Dry leaves wrapped in a tea towel inside a bag on the warmest shelf. Cold injury starts below 10 °C, so this is damage control, not storage.

temperate.preserveNote: Basil is the herb that proves the rule: it turns black and tastes of hay when dried, and it blackens in the fridge, so the freezer is the only good home for it. Pesto is the best form — leave the cheese out and stir it in when you thaw — frozen in ice-cube trays or pressed flat in a bag, with a film of oil on top against browning. Chopped basil covered with oil in ice-cube trays is the quick version. Whole leaves blanched for 15 seconds, cooled and frozen flat keep their green for soup. Now the rule that matters: anything made of basil, garlic and oil must stay frozen or be eaten from the fridge within four days. Oil shuts out air, and basil and garlic are low-acid, which is exactly the setting where Clostridium botulinum grows; a jar of basil in oil on the counter or in the back of the fridge for weeks is a real hazard, and no tested process exists for canning pesto. Basil vinegar, by contrast, is acid and safe on the shelf.

seeds.how: Let one or two plants flower at the end of August and stand until the flower spikes go brown and dry. Strip the spikes into a bowl, crumble the dry calyxes between your fingers and the small black seeds fall out; blow the chaff away. Basil is insect-pollinated and different basils cross with each other — Genovese next to Thai or lemon basil gives you muddled seedlings — so save seed from a single variety, or from the plant furthest from the others. Most garden basils are open-pollinated and come true; a few disease-resistant ones are hybrids and the packet will say so.
seeds.viability: About 5 years, stored cool and dry.

temperate.nextYear: Warmth is everything: start seed indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost under lights, and do not plant out until a week or two after it, when nights stay above 10 °C and the soil is warm — a basil put out in a cold May never recovers. Full sun, fertile soil, 25–30 cm apart, steady water, and pinch the tops from the start. Sow a second batch in June for September. Basil downy mildew now reaches most of eastern Canada in late summer; resistant varieties (the packet will say) and airy spacing are the answer. In zones 3–4 it is a transplant-only, under-cover-until-late-June crop, and still the first thing to go in September.

sow.outdoors: Transplant 1–2 weeks after the last frost, once nights hold above 10 °C; direct-sown basil is a July crop in zone 4.

faqs.q: What temperature kills basil?
faqs.a: Frost kills it outright, but it is damaged long before that: below about 10 °C it stops growing, and one night around 5 °C blackens the leaves. In most of southern Canada that means the first week or two of September is basil’s last. When a single-digit night is forecast, cut the whole plant and make pesto rather than covering it.

faqs.q: How do you store fresh basil?
faqs.a: Not in the fridge — cold turns the leaves black within a day or two. Stand the stems in a glass of water on the counter out of direct sun, with a loose bag over the top, and change the water daily; it keeps three to five days that way and often roots. If it must go in the fridge, wrap dry leaves in a tea towel and use them within a day.

faqs.q: Can you freeze basil?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the only good way to keep it. Make pesto without the cheese and freeze it in ice-cube trays or flat in bags; or chop the leaves, pack them in ice-cube trays and cover with oil; or blanch whole leaves 15 seconds and freeze them flat. Thawed basil is limp and dark but tastes right in anything cooked. Keep the oil versions frozen until the day you use them.

faqs.q: Can you dry basil?
faqs.a: You can, and you will wish you had not: dried basil goes black-brown and loses nearly all its flavour, which is why the jar in the shop tastes of nothing. Thyme, oregano and sage dry well; basil, parsley, chives and cilantro do not. Freeze it instead.

faqs.q: Is basil in oil safe?
faqs.a: Only frozen, or in the fridge for no more than four days. Oil keeps air away from the basil and garlic, and both are low-acid, which is the combination that lets botulism bacteria grow without any sign of spoilage. Pesto follows the same rule — four days refrigerated or into the freezer — and there is no safe way to can it at home. If you want basil on the shelf, make basil vinegar: the acid does the work.

faqs.q: How do you save basil seeds?
faqs.a: Let a plant or two flower in late summer and dry on the stem until the spikes are brown. Crumble the dry flower heads between your fingers, pick out the small black seeds and blow away the chaff. Basil crosses with other basils by insects, so save from one variety grown on its own, and expect the seed to keep about five years.

faqs.q: What can kids do with basil?
faqs.a: Pinching off the flower buds is a perfect small job — it needs doing every few days all summer and it keeps the plant producing. Basil is safe to eat raw straight off the plant, and a leaf rubbed between the fingers is the best smell in the garden. Tearing leaves for the pesto bowl beats chopping, and a child can run the salad spinner.

temperate.name: Dill
temperate.tagline: Two crops from one plant — feathery dill weed in June, and the seed heads that make a pickle a pickle in August.
temperate.frostNote: Dill takes a light frost of −1 to −2 °C without much harm — seedlings sown in early spring come through several — but a hard frost blackens the foliage and ends it. The evening before a hard frost, cut the remaining fronds for the freezer and any brown seed heads into a paper bag. Leave a few heads standing: the seed that falls now is next year’s first dill, up in April before you could have sown it.
temperate.ready: Leaves (dill weed) from the time the plant is 20 cm tall until the flower stalk starts to rise, with the flavour at its best just as the first flower buds open — after that the plant puts everything into seed. Heads for pickling at the stage most recipes mean: the flowers finished, the seeds formed but still green and soft, the head flat and flexible. Seed for the jar or next year when the heads turn tan-brown and the seeds come off at a touch, about two or three weeks after flowering.
temperate.pick: Snip fronds from the outside of the plant in the morning. For pickle heads cut a 20–30 cm length of stalk with the umbel on it. For seed, cut the heads a little before they are fully brown — the ripe seed falls off at a shake — and hang them upside down inside a paper bag with a few holes in it in a warm, airy room for one to two weeks, then shake the bag. Umbels ripen at different times on one plant, so go over it twice.

store.keeps: 3–5 days for fronds; a week for heads
store.how: Stems in a jar of water with a bag over the top, or fronds rolled in a damp towel inside a bag.

store.keeps: A year for flavour, longer for sowing
store.how: Fully dry seed in a sealed jar out of the light.

temperate.preserveNote: Dill weed freezes: chop the fronds and pack them into ice-cube trays with water, or wrap three or four whole stems in plastic and foil and freeze them for snipping. It darkens a little and loses a touch of flavour frozen, and a great deal more dried — dill weed has enough moisture to mould in a bunch and most of its flavour is in oils that go in the drying, so dry it only on screens, fast, and expect a shadow of the fresh herb. The seed, on the other hand, dries perfectly in a paper bag and keeps a year in a jar. The famous use is the dill pickle, which is a water-bath pickle made by a tested recipe with 5 % vinegar and the dill head added at the amount given; dill is a flavouring there, and the vinegar does the preserving. Dill in oil is subject to the same rule as every herb in oil: refrigerate four days or freeze.

seeds.how: Dill is the easiest seed in the garden to save because it saves itself: let a few heads ripen and shatter and you will have volunteers forever. For a jar of seed, cut heads as they go brown, dry them upside down in a paper bag, shake, and winnow the chaff. It is an annual, insect-pollinated, and different dill varieties (Bouquet, Mammoth, Dukat, Fernleaf) cross with each other if they flower together — grow one variety for seed, or accept a mix. Whether dill crosses with fennel is argued over; keep them apart if you are saving either.
seeds.viability: 3–5 years, stored cool and dry.

temperate.nextYear: Direct sow — dill has a taproot and sulks when transplanted — a week or two before the last frost, 5 mm deep in full sun, and again every two to three weeks until midsummer for a steady supply of fronds. For pickle heads, sow a batch the week you plant the cucumbers: dill takes about eight to ten weeks from sowing to flower heads, which lines the heads up with the cucumber flush in August. Thin to 15–30 cm, do not feed it much, and let the last patch of the year self-sow where you want dill next spring. It is in the carrot family, so keep it out of the beds where carrots, parsnips, parsley and cilantro grew last year. Black swallowtail caterpillars eat dill; sow enough to share. In zones 3–4 it does everything it does elsewhere, a fortnight later.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 1–2 weeks before the last frost, then every 2–3 weeks until midsummer; it hates transplanting.

faqs.q: When do you harvest dill heads for pickles?
faqs.a: When the yellow flowers have finished and the seeds have formed but are still green and soft, with the head flat and flexible rather than brown and brittle — usually two weeks after flowering. That is the stage the tested pickle recipes mean by a ‘dill head’. If your cucumbers are ready and the dill is not, use the fronds plus a teaspoon of dill seed per jar from last year’s harvest.

faqs.q: How do you harvest and dry dill seed?
faqs.a: Cut the heads when they turn tan and the first seeds come off at a touch — a little early is better than losing them to the wind. Hang the heads upside down inside a paper bag with air holes in a warm room for one to two weeks, then shake the bag and winnow off the chaff. Store the seed in a jar; it keeps a year for cooking and three to five for sowing.

faqs.q: Can you freeze dill?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is better than drying it. Chop the fronds into ice-cube trays with water and top up, or wrap small bundles of whole stems in plastic and foil and snip from them frozen. The colour darkens a little but the flavour holds well in anything cooked. Add dill at the end of cooking either way; heat drives the flavour off.

faqs.q: Can you dry dill?
faqs.a: The seed, perfectly; the leaves, poorly. Dill weed holds a lot of water and moulds in a hanging bunch, and the flavour is in oils that evaporate as it dries, so dried dill weed is faint at best. If you must, dry it fast in a thin layer on a screen or in a dehydrator under 45 °C. Otherwise freeze the fronds and dry the heads.

faqs.q: Does dill come back every year?
faqs.a: The plant is an annual and dies with the hard frosts, but it self-sows so reliably that most gardens have dill forever once they have had it once. Leave a few heads to ripen and shatter in September; the seedlings come up in April, weeks before you could have sown them, and they are the best dill of the year. Pull the ones you do not want.

faqs.q: Is dill frost hardy?
faqs.a: Half-way. Seedlings sown before the last frost come through light frosts, and in autumn the plant takes −1 to −2 °C without much damage; a hard frost blackens it. Dill does not need covering — cut the last fronds for the freezer and the brown heads for seed the evening before a hard frost and let the rest go.

faqs.q: Is dill safe for kids in the garden?
faqs.a: Yes — the whole plant is edible, the flowers included, and a child who chews a few green dill seeds has found one of the garden’s best snacks. The thing to look for together is the black swallowtail caterpillar, green with black and yellow bands, which eats dill, parsley and carrot tops: plant enough to share and watch it turn into a butterfly in the fall rather than pulling it off.

temperate.name: Parsley
temperate.tagline: The herb that stands green through the first snows — and the one that is worthless dried.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it. Parsley shrugs off frost, keeps growing into November, and tastes exactly the same after a freeze; it is usually the last green thing standing in the bed. Before the ground freezes, cut a big batch for the freezer, then cover the crowns with 10–15 cm of straw or leaves. In zone 5, and often in zone 4 under snow, it comes back in April and gives a few weeks of early leaves before it bolts. Or pot one up for the kitchen windowsill, where it sulks but survives.
temperate.ready: When the plant has 20 cm stalks with three or more full leaf segments, about 70–90 days from sowing. The outer stalks are the ones to take; the centre keeps producing. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley has the stronger flavour for cooking; curly holds up better as a garnish and in the cold.
temperate.pick: Cut outer stalks at the base, close to the crown, leaving the inner ones to grow on; never shear the whole plant to a stub in midsummer. Pick in the morning. In October cut it back by a third for the freezer and leave the rest to stand.

store.how: Stand the bunch in a jar of water with a loose bag over the top, or roll it in a damp towel inside a bag.
In a glass of water like flowers.

store.keeps: Through November in most years; through winter to a spring flush in zone 5
store.how: Pick as needed until it is buried; then straw or leaves 10–15 cm deep over the crowns.

temperate.preserveNote: Freeze it: chop the leaves, pack them into ice-cube trays, top up with water (or a little oil) and bag the cubes; or chop and freeze flat in a bag so you can break off what you need; or freeze whole sprigs in a bag for soup. Thawed parsley is limp, so it is a cooking herb from the freezer, not a garnish. Drying is the method that does not work — parsley loses most of its flavour dried, and the brittle green dust in the jar tastes of nothing — though if you insist, do it fast under 45 °C in a thin layer. Parsley in oil follows the herbs-in-oil rule: four days in the fridge, or frozen.

seeds.how: Parsley flowers in its second year, in June, from a crown that overwintered; the seed ripens on the umbels in late summer and is gathered when the heads turn brown, dried in a paper bag, and rubbed out. It is insect-pollinated and different parsleys (curly, flat, Hamburg root) cross if they flower together, so let only one kind go to seed in a season. Second-year leaves are bitter, so a seed plant is a seed plant, not a kitchen plant. Sowing the seed is the hard part: it germinates slowly and unevenly, two to five weeks, and old seed worse than fresh — soak it in warm water for 24 hours before sowing, and sow more than you need.
seeds.viability: Short: 1–3 years. Use fresh seed and soak it.

temperate.nextYear: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost after a 24-hour soak, and transplant young — it has a taproot and resents being moved once it is big — or direct sow two to three weeks before the last frost and be patient for a month. Full sun or light shade, rich moist soil, 20–30 cm apart, and water in drought; it is unfussy once up. It is in the carrot family, so rotate it away from last year’s carrot, parsnip, dill and cilantro beds. Leave one overwintered plant to flower in June: the umbels feed hoverflies and parasitic wasps that work the rest of the garden, and the seed sows itself. Black swallowtail caterpillars will find it; plant enough for both of you. In zones 3–4 start it indoors and expect the fall mulch to work in some winters and not others.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost after a 24-hour soak; expect 3–5 weeks to germinate.

faqs.q: Is parsley frost hardy?
faqs.a: Yes. It takes repeated frosts without damage, stays green and usable into November in most of southern Canada, and tastes the same after a freeze. Nothing to cover on a frost night. Mulch the crowns with straw before the ground freezes and in zone 5 — often zone 4 under snow — it comes back for a spring flush before bolting.

faqs.q: Does parsley come back every year?
faqs.a: Once, sort of. Parsley is a biennial: the plant that overwinters comes back in April, gives three or four weeks of leaves, then throws up a flower stalk in June and the leaves turn bitter. Treat it as a new sowing every spring and the overwintered plants as a bonus — and as the seed and insect plants for the garden.

faqs.q: Why is my parsley seed not germinating?
faqs.a: It is slow, not dead: parsley takes two to five weeks to come up and old seed longer and worse. Soak the seed in warm water for 24 hours before sowing, keep the soil evenly moist the whole time (a board over the row helps outdoors), and use seed less than two years old. Starting it indoors under lights six to eight weeks before the last frost gets around most of the trouble.

faqs.q: Can you freeze parsley?
faqs.a: Yes — it is the right way to keep it. Chop it into ice-cube trays with water and bag the cubes, or chop and freeze flat in a bag to break pieces off, or freeze whole sprigs for the stock pot. It comes out limp and dark green but tastes right in anything cooked. Not for garnish.

faqs.q: Can you dry parsley?
faqs.a: You can, and it is not worth it: most of parsley’s flavour goes with the water, and dried parsley is green dust. The herbs that dry well are the woody ones — thyme, oregano, sage, rosemary. Freeze parsley instead.

faqs.q: How do you save parsley seed?
faqs.a: From a plant that has overwintered: it flowers in June of its second year and the seed browns on the umbels in August. Cut the heads when brown, dry them in a paper bag, rub the seed out and store it cool and dry — and use it within a year or two, because parsley seed does not keep. Let only one kind of parsley flower at a time, or they cross.

faqs.q: What is eating my parsley, and is it safe for kids?
faqs.a: If it is a fat green caterpillar with black and yellow bands, it is a black swallowtail, and the best thing you can do is leave it, plant more parsley, and watch for the butterfly. The parsley itself is safe to pick and eat raw; the one thing to teach is that parsley, carrot, dill and cilantro have wild look-alikes in the ditch that are not safe, so garden parsley is the only parsley a child picks.

temperate.name: Cilantro (coriander)
temperate.tagline: Leaves in the cool months, seed in the heat: cilantro bolts the moment summer arrives, and that is the second harvest.
temperate.frostNote: Leave it. Autumn cilantro is the best of the year: the plants take light frosts down to about −3 °C and keep making leaves through October, with none of the bolting that ruins a July sowing. Before a hard freeze, cut what is left for the freezer and cut any seed heads that are still ripening into a paper bag. Seed that has already fallen will come up on its own in spring.
temperate.ready: Leaves when the plant is 10–15 cm tall, while the leaves are still broad and flat and before the central stem starts to stretch — once the stem rises and the new leaves go thin and ferny, the plant is bolting and the leaf flavour fades. In warm weather that happens within four to six weeks of sowing, which is why cilantro is sown little and often. Seed (coriander) when the round heads turn brown and the seeds smell warm and citrusy rather than green, two or three weeks after the white flowers.
temperate.pick: Snip outer leaves, or cut the whole plant 3 cm above the crown and let it regrow once or twice. For seed, cut whole heads when half of them have browned, before they shatter, and dry them upside down in a paper bag for a week; rub the heads between your hands and winnow. Whole coriander keeps far better than ground.

store.how: Stems in a jar of water with a loose bag over the top; change the water every two days. A bunch in a damp towel in a bag lasts about as long.
Fully dry seed in a sealed jar; grind as you need it.

temperate.preserveNote: The leaves freeze and do not dry. Chop them into ice-cube trays with water or a little oil (oil cubes stay frozen until the day they are used), or freeze whole washed sprigs in a bag; thawed cilantro is limp but tastes like itself in salsa, soup and curry. Dried cilantro leaf has almost no flavour at all, so there is no point. The seed is the opposite: dry it fully on the plant or in a paper bag and it keeps a year or more whole, toasted and ground as you go. Fresh cilantro goes into canned salsa only in the amount the tested recipe gives — the herbs are low-acid ingredients and the recipe’s proportions are what make the jar safe — and never stirred into a jar after processing.

seeds.how: This is the one herb where saving seed and harvesting the crop are the same job. Let the plants flower, wait for the heads to brown, cut them into a paper bag, dry a week, rub out the seed and winnow. Cilantro is an annual, insect-pollinated, and crosses only with other cilantro — grow one variety if you want the slow-bolt trait kept — and it self-sows so freely that an August patch left to shatter is next year’s May crop. Keep the kitchen seed and the sowing seed in the same jar; they are the same thing.
seeds.viability: About 5 years, stored cool and dry.

temperate.nextYear: Treat it as a cool-season crop and stop fighting the bolting. Direct sow (it has a taproot) two to three weeks before the last frost and every two to three weeks until early June; skip high summer, when a sowing goes to flower in a month whatever you do; then sow again from early August for the fall crop, which is the best of the year. Slow-bolt varieties — the packet will say — buy a week or two. Light afternoon shade in summer, 15–20 cm apart, steady water. It is in the carrot family, so rotate it with the parsley, dill and carrots as a group. Leave one patch to seed itself where you want cilantro in April. In zones 3–4 the summers are cool enough that a June sowing may hold, but the spring and fall sowings are still the reliable ones.

sow.outdoors: Direct sow 2–3 weeks before the last frost, every 2–3 weeks until June, then again in August for the best fall crop.

faqs.q: Why does my cilantro bolt so fast?
faqs.a: Because it is a cool-season annual and heat and long days tell it to flower; in July a sowing can go from leaf to flower in four weeks no matter how it is watered. The answers are timing and acceptance: sow every two or three weeks in spring and again from August, pick slow-bolt varieties, give summer sowings afternoon shade — and let the bolted plants make coriander seed, which is the second crop, not a failure.

faqs.q: How do you harvest coriander seed?
faqs.a: Let the plant flower and wait two or three weeks for the round seed heads to turn brown and smell warm rather than green. Cut whole heads into a paper bag before they shatter, dry them a week, rub the heads between your hands and blow off the chaff. Store the seed whole and grind it as you need it; the same jar is next year’s sowing seed.

faqs.q: Can you freeze cilantro?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the only way to keep the leaves. Chop them into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or freeze whole sprigs flat in a bag; the thawed herb is limp but the flavour is there in salsa, soup and curry. Oil cubes must stay frozen until they are used. Dried cilantro leaf, by contrast, tastes of nothing.

faqs.q: Can you dry cilantro?
faqs.a: The seed, yes — that is coriander, and it dries perfectly on the plant or in a paper bag. The leaves, no: dried cilantro loses essentially all its flavour, which is why you never see a good jar of it. Freeze the leaves and dry the seed.

faqs.q: Is cilantro frost hardy?
faqs.a: Enough to make autumn its best season: the plants take light frosts to around −3 °C and go on producing leaves into October, and fall sowings do not bolt. A hard freeze ends it. Nothing to cover — cut the last leaves for the freezer and the seed heads for the jar the evening before a hard frost.

faqs.q: Why does cilantro taste like soap to some kids?
faqs.a: Genetics, not fussiness: a known variation in smell receptors makes the leaf taste soapy to a share of people, and no amount of exposure changes it. Let that child grow it for the coriander seed instead, which tastes different and warm, and which they can harvest, dry and grind themselves. The plant is safe to eat at every stage.

temperate.name: Thyme, oregano, sage and rosemary
temperate.latin: Thymus vulgaris, Origanum vulgare, Salvia officinalis, Salvia rosmarinus
temperate.tagline: The woody Mediterranean herbs: they dry as well as basil dries badly, and three of the four will sleep through a Canadian winter.
temperate.frostNote: Leave thyme, oregano and sage: frost does not hurt them, and sage and thyme can be picked under the snow all winter. What the frost night is for is the rosemary. It handles light frosts but not a Canadian winter — it is hardy only to about zone 8a, so no Canadian garden north of the coast keeps it outdoors — so pot it up two or three weeks before the first frost and bring it to a bright cool window, or take your last big harvest and let it go as an annual. Do not shear the hardy three after mid-September; a hard late cut pushes soft growth that winter kills.
temperate.ready: All four are at their best just before they flower, when the oils are highest: thyme and oregano in June and again in late summer, sage from about 75 days after planting with two main cuts a season, rosemary any time. Mid-morning, once the dew has dried. Take a light harvest from first-year plants and never more than a third to half of a plant at once — a fifth, for rosemary.
temperate.pick: Snip stems 10–15 cm long with scissors, cutting just above a pair of leaves so the plant branches; strip the leaves after drying, not before. For sage cut 15–20 cm from the tops of the stems. Make the last big cut of the hardy three by early to mid-September and take only sprigs after that.

store.keeps: 1–2 weeks fresh; oregano cuttings in a jar for several weeks
store.how: Dry sprigs in a bag or a jar in the door. Woody herbs keep far better than soft ones.

store.keeps: About a year before the flavour fades
store.how: Whole dried leaves in a sealed jar out of the light; crumble when you cook, not when you pack.

store.keeps: Thyme and sage can be picked all winter
store.how: Brush the snow off and snip; the leaves are leathery and fine.

temperate.preserveNote: These are the herbs that dry: tie small loose bunches and hang them upside down inside paper bags with holes punched in them, in a warm, dark, airy room for one to two weeks, or lay sprigs on screens, or run a dehydrator at 35–45 °C (95–115 °F) for a few hours. They are done when a leaf crumbles between your fingers and the stem snaps; strip the leaves and store them whole in jars, because flavour lives in the whole leaf and leaves the crumbled one. Rosemary and thyme also freeze well on the stem in a bag, and sage leaves frozen in butter are winter’s best roast-chicken butter. Herb-infused oil is the thing to be careful with: oil plus a low-acid herb is the botulism setting, so an oil you have put fresh or dried herbs or garlic into lives in the fridge for four days or in the freezer, never on the shelf. Herb vinegars are acid and are safe on the shelf. What does not work: drying in the sun, in a hot oven, or anywhere over 45 °C, which drives off the oils you were trying to keep.

seeds.how: These are grown from cuttings and divisions, not seed: thyme and oregano from seed are variable and seed-grown oregano is often bland, and rosemary cultivars do not come true. Take 10–15 cm softwood tip cuttings from flower-free shoots in late spring or early summer, strip the lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, set them in damp perlite or a gritty mix under a plastic bag out of direct sun, and they root in two to four weeks — ten to twenty days for rosemary with bottom heat. Divide clumps of thyme and oregano in early spring as growth starts; layer or divide sage, which is short-lived and worth replacing every three to five years. Cut old woody thyme back hard in spring every few years to renew it.
seeds.viability: Not from seed in practice. June cuttings are garden plants by autumn; sage is the one worth sowing if you must, 6–8 weeks before the last frost.

temperate.nextYear: They want the opposite of the vegetable garden: full sun, lean soil, and sharp drainage above all — wet feet in winter, not cold, is what kills a Mediterranean herb in Canada, so a raised bed, a slope, a gravel mulch instead of wet leaves. No rich compost, no fertiliser to speak of. Thyme and sage are reliably hardy to zone 5 (sage to zone 4), and oregano is marginal in zone 5 without a winter mulch; all three usually make it through zone 4 with snow or a winter mulch of evergreen boughs laid on after the ground freezes and lifted in April; Greek oregano and ‘Profusion’ are the hardy, flavourful oreganos, and thyme varieties vary, so buy ones labelled hardy. Leave the winter-browned tips on until new growth shows in spring, then cut them back. Rosemary is a zone 7–8 plant (‘Arp’ and ‘Madeline Hill’ to zone 6 with shelter), so grow it in a pot of gritty mix that comes indoors to a cool bright window before the first frost, watered sparingly — or buy a new one each May. In zones 3–4 thyme and oregano under snow are usually fine, sage is a gamble, and rosemary is a houseplant.

sow.outdoors: Set out plants or rooted cuttings after the last frost; divide thyme and oregano as growth starts in April.

faqs.q: Does rosemary survive winter in Canada?
faqs.a: Not outdoors, except on the mildest parts of the coast. Rosemary is hardy to zone 7 or 8 (the toughest cultivars, ‘Arp’ and ‘Madeline Hill’, to zone 6 with shelter), so in the rest of the country it is a pot plant: bring it to a cool, bright window two or three weeks before the first frost, water sparingly, and expect it to sulk until spring. Many gardeners simply buy a new plant each May and dry the old one in September.

faqs.q: How do you dry thyme, oregano and sage?
faqs.a: Cut stems just before flowering, tie them in small loose bunches and hang them upside down inside paper bags with a few holes in a warm, dark, airy place for one to two weeks — or on screens, or in a dehydrator at 35–45 °C. They are dry when a leaf crumbles and a stem snaps. Strip the leaves, store them whole in sealed jars out of the light, and crumble them as you cook. They keep a year.

faqs.q: When do you harvest thyme, oregano and sage?
faqs.a: Any time for a sprig, but for drying cut them just before they flower, when the oils are strongest — June and again in late summer for thyme and oregano, two main cuts a season for sage. Mid-morning after the dew dries. Take no more than a third to half of the plant, go lightly on first-year plants, and make the last big cut by early to mid-September so the plant hardens before winter.

faqs.q: Can you freeze rosemary and thyme?
faqs.a: Yes: whole sprigs in a freezer bag, snipped off frozen as you need them, keep their flavour well, and sage leaves chopped into softened butter and frozen in a log are better than dried sage for roasts and stuffing. Freezing is the alternative, not the improvement — these are the herbs that genuinely dry well, so dry the bulk and freeze a bag for convenience.

faqs.q: Is herb-infused oil safe to keep?
faqs.a: Only in the fridge for up to four days, or in the freezer. Oil keeps air away from the herbs and garlic, which are low-acid, and that is the setting in which botulism bacteria grow without any smell or sign; dried herbs in oil are no safer than fresh. The shelf-stable versions in shops are acidified by a process you cannot copy at home. Herb vinegars are acid and keep safely on the shelf.

faqs.q: How do you winter thyme, oregano and sage?
faqs.a: Drainage first: they die of wet roots far more often than of cold, so plant them in a raised or sloping bed with a gravel mulch rather than wet leaves. Stop hard cutting by mid-September. After the ground freezes, lay evergreen boughs or straw over oregano and thyme in zones 4–5 and lift it in April. Leave the browned tips on until new growth shows in spring, then cut back. Sage is short-lived; replace it every three to five years from cuttings.

faqs.q: What can kids do with these herbs?
faqs.a: Rub a leaf of each between their fingers and name the smell — pizza (oregano), stuffing (sage), roast potatoes (rosemary), and thyme, which smells like all of them — and all four are safe to taste straight from the plant. Children are good at the two jobs that matter: stripping dried leaves off stems into a bowl, and tying the bunches. Sage leaves are furry and a favourite to stroke; a bee on a thyme flower in June is the first bee most kids watch up close.

world.name: Cassava
world.tagline: The root that feeds much of tropical Africa — generous in poor soil and drought, and never to be eaten raw.
world.frostNote: Cassava needs eight to eleven frost-free months to make usable roots, and frost kills the leaves and stems at 0 °C. Near the cold edge of its range — the KwaZulu-Natal interior, high ground in East Africa, northern Florida — a plant cut back by frost may resprout from the base, but it loses months of growth. There is nothing worth covering: if a hard frost is forecast and the roots are a useful size, lift what you need.
world.ready: Most cultivars are ready 9–12 months after planting, and some take 15–18 months. There is no single ripe day: the lower leaves yellow and drop as the plant matures, and scraping the soil from the base of one plant shows whether the roots have filled out. Roots can be left in the ground for months past maturity and dug as needed, which is why cassava is grown as a food reserve, though roots left too long turn woody.
world.pick: Cut the stems back to knee height, keeping the best mature stems for planting, then loosen the soil around the plant with a fork and lever it out by the stump so the roots come up whole. A snapped root starts to spoil at the break. Lift only what you can peel and process within a day or two: roots begin to deteriorate within 2–3 days of harvest, and lose quality within 24–48 hours.

store.how: Leave plants standing and dig to order — the traditional store across Africa. Lift before the roots turn woody.
Unwashed, out of the sun. Fresh roots discolour inside and spoil within 2–3 days; peel and process or cook them the day they are dug.

store.where: Moist sawdust, lined pit or refrigerator
store.how: Improved storage — packing sound roots in moist sawdust or a lined pit, refrigerating them, or waxing them — extends their life to between two and six weeks.

world.preserveNote: Cassava is preserved by processing rather than by putting fresh roots in jars, and the same processing is what makes it safe. Every cassava root contains cyanogenic glycosides, chiefly linamarin, which release hydrogen cyanide when the tissue is broken; they are concentrated in the peel and outer layers, bitter cultivars carry far more than sweet ones, and bitterness is not a reliable guide to toxicity. So every cassava is peeled, and bitter cassava must also be soaked, grated or fermented and then cooked — it is never eaten raw. The traditional products do exactly that: grating and pressing for gari breaks down more than 95% of the toxin within three hours, and soaking for six days then grating and fermenting the mash for four removes about 98%. For flour, the tested wetting method is to mix peeled, ground cassava flour with water at 1 part flour to 1.25 parts water by weight, spread it no more than 1 cm thick and leave it 5 hours at 30 °C. Boiling, steaming, baking or frying on their own remove only 10–75% and are not reliable for bitter roots. Sweet cassava for boiling should be peeled, cut up and started in cold water, with the water thrown away: in FAO trials, 30 minutes’ cooking from cold left 8% of the cyanide, against about 30% when the pieces went straight into boiling water. Short sun-drying of fresh chips removes only 60–70%, so chips and flour are made from soaked or fermented roots. There is no tested home-canning process for cassava.

seeds.how: Cassava is grown from stem cuttings, not seed. Take stems from healthy, mature plants 10–12 months old and cut them into 25 cm lengths with 5–7 nodes. Plant them upright where rainfall is high, or laid flat in dry areas, with the buds pointing up. Take cuttings only from vigorous plants free of leaf mottling and root streaking: cassava’s virus diseases travel in the stems, and a farmer’s own sick cuttings are how they spread.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — the variety lives in the stems. Plant cuttings from freshly cut mature stems.

world.nextYear: Cassava grows on land too poor or dry for most crops, but it takes a great deal from the soil, so follow it with a legume — groundnuts or cowpeas — or a fallow, and add compost where you can. Plant at the start of the rains, when at least two months of good soil moisture lie ahead: March–May in southern Nigeria and Ghana, May–June in the savanna, with the long rains in March–April or the short rains in October–November in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, and from October to December on the KwaZulu-Natal and Mozambique coast. Space plants about 1 m apart each way. It needs 8–11 frost-free months and does poorly above about 2,000 m or where the monthly mean falls much below 18 °C, so Nairobi-height gardens grow it slowly. Grow sweet cultivars for the garden and the kitchen, and learn which cultivars your neighbours plant before you take cuttings: bitter ones look the same.

sow.outdoors: Plant 25 cm stem cuttings at the start of the rains, when at least two months of moist soil are expected; in frost climates only after nights stay above 15 °C, and only where 8–11 frost-free months follow.

faqs.q: Can you eat cassava raw?
faqs.a: No. All cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides that release hydrogen cyanide, mostly in the peel and outer layers, and bitter cultivars carry far more than sweet ones. Sweet cassava must be peeled and thoroughly cooked; bitter cassava must be peeled and then soaked, grated or fermented — as gari and fufu are — before cooking. Bitterness is not a reliable test of how toxic a root is.

faqs.q: What is the difference between sweet and bitter cassava?
faqs.a: The amount of cyanogenic glycoside: sweet cultivars contain only small amounts and can be peeled and boiled, while bitter cultivars, often planted as a high-yielding food reserve, need full processing. Root content ranges from about 15 to 400 mg of hydrogen cyanide per kilogram. You cannot tell the two apart reliably by taste or appearance, so know your cultivar.

faqs.q: How do you remove cyanide from cassava at home?
faqs.a: Peel it, then use a method that breaks the tissue and lets the toxin escape: grate and press it (gari), soak it for days and ferment the mash (fufu), or for flour use the wetting method — 1 part flour to 1.25 parts water by weight, spread 1 cm thick, left 5 hours at 30 °C. For sweet cassava, boil peeled pieces from cold water and discard the water. Boiling alone is not enough for bitter cassava.

faqs.q: Can you eat cassava leaves?
faqs.a: Yes, and they are richer in protein and vitamins than the roots, but they contain even more cyanogenic glycoside and must never be eaten raw. Pound them for at least 10 minutes and wash them in twice their weight of water, or boil them well for 15–30 minutes and discard the water, before cooking into a stew such as saka-saka or matapa.

faqs.q: Is cassava safe for children?
faqs.a: Properly processed cassava is a safe staple, but children and women are the people most affected by konzo, the spastic paralysis of the legs that has broken out in drought years when bitter cassava was eaten under-processed and without enough protein alongside it. Never let children chew raw roots or leaves, never shorten soaking or fermenting times, and serve cassava with beans, fish or groundnuts.

faqs.q: How long does cassava keep after digging?
faqs.a: Only a day or two. Fresh roots start to deteriorate within 2–3 days and discolour inside, so lift only what you can peel and cook or process the same day. Packing in moist sawdust or refrigeration extends that to two to six weeks; the best store is the ground itself.

world.name: Sweet potatoes
world.tagline: Grown from slips, cured in the warmth, kept in a cupboard — and the leaves are a hot-season green in their own right.
world.frostNote: The vines blacken at the first frost, and the roots underneath are sensitive well before that: sweet potatoes are chill-damaged below about 10 °C, and roots that sit in cold soil store badly. Dig immediately before or just after a vine-killing frost; in a cold autumn, do not wait for the frost at all — lift once the nights head towards 10 °C.
world.ready: Most varieties need at least 120 days from planting the slips, and can be left to 150 if the weather allows; Ontario growers count 100–130 days. Dig one plant as a test, and lift the crop once the roots have reached a useful size. In the tropics, where the plants never stop, dig the whole crop rather than leaving it in for months: old roots toughen, and pests build up in a planting left too long.
world.pick: Cut the vines away first, then dig with a fork from well outside the plant and lift rather than lever: the skin is thin, and every cut or bruise is an entry for rot. Handle the roots as little as possible. The young leaves and shoot tips can be picked all season as a cooked green; take a few from each plant rather than stripping one.
world.cure: Curing heals small wounds, sets the skin and converts starch to sugar — a sweet potato eaten the day it is dug is starchy and bland. Hold the roots for about a week at 27–29 °C (80–85 °F) and 90–95% relative humidity; UF/IFAS gives a warmer cure of about 35 °C (95 °F) and 90% humidity for around ten days. A warm shed with the roots in boxes under damp sacking does the job in a tropical or Mediterranean autumn; in Canada, a small room with a heater and a pan of water.

store.where: Cool cupboard, pantry or basement corner
store.how: In crates or paper-lined boxes, off the floor, in the dark, at 85–90% humidity. Below 13 °C (55 °F) the flesh discolours and develops an off flavour; above 16 °C the roots sprout. Never refrigerate them.

world.preserveNote: A cured sweet potato kept at 13–16 °C lasts four to six months, which is preservation enough for most households. For the freezer, cook them first — boiled, steamed, pressure-cooked or baked until almost tender — then cool, peel, and halve, slice or mash; dip slices for 5 seconds in 125 ml (½ cup) of lemon juice per litre (quart) of water, or stir 2 tablespoons of lemon or orange juice into each litre (quart) of mash, to stop darkening. Pressure canning works for pieces only: boil or steam them 15–20 minutes until partly soft, peel, cut into even pieces, pack with 2.5 cm (1 in) headspace in boiling water or syrup, and process 65 minutes for 500 ml (pint) jars or 90 minutes for litre (quart) jars at 10 lb in a weighted-gauge canner at 0–300 m (0–1,000 ft). What does not work: mashing or puréeing before canning, which the USDA guide forbids because the dense mass will not heat through; dry-packing pieces without liquid; and any water-bath method, since sweet potato is a low-acid vegetable.

seeds.how: Sweet potatoes are grown from slips — leafy shoots that sprout from a stored root — not from seed. Keep a few sound, medium-sized cured roots, and a few weeks before planting time bed them half-buried in moist sand somewhere warm and bright. Snap or cut the sprouts off when they are 20–30 cm long with at least four nodes, and plant them with two nodes below ground. Vine-tip cuttings from a growing crop root just as easily, which is how gardeners in the tropics keep a planting going season after season. Where sweet potato weevil or virus is a problem, start again from certified clean slips rather than your own.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — the variety is carried in the roots and vines. A cured root kept at 13–16 °C stays sound for slipping until the next planting season.

world.nextYear: Rotate: at least two years away from the same bed, to keep sweet potato weevil and nematodes down. Full sun, light sandy or sandy-loam soil, ridges or hills about 15 cm high and 40 cm wide, and go easy on fertiliser — too much feeds the vine and stops roots forming. Plant slips 30–40 cm apart in rows about a metre apart once the soil holds above 18 °C. In the tropics plant at the start of the rains, or at any time with irrigation; in Kenya and Uganda with the long rains (March–April) or the short rains (October–November); in summer-rainfall southern Africa from October to December; in the Mediterranean once the soil warms in May. Water steadily for the first four to six weeks and then less: drought in the last month splits the roots. In Canada and Britain, choose a short-season variety such as Beauregard, warm the soil with black plastic and plant after the last frost.

sow.outdoors: Plant slips at the start of the rains, or once the soil holds above 18 °C; in cold-winter countries after the last frost, into soil warmed under black plastic.

faqs.q: When are sweet potatoes ready to dig?
faqs.a: About 120 days after planting the slips for most varieties, and up to 150 if the season allows — dig one plant to check. In Canada lift them in September or early October, immediately before or just after the first frost blackens the vines, and before the soil turns cold, because roots are chill-damaged below about 10 °C.

faqs.q: Why do you have to cure sweet potatoes?
faqs.a: Because a freshly dug sweet potato is starchy and bland and its thin skin is easily infected. About a week at 27–29 °C and 90–95% humidity heals cuts, sets the skin and converts starch to sugar; after that the roots keep four to six months at 13–16 °C.

faqs.q: Should sweet potatoes go in the fridge?
faqs.a: No. Below 13 °C (55 °F) the flesh discolours and develops an off flavour, and chilled roots rot sooner. A cool, dark cupboard or basement corner at 13–16 °C is the right place for cured roots.

faqs.q: Can you eat sweet potato leaves?
faqs.a: Yes. The young leaves and shoot tips are a mild cooked green that keeps coming through the hot season while the roots grow — a common vegetable in East Africa and Southeast Asia. Pick a few tips from each plant rather than stripping one, because the leaves are what feed the roots.

faqs.q: Can I grow sweet potatoes in Ontario or the UK?
faqs.a: Yes, with a short-season variety and the warmest spot you have. Ontario growers plant Beauregard and Covington slips in late May or early June into soil above 18 °C and dig in September and October. The RHS notes that sweet potatoes crop best at 21–26 °C and only reliably outdoors in very warm, sheltered sites, so in Britain a greenhouse or polytunnel is safer.

faqs.q: Can you can mashed sweet potatoes?
faqs.a: No. The tested method is for pieces only — pressure-canned 65 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge near sea level — and the USDA guide warns not to mash or purée them first. Freeze mash instead, with 2 tablespoons of lemon or orange juice per litre to hold the colour.

world.name: Okra
world.tagline: West Africa’s gift to the soup pot — a pod to pick every second day, small, before it turns to wood.
world.frostNote: Okra is finished by frost and sulks long before it: it needs temperatures above about 20 °C for normal growth, and its pods are cold-sensitive. When a frost is forecast, pick every pod worth having that evening; covering the plants late in the season buys nothing.
world.ready: Pods are picked young — about a week after the flower opens, when they are 5–8 cm (2–3 in) long for most varieties and no more than about 12 cm for long-podded types. A ready pod snaps cleanly at the tip and a knife slides through it easily; once it resists the knife it has gone fibrous.
world.pick: Cut the stalk just above the cap with secateurs or a sharp knife — the stems are tough, and pulling tears the plant. Pick every two days in hot weather, daily at the peak, and take any pod you missed: plants left carrying old pods slow down. Wear long sleeves and gloves, because the fine hairs on the leaves, stems and pods irritate skin.

store.where: Cool room or the warmest shelf of the fridge
store.how: Unwashed and dry, in a paper bag inside a perforated plastic one. The pods are cold-sensitive, so keep them out of the coldest part of the fridge; commercial storage is 8–10 °C at 90–100% humidity. In a household fridge, use them within the week.

world.preserveNote: Freezing is the easiest: trim the stems without opening the seed cells, water-blanch pods up to 10 cm for 3 minutes and larger ones for 4, cool, and freeze whole or sliced; for frying, slice after blanching, dredge in meal or flour and tray-freeze before bagging. Pickled dilled okra is a tested water-bath recipe — 3.2 kg (7 lb) of small pods to 1.4 L (6 cups) each of water and 5% vinegar with 160 ml (⅔ cup) of pickling salt, garlic, dill seed and small hot peppers, processed 10 minutes for 500 ml (pint) jars at 0–300 m. Drying is the West African way: whole or sliced pods are sun-dried and usually ground to a powder that thickens soup through the dry season. Plain okra can be pressure-canned — boil 2 minutes, pack hot with 2.5 cm headspace and process 25 minutes for 500 ml jars or 40 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge — but it comes out soft, and there is no safe water-bath method for unpickled okra.

seeds.how: Okra is basically self-pollinating, which makes it a good first seed crop, though bees do carry some pollen between plants; Seed Savers Exchange advises 150–500 m (500–1,600 ft) between varieties for purity. Leave a few of the best early pods on the plant until they turn brown and brittle — about a month after flowering — clipping them as they ripen from the bottom of the plant upward, and finish drying them under cover. Crack them open by hand, or snip off the stem end and pour the seed out; gloves help, because dry pods are spiny. West African farmers often keep the seed in the dried pod until sowing time.
seeds.viability: 1–3 years cool, dark and dry. Okra seed is short-lived, so save a little every year.

world.nextYear: Rotate where root-knot nematode is about — okra is highly susceptible, and moving it each year keeps numbers down. Full sun, well-drained soil with plenty of organic matter at pH 6–7, and steady water: okra survives drought but crops far better watered. Soak seed for six hours before sowing and sow 1–2 cm deep when the soil is above 20 °C; germination is fastest at 30–35 °C. In West Africa sow with the rains, and again in the dry season where there is water; in East Africa with the long rains in March–April or the short rains in October; in summer-rainfall southern Africa from October to January; around the Mediterranean from May, once the nights are warm. Thin to 30–45 cm apart in rows about 90 cm apart; a balanced, slow-release fertiliser is enough.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct once the soil is above 20 °C — with the rains in the tropics; in cold-winter countries transplant two to three weeks after the last frost, into soil warmed under black plastic.

faqs.q: Can I grow okra in Toronto?
faqs.a: Yes, in a warm summer and as a transplant. Ontario trials show okra starts cropping 40–50 days after transplanting and keeps going until frost if it goes into soil above 20 °C, ideally through black plastic mulch. Start seed indoors in pots about four weeks before planting out, harden the plants off, and set them out two or three weeks after the last frost in the warmest bed you have, with a variety such as Clemson Spineless or Annie Oakley II.

faqs.q: How big should okra be when you pick it?
faqs.a: Small — about 5–8 cm (2–3 in) for most varieties, a few days after the flower petals fall. If a knife will not slide through the pod easily, it is too old to eat; leave it for seed or the compost.

faqs.q: Can you eat okra leaves?
faqs.a: Yes. Young okra leaves are cooked like spinach in many parts of Africa, and the pods are only half the crop. Pick a few young leaves from each plant rather than stripping one, since the leaves feed the pods.

faqs.q: How do you freeze okra?
faqs.a: Trim the stems without cutting into the seed cells, water-blanch small pods for 3 minutes and large ones for 4, cool in iced water, drain, and freeze whole or sliced with 1 cm headspace. For frying later, slice after blanching, coat in cornmeal or flour, freeze on a tray and bag once firm.

faqs.q: Why does okra make my skin itch?
faqs.a: The leaves, stems and pods carry fine hairs that irritate skin, especially in the heat of a picking session. Wear long sleeves and rubber gloves and cut with shears; spineless varieties such as Clemson Spineless are easier to handle.

faqs.q: How do I save okra seeds?
faqs.a: Leave a few early pods to grow on until they are brown and brittle, about a month after flowering, then dry them further under cover and break them open. Okra is mostly self-pollinated, but keep varieties 150 m or more apart for pure seed. Seed keeps one to three years.

world.name: Leaf amaranth
world.latin: Amaranthus cruentus, A. dubius, A. tricolor
world.tagline: Morogo, efo tete, mchicha, callaloo — the hot-weather spinach of Africa, ready to cut a month after sowing.
world.frostNote: Amaranth is frost-sensitive and slows well before frost, growing best with days above 25 °C and nights no lower than 15 °C. Cut or pull the whole planting before the first frost and blanch the surplus for the freezer; covering it is not worth the trouble.
world.ready: Ready to eat from three to five weeks after sowing: direct-sown crops are pulled whole at that stage, and transplanted market crops are uprooted 20–30 days after planting out. Cut while the stems are still soft enough to snap and before the flower heads show. Once a plant flowers — four to eight weeks after sowing, depending on variety and day length — the new leaves are smaller and tougher.
world.pick: Either pull young plants whole, roots and all, as most growers do for market, or cut them 10–15 cm above the ground, leaving at least two leaves and their buds to regrow. A widely spaced, well-fed planting can be cut every two or three weeks, up to ten times; cutting low delays flowering. Pick in the cool of the morning — uprooted bunches stay fresh for a day or two stood roots-down in a basin of water.

store.how: Unwashed, loosely bagged. Commercial storage is 0–2 °C at 95–100% humidity; it wilts in hours in dry air.
Whole uprooted plants with the roots in a basin of water, as they are kept in African markets.

world.preserveNote: Treat amaranth as you would spinach: strip the leaves and tender tips, water-blanch 2 minutes, cool, squeeze out the water and freeze flat or as pucks for stews and sauces. The traditional dry-season store is sun-dried leaf, often pounded to a powder and stirred into sauces. Greens can be pressure-canned — steamed until well wilted, packed loosely in boiling water and processed 70 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge — but the freezer gives a far better product, and there is no safe water-bath method. Like spinach, amaranth contains oxalate, and leaves grown with heavy nitrogen fertiliser can carry high nitrate, mostly in the stems; cooking in plenty of water and pouring the water away, as most African cooks do, removes much of both.

seeds.how: Amaranth is wind-pollinated and mostly self-fertilised, but up to 40% of seed can be crossed, so save from one leaf variety at a time or keep varieties well apart, and do not let weedy pigweeds flower nearby. Let a few of your best plants run to flower; the seed matures three to five months after sowing, and the plant then dies. Cut the heads on a dry morning before they shatter, dry them on a sheet, then rub and winnow out the tiny seeds — 2,500–3,500 of them to the gram. Light and warmth break the seed’s dormancy, which is why it is sown barely covered.
seeds.viability: Several years kept cool, dark and dry; sprout a pinch on damp paper before relying on older seed.

world.nextYear: Amaranth has no serious soil-borne diseases, so it does not strictly need rotating, but it is a heavy feeder that removes a lot of potassium and nitrogen: dig in plenty of manure or compost before each crop, and avoid heavy chemical nitrogen, which raises the nitrate in the leaves. Sow barely covered, in rows 20 cm apart or broadcast, once the soil is above 15 °C; seedlings are up in three to five days. In the tropics sow with the rains and again every two or three weeks; in Kenya and Tanzania it is a staple of both the long and the short rains; on the South African highveld sow from October to February; in Lagos and Accra it grows year-round with water. Water daily in dry spells — drought makes it flower early. In Canada sow outdoors from late May, or set out transplants once frost is past; it tends to bolt as the days shorten in late summer.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct, barely covered, once the soil is above 15 °C — with the rains in the tropics, and every two or three weeks for a steady supply.

faqs.q: What is morogo?
faqs.a: Morogo is the name used across much of South Africa for leafy greens, wild and cultivated, cooked as a relish to eat with pap — and amaranth is one of the most important of them. The same plants are efo tete in Yoruba, mchicha in Swahili, and callaloo or African spinach elsewhere. Several species are grown, including Amaranthus cruentus, A. dubius and A. tricolor, and all are cooked the same way.

faqs.q: How long does amaranth take to grow?
faqs.a: Three to five weeks from sowing to the first harvest of whole young plants. A widely spaced planting cut at 10–15 cm regrows and can be cut every two to three weeks for another month or two. Ontario growers give 30–60 days.

faqs.q: Can I grow leaf amaranth in Canada?
faqs.a: Yes. Ontario growers sow it outdoors in May and June, or transplant in early May, into soil around 15 °C; it grows best at 18–24 °C and is ready in 30–60 days. It is frost-sensitive and tends to bolt as the days shorten, so sow small batches every couple of weeks through June and July.

faqs.q: Does amaranth contain oxalate?
faqs.a: Yes, at levels similar to spinach, and the stems can carry nitrate if the crop has been heavily fed with nitrogen fertiliser. Cooking the leaves in plenty of water and discarding the water removes much of both, which is how amaranth is usually cooked in Africa.

faqs.q: How do you freeze amaranth leaves?
faqs.a: Strip the leaves and soft tips from the stems, water-blanch them for 2 minutes, cool in iced water, squeeze out the water and freeze in flat bags or pucks with 1 cm headspace. Use them straight from frozen in stews and sauces.

faqs.q: Is leaf amaranth the same as the pigweed in my garden?
faqs.a: They are close relatives in the same genus. Weedy pigweeds such as Amaranthus hybridus and A. spinosus are eaten young in many places, but the garden leaf amaranths have been selected for large, tender leaves. If you save seed, keep the weedy kinds from flowering nearby.
