world.name: Cowpeas
world.tagline: Leaves at four weeks, green pods at eight, dry black-eyed peas at twelve — the Sahel’s pulse, and a crop that feeds the soil.
world.frostNote: Cowpea does not tolerate frost and stops growing on cold nights; it wants nights above 15 °C. If frost threatens a late crop, pick the green pods and any dry ones that evening, or pull whole plants and hang them under cover to finish drying.
world.ready: Leaves from about four weeks after the seedlings emerge until flowering begins. Green pods 12–15 days after the flower, while the seeds are still soft and the pod snaps. For dry peas, wait until the pods have turned yellow to tan and at least two-thirds of them are dry.
world.pick: Take young shoot tips and a few leaves from each plant; picking more than 10–20% of the leaves before flowering starts to cut the pod crop. Leafy varieties can be cut back to about 10 cm to regrow. Pull green pods with a twist, holding the stem. Many varieties split and drop their seed when dry, so check dry pods every few days, or pull whole plants when most pods are mature and spread them under cover to finish.

store.where: Fridge, green pods and fresh-shelled peas
store.keeps: About a week; yard-long pods up to two
store.how: In a perforated bag. Fresh shelled cowpeas keep about 8 days at 8 °C, and yard-long bean pods 7–14 days at 4–7 °C; colder than that injures the pods.

store.where: Airtight jar or tin, dry peas
store.how: Dried until a fingernail will not dent them — below about 14% moisture — then sealed against damp and weevils.

world.preserveNote: Dry peas are the point of the crop: dried hard and kept airtight, they last for years. The leaves are dried for the dry season across Africa — whole, crumbled or powdered, or boiled, kneaded and squeezed into balls and sun-dried, as in Botswana and Zimbabwe. Fresh green-shelled peas freeze well: shell, sort out over-mature, immature and insect-damaged ones, water-blanch 2 minutes, cool and pack with 1 cm headspace. Dry peas can be pressure-canned: soak 12–18 hours, boil 30 minutes, pack with 2.5 cm headspace in the cooking water and process 75 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge. There is no water-bath method for any bean or pea, and dried cowpeas must be soaked and boiled before eating.

seeds.how: Cowpea flowers open in the morning and close by noon, and in dry climates they are almost entirely self-pollinated; in humid places insects can cross up to 40%. Seed Savers Exchange suggests just 3–6 m (10–20 ft) between varieties, so a gardener can save two kinds in one season. Leave pods on the plant until tan and dry, or pull plants when most pods are yellow and finish drying them under cover; shell, winnow, and dry the seed until a fingernail will not dent it.
seeds.viability: 3–4 years cool, dark and dry in an airtight container.

world.nextYear: Cowpea fixes its own nitrogen and can leave 75–150 kg per hectare in the soil for the next crop, so it belongs before maize, millet or a hungry leafy crop. Give it full sun, any well-drained soil, half the fertiliser of other vegetables — too much nitrogen limits pods — and keep it weeded for the first six weeks. Sow 1–2 cm deep in soil above 20 °C; seedlings appear in three to five days above 22 °C. In the West African savanna sow early in the rains for a harvest from late August to November; in East Africa with the long or short rains; in summer-rainfall southern Africa from November to January; around the Mediterranean in late spring as a summer crop. Climbing and yard-long types need stakes 2 m tall.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct once the soil is above 20 °C — early in the rains in the tropics; after the last frost elsewhere.

faqs.q: Are black-eyed peas the same as cowpeas?
faqs.a: Yes. Black-eyed peas, crowder peas, cream peas and southern field peas are all cowpeas, Vigna unguiculata, and the yard-long bean is a climbing form of the same species grown for its long green pods.

faqs.q: Can you eat cowpea leaves?
faqs.a: Yes, and across much of Africa the leaves matter as much as the peas. Pick young tips from about four weeks after the seedlings emerge until flowering, boil or fry them, and dry the surplus for the dry season. Do not take more than a fifth of the leaves if you also want a pea crop.

faqs.q: How do you freeze black-eyed peas?
faqs.a: Pick pods when the seeds are tender and well filled, shell them, discard any that are over-mature, immature or insect-damaged, water-blanch for 2 minutes, cool, drain and freeze with 1 cm headspace.

faqs.q: Do cowpeas need fertiliser?
faqs.a: Very little. Cowpea fixes nitrogen from the air through its root nodules, so give it about half the fertiliser of other vegetables — too much nitrogen gives leaves and few pods. On phosphorus-poor soil a little phosphate helps nodules and roots.

faqs.q: Can I grow cowpeas in Canada?
faqs.a: In the warmer parts of southern Canada, yes, with a short-season variety. Ontario growers sow yard-long beans directly after frost into soil above 20 °C and pick 60–80 days later; bush black-eyed types are similar. They need heat — a cool, wet summer gives a poor crop.

faqs.q: How do I save cowpea seed?
faqs.a: Leave pods on the plant until tan and dry, shell them, and dry the seed until a fingernail will not dent it. Cowpeas rarely cross, so 3–6 m between varieties is enough. Seed keeps three to four years cool and dry.

world.name: Groundnuts (peanuts)
world.tagline: Flowers above ground, nuts below — a hot-season legume that wants loose sandy soil and a dry spell to finish.
world.frostNote: Groundnuts are frost- and cold-sensitive, and growth stops when the temperature falls below about 15 °C. A frost kills the tops and stops the pods filling; if one is forecast and most pods are mature, lift the plants that day and cure them under cover.
world.ready: Pull up one plant and open a dozen pods: they are ready when the inside of most shells has turned from white to brown or blotched black and the seed coats have gone pink or tan — harvest when 60–80% of the pods look like that. Valencia types grown for boiling can be dug green from about 75 days; Spanish types take about 120 days, and runner and Virginia types 135–155.
world.pick: Loosen the soil along the row with a fork, then lift whole plants by the base and shake off the soil; pods snapped off and left in the ground are lost. Lift in dry weather, never after rain.
world.cure: Cure the whole plants before picking off the pods: pile them loosely or hang them, pods upward, in warm, dry, airy conditions for 5–10 days with no rain on them, until the pods rattle. Then pick the pods and finish drying them to about 10% moisture — shells brittle, kernels firm but not shrivelled. Fast, thorough drying is the main defence against aflatoxin, the liver-damaging poison made by Aspergillus moulds on damp groundnuts.

store.where: Cool, dry, ventilated cupboard or store, in the shell
store.how: Cured pods in mesh or cloth bags with air moving around them: ventilation stops moisture building up, which is what lets moulds and aflatoxin develop. Shell only what you will eat within a few weeks.

world.preserveNote: Drying is the method. Cured groundnuts dried to about 10% moisture and kept cool, dry and ventilated store for months. To finish them at home, dry shelled or unshelled nuts in a single layer at 54 °C (130 °F) until the shells are brittle and the kernels tender but not shrivelled; to roast, give them 150 °C (300 °F) for 30–40 minutes in the shell or 20–25 minutes shelled, stirring often. Green — freshly dug, undried — groundnuts for boiling can be pressure-canned in brine by the tested NCHFP method: three one-hour soaks in fresh water, 10 minutes’ parboiling, a brine of 1 cup of salt to 3.8 L (1 gallon) of water, then 45 minutes for 500 ml jars or 50 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge; never water-bath them. The rule that matters most is to throw away mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled nuts rather than eat or press them: aflatoxin is invisible, has been linked to liver cancer in Africa, and can contaminate small-scale, unrefined groundnut oil.

seeds.how: Groundnuts are self-pollinating, with only occasional crossing by bees, so a variety comes true. Keep the best fully mature pods from healthy plants, store them in the shell, and shell them by hand only one or two weeks before sowing; plant raw, never roasted, kernels. Spanish and Valencia types have no seed dormancy and can sprout in the ground if harvest is held up by rain, while Virginia types are dormant for one to three months.
seeds.viability: Sow the following season, from seed kept in the shell, cool and dry. Mouldy or aflatoxin-damaged seed germinates poorly and gives weak seedlings.

world.nextYear: Rotate: groundnuts in the same bed no more than one year in three, and not straight after cotton or tobacco, to limit soil-borne disease and nematodes. Deep, loose, well-drained sandy loam with calcium is what they want; on poor soil, apply gypsum beside the row once the plants flower, because the developing pods take calcium straight from the soil around them, and calcium shortage gives empty shells. Sow raw seed 4–7 cm deep, about 10 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart, into soil above 15 °C; germination is best at 25–30 °C. Keep weeds out for the first six weeks, then stop hoeing deeply once the pegs go into the soil. In the West African savanna sow with the first reliable rains so the crop finishes into the dry season; in East Africa with the long rains; in summer-rainfall southern Africa from October to December; around the Mediterranean in May. In Ontario only the early Spanish and Valencia types reliably mature.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct into loose soil above 15 °C — at the start of the rains in the tropics, so the crop ripens into a dry spell; after frost, in mid-May, in southern Ontario.

faqs.q: How do peanuts grow underground?
faqs.a: The yellow flowers bloom above ground; once one is pollinated, a stalk called a peg grows down from its base and pushes into the soil, and the pod forms at its tip. That is why groundnuts need loose soil and why you stop hoeing deeply once pegging begins.

faqs.q: When do you harvest groundnuts?
faqs.a: When 60–80% of the pods on a test plant have darkened inside the shell and the seed coats have turned pink or tan — about 120 days for Spanish types and 135–155 days for runner and Virginia types. Valencia types for boiling can be dug green from about 75 days.

faqs.q: What is aflatoxin, and how do I avoid it?
faqs.a: Aflatoxin is a poison made by Aspergillus moulds that invade groundnuts left damp, and it has been linked to liver cancer. Avoid it by lifting in dry weather, curing quickly, drying the nuts to about 10% moisture, storing them where air moves, and throwing away any nut that is mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled.

faqs.q: Can I grow peanuts in Ontario?
faqs.a: Yes, with an early Spanish or Valencia variety. Commercial production needs at least 3,000 crop heat units; gardeners sow in mid-May into soil above 15 °C and harvest from late September to early October, 100–120 days later. A sandy, warm bed makes the difference.

faqs.q: How do you make boiled peanuts that keep?
faqs.a: Use freshly dug green peanuts, soak them three times for an hour in fresh water, parboil 10 minutes, pack into jars with boiling brine (1 cup of salt per gallon of water) and pressure-can 45 minutes for 500 ml jars or 50 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge. There is no safe water-bath method.

faqs.q: How do you roast peanuts at home?
faqs.a: Spread dried peanuts in a shallow pan and roast at 150 °C (300 °F) — 30–40 minutes in the shell, 20–25 minutes shelled — stirring often so they do not scorch. Dry them first at a low heat if they are freshly dug.

world.name: Taro (cocoyam, madumbe)
world.tagline: Cocoyam, madumbe, dasheen, eddoe — a corm for the wet corner of the garden, with leaves to cook as well, and always eaten cooked.
world.frostNote: Taro is a tropical plant and frost kills its leaves. Eddoe types, with a cluster of small cormels, stand cold better than dasheen types with one big corm, which is why eddoes are grown as far north as Korea and Japan. In a garden with frost, lift the corms before the first one and keep a few for replanting.
world.ready: Leaves can be picked from about two months after planting. Corms are ready 8–10 months after planting for dasheen types and 5–7 months for eddoes, and a few months later where taro grows in flooded beds. The signs are yellowing leaves and corms lifting slightly at the soil surface; immature corms can be dug from five months.
world.pick: Lift corms with a fork in dry weather — dry corms store better — and handle them gently, because bruised corms rot within days. Cut off the tops; the top 1–2 cm of the main corm with 15–20 cm of leaf stalk can be replanted as a sett. Dasheen types can be ratooned by lifting the main corm and leaving the small ones to grow on. For greens, pick young leaves that are unfolding or just opened; heavy leaf picking reduces corm size and yield.

store.how: Planting corms, and corms for the kitchen, are often simply left in the ground and lifted as needed.
Sound, unbruised corms keep up to six weeks at ambient temperature, though often only two. Leaves keep a few days at most.

store.keeps: Up to 6 months for dasheen types
store.how: Dasheen corms store up to six months at about 10 °C.

world.preserveNote: Taro is eaten cooked, always. The corms, leaves and leaf stalks are full of needle-like bundles of calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) that make the mouth and throat itch and burn when raw, and cooking removes this; some cocoyam carries about 780 mg of calcium oxalate per 100 g, and high-oxalate cultivars are made milder by peeling, grating, soaking and fermenting, as in West African fufu and Hawaiian poi. Taro also contains enzyme inhibitors that cooking largely destroys. The best preservation is storage: dasheen corms keep up to six months at about 10 °C, and corm slices can be sun-dried into chips. There is no tested home-canning process for taro, so cook it fresh and freeze cooked dishes if you have a surplus.

seeds.how: Taro is propagated vegetatively, from side suckers, small unmarketable cormels of 60–150 g, pieces of corm, or setts — the top 1–2 cm of the main corm with 15–20 cm of leaf stalk attached, the ‘huli’ of Hawaii. Plant cormels 5–7.5 cm deep. Take planting material only from healthy plants, because taro leaf blight and soft rots travel on infected corms. Most clones rarely flower, and seed is used only by breeders.
seeds.viability: Not applicable. Planting corms are usually left in the ground until needed; stored at 11–13 °C and 85–90% humidity they grow away better than corms held at 2 °C.

world.nextYear: Taro does best where water is never short — beside a river or tap, or in the low, wet corner of the garden — in fertile soil rich in organic matter at pH 5.5–6.5, with plenty of potash. It tolerates shade, so it can grow under bananas, coconut or coffee. Dasheen types like heavy, moisture-holding soil and can stand in shallow, moving water; eddoes prefer well-drained loam and tolerate drought better. Plant at the start of the rains: around March in southern Ghana and Nigeria, with the long rains in East Africa, and in spring, from September to November, in KwaZulu-Natal, where it is madumbe; around the eastern Mediterranean (Cyprus, Egypt), in spring once the soil is warm. Space plants 50–80 cm apart in rows 70–120 cm apart and weed until the leaves close over. Rotate beds every few years.

sow.outdoors: Plant cormels, suckers or setts 5–7.5 cm deep at the start of the rains, in warm, moist soil; in frost climates only once the soil is warm in late spring.

faqs.q: Can you eat taro raw?
faqs.a: No. Raw taro corms and leaves contain bundles of needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that make the mouth and throat itch and burn; cooking removes the problem. Boil, steam, roast or fry the peeled corms thoroughly, and cook the leaves well.

faqs.q: Are taro leaves edible?
faqs.a: Yes, cooked. Taro leaves and leaf stalks are a popular potherb in West Africa, north-eastern India and the Caribbean, where they are one form of callaloo. Pick young leaves from two months after planting, and never eat them raw — dasheen types are less acrid than eddoes, but all need cooking.

faqs.q: What is the difference between taro, cocoyam and madumbe?
faqs.a: They are names for the same plant, Colocasia esculenta: madumbe (amadumbe) is the Zulu name and cocoyam the West African one, though in West Africa ‘cocoyam’ also covers tannia, Xanthosoma sagittifolium, a related crop. Dasheen types form one large main corm; eddoes form a cluster of smaller cormels.

faqs.q: How long does taro take to grow?
faqs.a: Eight to ten months for dasheen types and five to seven months for eddoes, and longer in flooded beds. Leaves can be picked from about two months, and immature corms dug from five.

faqs.q: How do you store taro?
faqs.a: Leave the corms in the ground until you need them, or lift them in dry weather and keep unbruised corms in a cool, airy place, where they last two to six weeks. Dasheen corms keep up to six months at about 10 °C.

faqs.q: Can I grow taro in a cold-winter country?
faqs.a: Only as a summer crop with a long, warm season, and expect small corms. Eddoe types tolerate cool weather best. Start corms indoors in pots in spring, plant them out into warm, wet soil after the last frost, and lift them before the first one.

world.name: Bananas and plantains
world.tagline: A giant herb that fruits once per stem — cut the bunch green, hang it in the shade, and let the next sucker take over.
world.frostNote: Bananas slow below 16 °C and stop growing at 10 °C, and chilling between 0 and 16 °C can stop the bunch emerging (‘choking’), turn ripening fruit dull grey-green and increase rot. Frost at 0 °C kills leaves, stems and fruit, and below −2 °C the plant is usually killed to the ground, though it regrows from the underground rhizome when warmth returns. If frost threatens, cut any bunch that is full and plump and ripen it indoors.
world.ready: A bunch is ready when the fingers have filled out to full size for the variety — the ridges along each finger have rounded off and the sides have swollen — but before any turn yellow. The flowering stalk emerges 10–15 months after planting, and the first harvest comes 10–24 months after planting, depending on variety and care.
world.pick: Cut the whole bunch while the fingers are plump and still green, 7–14 days before they would ripen on the plant, and hang it in a cool, shady place to ripen; the flavour develops better that way. Each stem fruits only once: after harvest, cut it off at the base and chop it as mulch, keeping one half-grown follower and one small sucker in each clump to carry the next crops.

store.where: Shaded, airy porch or kitchen, hanging
store.keeps: 1–3 weeks as the hands ripen in turn
store.how: Hang the whole bunch out of the sun. Not all the hands ripen at once, which spreads the eating over a week or two.
Never refrigerate green bananas or plantains: chilled before ripening, they fail to ripen properly, discolour and lose flavour.

world.preserveNote: Bananas are a fruit to eat as they ripen, but a glut freezes well: peel firm-ripe fruit, mash it thoroughly with ½ teaspoon (1,500 mg) of ascorbic acid per 250 ml (cup) of mash, and freeze in airtight containers for baking and smoothies. Dried slices are easy: cut 3 mm (⅛ in) slices, dip them for 10 minutes in a citric acid or lemon juice solution, and dry at 60 °C (140 °F) for 6–10 hours until tough and leathery. Plantains and cooking bananas are always cooked — boiled, fried, roasted or pounded. There is no tested home-canning process for plain bananas.

seeds.how: Edible bananas set fruit without pollination and have no viable seed; they are grown from suckers or pieces of rhizome. Choose sword suckers — 30–120 cm tall, with narrow, sword-shaped leaves, firmly attached to the parent — or a large non-fruiting ‘maidenhead’, and avoid broad-leaved water suckers, which are weakly attached and give poor bunches. Dig them out with a sharp spade and a piece of rhizome. Clean tissue-culture plantlets from a nursery are the safest start, because nematodes, weevils and Panama disease travel on suckers.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — each clump is a clone, propagated from suckers or tissue culture.

world.nextYear: Pick the warmest, most sheltered spot that never floods: bananas survive only a day or two of moving floodwater, stagnant water kills them quickly, and wind shreds the leaves and topples tall varieties. They want full sun, deep soil rich in organic matter, and a great deal of water — about 100–150 mm a month, or 25–40 mm a week in dry weather — with feeding every two months while young. Plant suckers at the start of the rains, or earlier with irrigation, in a hole about 90 cm wide and 60 cm deep with compost mixed in, and mulch heavily. Keep each clump to one fruiting stem, one half-grown follower and one small sucker, killing the rest at ground level. Plantain is the starch of the humid zone in West and Central Africa and highland cooking bananas are a staple in East Africa; in the subtropics bananas crop commercially only in the warmest pockets — the Canary Islands, Morocco, Egypt, Israel and South Africa among them. Never take suckers from a clump showing Panama disease, which yellows and kills the leaves from the oldest upward.

sow.outdoors: Plant sword suckers or tissue-culture plantlets at the start of the rains, or at any time with irrigation, once the soil is warm.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a banana and a plantain?
faqs.a: Plantains are starchy bananas that are always cooked before eating — boiled, fried, roasted or pounded — whereas dessert bananas are eaten raw when ripe. Plantains, in their French and Horn groups, carry fewer fruit per bunch than sweet bananas, and are a staple across West and Central Africa, southern India and tropical America.

faqs.q: How long does a banana plant take to fruit?
faqs.a: Usually 10–15 months from planting to the emergence of the flowering stalk, and 10–24 months to the first ripe bunch, depending on variety, warmth and care. The first bunch from a newly planted sucker is often smaller than later ones.

faqs.q: Why shouldn’t green bananas go in the fridge?
faqs.a: Because unripe bananas are chill-injured below about 16 °C: they fail to ripen properly, the peel and flesh discolour and the flavour suffers. Ripen them at room temperature and refrigerate only fully ripe fruit, for a few days.

faqs.q: Does a banana plant die after fruiting?
faqs.a: The stem does — each pseudostem fruits once — but the clump lives on through its suckers. Cut the spent stem off at the base after harvest, chop it as mulch, and let the next sucker take over.

faqs.q: Can I grow bananas in a cold-winter country?
faqs.a: Only as a foliage plant, or in a heated greenhouse. Growth stops at 10 °C, frost kills the leaves at 0 °C and the plant is cut to the ground below −2 °C, and a bunch takes 10–24 months of warmth to form and fill.

faqs.q: How do you freeze bananas?
faqs.a: Peel firm-ripe bananas, mash them thoroughly, stir in ½ teaspoon of ascorbic acid per cup of mash so they do not brown, and freeze in airtight containers. Use the mash for banana bread, pancakes and smoothies.

world.name: Papaya
world.tagline: From seed to fruit in under a year — grow three plants to be sure of one that bears, and pick when the first yellow streaks show.
world.frostNote: Papaya is damaged or killed below about −0.6 °C (31 °F) and sulks long before: below 15 °C flowering stops or the fruit comes misshapen, roots barely grow in soil below 15.5 °C, and new leaves stop forming in cold weather. When frost threatens, pick any fruit showing colour, and the full-sized green ones to cook.
world.ready: Fruit can be picked green, as a vegetable, or for eating ripe once yellow covers a tenth to a third of the skin; the longer it colours on the tree, the sweeter it is. Well-grown plants flower about four months after planting and bear their first fruit 7–11 months after.
world.pick: Twist or cut the fruit off with a short stalk and handle it gently — scratched skin weeps latex, which stains the fruit. Wear gloves when picking green fruit or cutting the stem, because the milky latex irritates skin. Where papaya fruit fly is a problem, bag each fruit while small in a paper bag or cloth and leave it on until harvest.

store.how: Part-coloured fruit finishes ripening at room temperature.
Refrigerate only once the fruit is fully ripe.

world.preserveNote: Ripe papaya cans safely only with added acid. The tested NCHFP method makes a medium or heavy syrup with 60 ml (¼ cup) of lemon juice to each litre (quart) of syrup, cooks peeled, seeded cubes gently in it for 2–3 minutes, packs them hot with 1 cm (½ in) headspace, and processes them 15 minutes for 500 ml (pint) jars or 20 minutes for litre (quart) jars in a boiling-water canner at 0–300 m. Do not leave out the lemon juice. Ripe flesh is also dried, candied, or made into jam and jelly. Green papaya is a vegetable — boiled, cooked in soups, or shredded raw into the salads of Thailand and Vietnam — but it is rich in latex containing the enzymes papain and chymopapain, so most green papaya is cooked.

seeds.how: Papaya grows easily from seed, but plants come in three sexes — male, female and bisexual — and only female and bisexual plants bear fruit, so raise two or three plants to be sure of one that crops. Bisexual plants pollinate themselves; female plants need pollen carried by insects or wind. Scoop the seeds from a ripe fruit, press them against the side of a colander to break the jelly-like sac around each one (it inhibits germination), rinse, and dry them out of the sun. Where papaya ringspot virus is about, avoid seed from small, pear-shaped Solo-type fruit, which are more susceptible.
seeds.viability: Several years, dried and kept in a sealed bag in the fridge. Fresh seed germinates in two to three weeks.

world.nextYear: Papaya is called pawpaw in much of Africa, Britain and Australia; it is unrelated to the North American pawpaw, Asimina triloba. Give it the warmest, sunniest spot in the garden that never floods, 2–3 m from buildings and other plants, in deep, well-drained soil; waterlogging and lawn sprinklers on a timer cause root rot. Sow two to four seeds in each 4-litre pot, keep the strongest seedling, and plant out at 15–30 cm tall. Feed little and often — every two weeks while young — and water every day or two in hot, dry weather on sandy soil, every three or four days on loam; drought drops flowers and young fruit. Plant out at the start of the rains in the tropics. In Mediterranean and subtropical climates it needs the warmest frost-free site or a greenhouse, because a winter below 15 °C stops flowering.

sow.outdoors: Sow in pots in warm conditions and plant out at the start of the rains, or once nights stay above 15 °C.

faqs.q: Why does my papaya flower but never fruit?
faqs.a: It is probably a male plant. Males carry small, tubular flowers on long dangling stalks and rarely set fruit; females and bisexual plants carry larger flowers tight against the trunk. Raise two or three seedlings from each sowing so that at least one bears.

faqs.q: When should I pick papaya?
faqs.a: For eating ripe, once yellow covers a tenth to a third of the skin; the more colour it gains on the tree, the sweeter it is. Ripen it fully at room temperature, then refrigerate, and eat within four to seven days.

faqs.q: Can you eat green papaya?
faqs.a: Yes — it is a vegetable in much of the tropics, boiled, cooked in soups, or shredded raw into Thai and Vietnamese salads. Green fruit is rich in latex, so most of it is cooked, and the latex irritates the hands of whoever peels it.

faqs.q: How do you grow papaya from seed?
faqs.a: Take seeds from a ripe fruit, rub them against a colander to break the jelly coat, rinse and dry them, and sow two to four in a 4-litre pot somewhere warm. They germinate in two to three weeks; keep the strongest seedling and plant it out at 15–30 cm tall.

faqs.q: Is papaya sap harmful?
faqs.a: It irritates the skin. The milky latex in the stem, leaves and green fruit contains protein-digesting enzymes, so wear gloves and long sleeves when picking green fruit or pruning.

faqs.q: How do you can papaya?
faqs.a: In a boiling-water canner, with added lemon juice: cube peeled, seeded fruit, cook it 2–3 minutes in syrup with ¼ cup of lemon juice per quart of syrup, pack hot with ½ inch headspace, and process 15 minutes for pints or 20 minutes for quarts near sea level.

world.name: Mangoes
world.tagline: The fruit that needs a dry season to flower — picked firm and mature, ripened in the kitchen, and handled with respect for its sap.
world.frostNote: Mango trees do not harden off to cold. Flowers and small fruit are damaged if the temperature falls below about 4.4 °C (40 °F) for a few hours; young trees can be killed at −1 to −2 °C, and mature trees survive about −4 °C for a few hours with damage to leaves and small branches. In a marginal garden cover young trees on frost nights and plant in the warmest corner.
world.ready: Mangoes ripen on the tree but are best picked firm and mature: the shoulders and the nose — the end away from the stem — have filled out and broadened, coloured varieties show their first blush or yellowing, and the flesh next to the seed has turned from white to yellow. Fruit matures 100–150 days after flowering. Pick as you need it through the season; once ripe, fruit begins to drop.
world.pick: Cut the fruit with secateurs, leaving about 10 cm of stalk, so the milky, resinous sap does not spurt from the stem end onto the skin — it burns the fruit, causing black blemishes that lead to rot, and it blisters human skin as well. Use a picking pole with a bag for high fruit rather than climbing.

store.how: Mature fruit ripens 3–8 days after picking. Warmer than this, it shrivels and develops off flavours.
Chilling unripe mangoes causes chilling injury — grey or brown skin, pitting, uneven ripening and off flavours that may not show until the fruit warms up.

world.preserveNote: Mangoes freeze beautifully: slice firm-ripe fruit and tray-freeze it unsweetened, pack slices in a 30% syrup, or purée the flesh with or without sugar. Tested NCHFP recipes cover the jars. Green, firm, non-fibrous mangoes can be sliced, boiled 2 minutes in light or medium syrup and canned 15 minutes for 500 ml jars or 20 minutes for litre jars in a boiling-water canner at 0–300 m. Mango chutney uses unripe mangoes with onion, ginger, garlic, raisins, sugar, chilli and 5% vinegar, processed 10 minutes for 250 or 500 ml jars; mango sauce, a purée of slightly under-ripe fruit heated to 93 °C (200 °F) with honey, sugar, bottled lemon juice and ascorbic acid, is processed 15 minutes for 250 ml jars. For mango leather, purée unripe fruit with honey and spices, spread it 6 mm (¼ in) thick and dry it at 60 °C (140 °F) for about 10 hours. Wear rubber gloves when peeling green mangoes, because the skin and sap irritate skin the way poison ivy, a relative, does, and do not touch your face until your hands are washed.

seeds.how: It depends on the variety. Many tropical mangoes, including the Indochinese types, have polyembryonic seeds: most of the embryos in one seed are genetically identical to the mother tree, so they come true, and sowing them is the usual way mangoes are propagated across much of the tropics. Indian types, which include many commercial varieties, have monoembryonic seeds that give a cross, and must be grafted — usually veneer- or cleft-grafted onto a vigorous polyembryonic seedling rootstock. Take seed from a fully ripe fruit and sow it fresh, not dried.
seeds.viability: Weeks, not years. Sow within a few days of taking the seed from the fruit; packed in moist sand, earth or sawdust it lasts a little longer.

world.nextYear: A mango is a tree for the long term: grafted trees bear three to five years after planting and grow very large unless pruned after each harvest. Choose full sun, the warmest spot, and soil that drains; mangoes tolerate occasional flooding but not poor drainage. Water young trees weekly in dry spells for their first three years; mature trees need little irrigation, and over-watering harms them. The key to fruit is dry weather before and during flowering: rain and heavy dew at bloom bring anthracnose and powdery mildew, which destroy the flowers and young fruit. That is why mangoes crop best in climates with a long dry season — the West African savanna, coastal Kenya and Tanzania, the Limpopo lowveld — and less reliably in places that are wet all year. In humid gardens choose anthracnose-resistant varieties. Plant at the start of the rains, so the tree roots in before the dry season.

sow.outdoors: Plant grafted trees at the start of the rains, in full sun, so they root in before the dry season.

faqs.q: Why does my mango tree flower but not set fruit?
faqs.a: Usually because rain or heavy dew during flowering let anthracnose and powdery mildew attack the flower panicles, or because a cold spell below about 4 °C hit the flowers. Dry weather before and during bloom gives the best set; in humid gardens, one or two sulphur and copper sprays starting when the panicles are a quarter grown protect them.

faqs.q: How do I know when a mango is ready to pick?
faqs.a: The shoulders and the end away from the stem have filled out, coloured varieties show a first blush or yellowing, and the flesh near the seed has turned from white to yellow. Pick firm and mature, and ripen at 21–24 °C for three to eight days.

faqs.q: Why do mangoes give some people a rash?
faqs.a: The sap and the skin of unripe fruit contain resinous compounds that irritate and can blister skin, with a delayed reaction like poison ivy, a relative of the mango. Sensitive people should wear gloves, and use one knife to peel and a clean one to slice, so the flesh does not carry resin from the peel.

faqs.q: Will a mango grown from a seed come true?
faqs.a: Only if it is a polyembryonic variety, as many tropical seedling mangoes and Indochinese types are — most of their seedlings are identical to the parent. Monoembryonic Indian types give a new, unpredictable tree and must be grafted.

faqs.q: Should mangoes go in the fridge?
faqs.a: Only once they are ripe. Unripe mangoes chilled in the fridge suffer chilling injury — grey or brown skin, pitting, uneven ripening and off flavours that show once they warm up.

faqs.q: How do you freeze mangoes?
faqs.a: Peel and slice firm, ripe fruit and freeze the slices on a tray before bagging them, or cover them with a 30% syrup, or purée the flesh with or without sugar. Leave headspace in rigid containers.

world.name: Avocados
world.tagline: A fruit that will not ripen on the tree — so the tree is the store, and the kitchen counter does the rest.
world.frostNote: Cold tolerance depends on the race: West Indian avocados are damaged at about −1 to −2 °C, Guatemalan types at −2 to −3 °C, and Mexican types, the hardiest, at −3 to −4 °C, with hybrids in between. Young trees are the most tender, and fruit on the tree is lost to a hard frost. When frost is forecast, pick mature fruit you want to ripen and cover or wrap young trees.
world.ready: Avocados do not ripen on the tree, so maturity is judged by the variety’s season and the size of the fruit. The easiest test is to pick one large fruit and leave it on the kitchen counter: a mature fruit softens in 3–8 days, while one that shrivels, turns rubbery or rots at the stem end was picked too early, so wait and try again. Fruit can hang for weeks through its season and be picked as needed, but eventually it drops.
world.pick: Clip the fruit with a short piece of stalk, using secateurs or a picking pole with a bag, rather than pulling it. Immature fruit is prone to stem-end rot as it softens, which is one more reason not to pick early.

store.how: The tree is the best store: pick a few at a time as you need them.
Ripens best at 16–24 °C. Warmer, it ripens unevenly and develops off flavours.
Refrigerate only ripe fruit. Hard fruit held below about 4 °C — 13 °C for West Indian types — suffers chilling injury: darkened skin and grey-brown flesh.

world.preserveNote: Avocados are eaten fresh; there is no tested home method for canning or drying them. They freeze satisfactorily only as purée, not whole or sliced: peel and stone fruit that yields to gentle pressure, mash it, add 1 tablespoon of lemon juice for every two avocados — or ¼ teaspoon (750 mg) of ascorbic acid per litre (quart) of purée — pack with headspace and freeze, unsweetened for guacamole and sandwiches, sweetened for desserts and smoothies.

seeds.how: Avocados do not come true from seed: a stone from a good fruit gives a tree of unknown quality. Named varieties are grafted — usually cleft- or veneer-grafted onto vigorous seedling rootstocks — and grafted trees begin to bear in three to four years. Seedlings are the usual rootstocks, though, so a stone is worth sowing if you plan to graft onto it.
seeds.viability: Short. Sow stones fresh; held in sealed polyethylene bags at about 4 °C they have stayed viable for up to five months.

world.nextYear: Drainage is everything: avocados will not tolerate flooding or waterlogged soil, and in wet ground they die of Phytophthora root rot, the most serious disease of the crop worldwide. Where drainage is doubtful, plant on a mound 60–120 cm high and 1.2–1.8 m across, in full sun and away from lawn sprinklers. Some varieties fruit well on their own; others set better with a variety of the opposite flowering type (A or B) blooming nearby, so look at what your neighbours grow. Water young trees once or twice a week in dry spells for their first three years, and avoid drought while flowers and fruit are developing. Plant at the start of the rains in the tropics, or in spring after frost in Mediterranean climates. Guatemalan and Mexican types and their hybrids suit cool highlands and Mediterranean coasts; in the hot, humid lowlands, West Indian types do better.

sow.outdoors: Plant grafted trees at the start of the rains in the tropics, or in spring once frost is past, on a mound if drainage is doubtful.

faqs.q: Do avocados ripen on the tree?
faqs.a: No. Avocados soften only after they are picked or fall, which is why the tree can be used as a store through the variety’s season. A mature fruit picked and left at room temperature ripens in three to eight days.

faqs.q: How do I know when to pick my avocados?
faqs.a: Pick one large fruit during the variety’s season and leave it on the counter. If it softens evenly within about a week, the crop is mature; if it shrivels, turns rubbery or rots at the stem end, wait a few weeks and test again.

faqs.q: Will an avocado grown from a stone produce fruit?
faqs.a: It may eventually, but not the fruit you planted: avocados do not come true from seed. For a known variety and a crop in three to four years, buy a grafted tree, or graft a named variety onto your seedling.

faqs.q: Do I need two avocado trees?
faqs.a: Not always. Avocado flowers open as female and male at different times of day, and varieties are classed as A or B types by that timing. Some varieties fruit well alone, but others set better with an opposite type blooming nearby; a neighbour’s tree often does the job.

faqs.q: Can you freeze avocado?
faqs.a: Yes, as purée only. Mash ripe flesh with 1 tablespoon of lemon juice per two avocados, pack with headspace and freeze. Whole or sliced avocados do not freeze satisfactorily.

faqs.q: How cold can an avocado tree take?
faqs.a: It depends on the race: West Indian types are damaged at about −1 to −2 °C, Guatemalan at −2 to −3 °C and Mexican, the hardiest, at −3 to −4 °C. Young trees are more tender than established ones, so wrap or cover them on frost nights.

world.name: Passion fruit
world.tagline: A vigorous vine that drops its fruit when it is ready — the purple for cool highlands, the yellow for the hot lowlands.
world.frostNote: The purple passion fruit is subtropical: in Florida, vines with their lower stems wrapped came through freezes, were cut back, and fruited heavily again. Frost still kills unprotected young growth, and the yellow form is tropical and more tender. When frost is forecast, gather coloured and fallen fruit and wrap the base of the vine.
world.ready: Ripe fruit falls to the ground: purple fruit turns deep purple, almost black, and yellow fruit deep gold. Fruit ripens 70–80 days after pollination. Fruit picked from the vine when just turning light purple finishes ripening indoors and does not sunburn on hot ground.
world.pick: Gather fallen fruit every day, before soil organisms spoil it; in hot weather, pick from the vine two or three times a week once fruit starts to colour, and once a week in the cool season. Wrinkled fallen fruit is fully ripe and good to eat.

store.how: Ripe fruit keeps about a week at 2–7 °C; the skin wrinkles but the pulp stays good.
Part-coloured fruit ripens well at about 20 °C; at 30 °C it ripens too fast.

world.preserveNote: The pulp and juice freeze well and keep their flavour: scoop out the seedy pulp and freeze it as it is, or press it through a sieve or two layers of cheesecloth for juice and freeze that — frozen juice keeps for a year at −18 °C without deteriorating. Heat damages the flavour, which is why the traditional preserves are jellies and jams made from the seeded pulp, often with pineapple, rather than canned fruit. Eat only ripe fruit: passion fruit contains a cyanogenic glycoside that is highest in very young, unripe fruit and so low in fallen, wrinkled fruit as to be of no concern.

seeds.how: Passion fruit grows easily from seed taken from a fully ripe fruit: sown soon after extraction it germinates in two to three weeks, and fermenting the pulp for a few days, or rubbing the seed with sandpaper, speeds it up. Purple passion fruit and its hybrids pollinate themselves; the yellow form is largely self-incompatible and needs a second vine and carpenter bees or hand-pollination. Many growers plant vines grafted onto yellow passion fruit rootstock, which resists Fusarium wilt and nematodes; set grafted vines with the union well above the soil and keep mulch away from it, or the resistance is lost.
seeds.viability: Best sown fresh: stored seed germinates more slowly and less well.

world.nextYear: A passion fruit vine needs a strong trellis or fence at least 2 m high in full sun, shelter from wind, and well-drained soil — root and collar rots kill vines in waterlogged ground. Water regularly, especially as the fruit approaches maturity, when drought makes it shrivel and drop, and go easy on nitrogen, which gives empty fruit. Prune once a year from the second year to stimulate new growth, which carries the flowers. Vines decline after a few years — commercial plantings last from three to eight — so plant a replacement before the old one fails. The purple form suits cooler highlands: Kenyan growers plant it at 1,200–2,000 m with 900–2,000 mm of rain, and South African plantings at 1,200–1,460 m in Limpopo have stayed productive for eight years. The yellow form suits hot lowlands. Plant at the start of the rains.

sow.outdoors: Plant vines at the start of the rains, against a trellis in full sun; in frost climates only after frost, in a sheltered spot.

faqs.q: How do you know when passion fruit is ripe?
faqs.a: It falls off the vine. Purple fruit turns deep purple to almost black and yellow fruit deep gold; collect fallen fruit daily, or pick from the vine when it has started to colour and let it finish ripening at room temperature.

faqs.q: Is wrinkled passion fruit still good?
faqs.a: Yes. A fallen fruit with a wrinkled skin is fully ripe, and its cyanogenic glycoside content is at its lowest; the pulp keeps well inside the shell. Discard any that are mouldy or leaking.

faqs.q: Why are my passion fruit empty or dropping?
faqs.a: Irregular watering is the usual cause of fruit drop, because demand for water is highest as the fruit matures. Fruit with soft seeds but no juice points to too much nitrogen, poor pollination, boron deficiency or damage by fruit flies or stink bugs.

faqs.q: Purple or yellow passion fruit — which should I grow?
faqs.a: Purple in cool highland and subtropical gardens: it is more aromatic and pollinates itself. Yellow in the hot lowland tropics: it is more vigorous and disease-resistant, but largely self-incompatible, so it needs a second vine and bees or hand-pollination.

faqs.q: How long does a passion fruit vine last?
faqs.a: Usually three to eight years. Pruning laterals after fruiting and keeping the base free of wounds extends its life, but plan to plant a replacement every few years.

faqs.q: Can I grow passion fruit in a cold-winter country?
faqs.a: Only in a pot that comes into a frost-free greenhouse or sunroom for winter, or in a heated conservatory. The purple form survives a light frost if its base is wrapped, but it will not crop outdoors through a Canadian or northern European winter.

world.name: Moringa (drumstick tree)
world.tagline: A fast, drought-hardy tree kept low for its leaves — the young pods are ‘drumsticks’, and the roots are not food.
world.frostNote: Moringa tolerates a light frost but no more, and it is at its best at lower elevations — up to about 1,350 m in East Africa, though it survives higher. When a frost is forecast, pick the young leaves you want; a young tree in a pot should come under cover.
world.ready: Leaves can be picked about two and a half months after sowing, and again about three weeks after each pruning. Young green pods, cooked like green beans, can be picked from about seven months after planting, and mature dry pods for seed about six weeks later. Trees grown from seed flower from their second year; trees grown from cuttings can fruit 6–12 months after planting.
world.pick: Strip leaves from the branches, or cut whole leafy shoots, about twice a month in the growing season. Keep the tree within reach by cutting it back once or twice a year once it is 1.5 m tall — to about 50 cm from the ground, or to ground level for older trees — which makes it branch and produce far more leaf. Pick the pods young and tender.

store.how: Fresh leaves wilt quickly; keep them loosely bagged and cook them soon.

store.where: Airtight jar, dried leaf or powder
store.how: Leaves dried in the shade, crumbled or powdered, in a sealed jar away from light.

world.preserveNote: The leaves are dried and powdered for storage across West Africa, and the young pods and leaves are cooked fresh. Dry leaves in an airy, shaded place until they crumble, then keep them in an airtight jar; leaves blanched 2 minutes can also be frozen like other greens. Treat moringa as a vegetable rather than a supplement. The leaves have long been eaten cooked in Africa and Asia, but in December 2025 Food Standards Australia New Zealand reviewed moringa leaves, young pods and seed oil as a novel food and could not conclude they were safe, citing animal studies in which high doses of leaf powder harmed the liver and kidneys and caused loss of pregnancies. So eat the leaves in ordinary cooked portions, and avoid concentrated leaf powder in pregnancy. Eat the seeds only in moderation: they are fried and eaten like groundnuts in Nigeria, but they contain glucosinolates whose breakdown products have both helpful and toxic effects. Do not use the root as a horseradish substitute — the root bark contains toxic alkaloids, including moringinine, that act on the heart and the nervous system.

seeds.how: Moringa is cross-pollinated, so seedlings vary in form and yield; good trees are therefore propagated from cuttings, which Indian growers prefer because seedlings bear inferior pods. For seed, leave pods on the tree until dry and brown, shell out the winged seeds and sow them 2 cm deep. Branches 1–1.5 m long and up to 4 cm thick root readily within a few months and are used to make living fences. Stored seed is attacked by insects, so keep it in a sealed jar.
seeds.viability: About 80% of fresh seed germinates, about 50% after 12 months’ storage, and none survives two years.

world.nextYear: Moringa is drought-tolerant, grows where the annual rainfall is as little as 500 mm, and takes almost any soil that drains, though fertile soil and manure give the best leaf. Sow seed direct at the start of the rains, or in a shaded, watered nursery in the dry season and plant out at about 40 cm tall, three months later, as the rains arrive. For leaf, plant densely — 0.7–1 m apart — and cut back hard; for trees, 3–5 m apart. Early growth is fast, often 3–4 m in a year, so plan the pruning from the start. It is a lowland tree, at home in the Sahel — Niger grows it as a field crop — and the savanna, and slower in cool highlands. Its light shade suits alley-cropping with vegetables.

sow.outdoors: Sow seed 2 cm deep at the start of the rains, or raise seedlings in a shaded nursery in the dry season and plant them out as the rains begin.

faqs.q: Which parts of moringa can you eat?
faqs.a: The leaves, flowers and young pods, cooked — the leaves in sauces and soups, the young pods (‘drumsticks’) like green beans — and the seeds in moderation, usually fried. Do not eat the roots or bark: the root bark contains toxic alkaloids.

faqs.q: Is moringa safe to eat?
faqs.a: Cooked leaves and young pods eaten as a vegetable have a long history of use in Africa and Asia. Concentrated leaf powder is another matter: Food Standards Australia New Zealand could not conclude in 2025 that moringa sold as a food was safe, after animal studies found liver, kidney and pregnancy effects at high doses. Eat it in ordinary portions, and avoid leaf powder in pregnancy.

faqs.q: How do you harvest moringa leaves?
faqs.a: Strip the leaves or cut leafy shoots about twice a month, starting about two and a half months after sowing. Prune the tree back to about 50 cm once or twice a year once it reaches 1.5 m; new leaves are ready to pick about three weeks after each pruning.

faqs.q: Can I grow moringa from cuttings?
faqs.a: Yes. Branches 1–1.5 m long and up to 4 cm thick root readily in a few months, and trees grown from cuttings can bear pods within 6–12 months, against two years from seed. Cuttings also keep the qualities of a good tree, which seed does not.

faqs.q: Can moringa grow in a cold climate?
faqs.a: Only as a summer pot plant that comes indoors before frost. It tolerates no more than a light frost and grows best in warm lowlands; it is slow even in cool tropical highlands.

faqs.q: How do you dry moringa leaves?
faqs.a: Strip the leaflets from the stalks, spread them thinly in an airy, shaded place, and turn them until they crumble. Rub them to a powder if you like and store them in an airtight jar away from light.

world.name: African eggplant (garden egg)
world.tagline: The garden egg of Ghana and Nigeria — small, firm, often bitter fruit picked pale and unripe, with leaves for the pot as well.
world.frostNote: African eggplant does not survive cold: the garden-egg types thrive at 25–35 °C by day and 20–27 °C at night, and none of its forms survive cold or very wet conditions. Pick every usable fruit before a frost. In the tropics, plants that go dormant in the dry season can revive with the rains, but they are rarely productive.
world.ready: Pick fruit at full size but still immature — white, pale green or cream for most garden eggs — while the seeds are soft; some sweet cultivars are picked as they begin to turn orange. Left on the plant, the fruit turns creamy or yellow to red, fills with seed and becomes less palatable. Flowering begins 70–100 days after sowing, earlier in the hot-savanna types. Leafy types are picked before they flower.
world.pick: Cut the fruit with a short stalk once a week, and keep picking even when you cannot use it all: fruit left on the plant holds back new fruit. For greens, pick young shoots with several leaves; leafy types can be cut back and allowed to regrow up to six times if they are watered and fed with nitrogen, or pulled whole when 40–50 cm tall.

store.how: Sound, undamaged fruit keeps for days or even weeks with good ventilation; the large garden-egg types stay firm longest.
Like other eggplants, the fruit is chill-sensitive below about 8 °C.

world.preserveNote: Garden eggs are mostly eaten fresh — cooked in stews and sauces, often with palm oil, or sometimes raw — and are not usually kept long. Like eggplant, they freeze: peel, slice 8 mm (⅓ in) thick, blanch 4 minutes in 4 litres (1 gallon) of boiling water with 125 ml (½ cup) of lemon juice to stop darkening, cool, drain and freeze. The leaves are sun-dried and ground to a powder for soup in the dry season. The leaves contain oxalate and alkaloids such as solasodine, which cooking reduces, so cook them rather than eating them raw. There is no tested home-canning process for any eggplant.

seeds.how: All the flowers are bisexual and can set fruit, and they are bee-pollinated, so nearby varieties cross to some extent; Seed Savers Exchange advises 100–500 m (300–1,600 ft) between eggplant varieties for pure seed. Leave a few of the best fruit on the plant until fully ripe and softening, then wash the seeds out of the pulp and dry them on cloth or paper out of direct sun. Farmers traditionally store the seed inside the air-dried fruit until sowing.
seeds.viability: Years, stored cool and dry; Seed Savers Exchange gives 4–6 years for eggplant seed.

world.nextYear: Treat it as part of the nightshade family: keep it off beds that grew tomatoes, eggplant, peppers or potatoes in the last two or three years. Full sun, deep, well-drained soil at pH 5.5–6.8 — it will not stand waterlogging — and manure or compost before planting. Sow in a nursery bed or trays and transplant after 30–35 days, at 5–7 leaves and 15–20 cm tall, 50–100 cm apart. In West Africa sow early in the rains; with irrigation it crops all year, and in the dry season it needs about 5 mm of water a day. In East Africa it is grown through the rains, and in Uganda in swamp margins in the dry season. In the Mediterranean or southern Africa treat it as a summer eggplant, planting out once nights stay above 15 °C. Steady moisture improves fruit quality.

sow.outdoors: Sow in a nursery bed or trays and transplant after 30–35 days, early in the rains in the tropics; in frost climates only once nights stay above 15 °C.

faqs.q: What is a garden egg?
faqs.a: A garden egg is the fruit of the African eggplant, Solanum aethiopicum — usually small, round to egg-shaped and white or cream when picked, turning yellow, orange or red as it ripens. It is grown across tropical Africa, above all in Ghana and Nigeria, where offering garden eggs is a traditional Igbo welcome to visitors.

faqs.q: Why are garden eggs bitter?
faqs.a: Bitterness comes from furostanol glycosides, and some cultivars are bred bitter on purpose — they are valued as medicine in many African countries. If you want mild fruit, choose a sweet cultivar and pick the fruit young.

faqs.q: Can you eat African eggplant leaves?
faqs.a: Yes, cooked. Leafy types are grown for their young shoots, which are picked repeatedly through the wet season, and the leaves of fruiting types are eaten too. They contain oxalate and alkaloids that cooking reduces, so do not eat them raw.

faqs.q: When do you pick garden eggs?
faqs.a: When the fruit is full-sized but still immature and pale, with soft seeds — usually weekly once cropping starts. Fruit left to colour on the plant fills with seed, becomes less palatable and slows the plant down.

faqs.q: Can I grow garden eggs in Canada?
faqs.a: Yes, as you would eggplant: sow indoors 7–10 weeks before planting out, and transplant into soil above 15 °C after all danger of frost, ideally through black plastic mulch in the warmest bed. Specialty eggplants in Ontario crop 55–80 days after transplanting.

faqs.q: How do you freeze garden eggs?
faqs.a: Peel and slice them 8 mm thick, blanch 4 minutes in boiling water with ½ cup of lemon juice per gallon to stop browning, cool, drain and freeze. For frying later, pack the slices with freezer wrap between them.

world.name: Broad beans (fava beans)
world.tagline: The cool-season bean of the Mediterranean, Ethiopia and the English allotment — sown where winters are mild, picked young and sweet in spring.
world.frostNote: Broad beans are the hardiest of the beans: hardy varieties such as Aquadulce Claudia are sown in autumn in mild regions and overwinter as young plants, protected by cloches or fleece in cold spells. Even so, frost is the limiting factor on the crop above about 3,000 m in the Ethiopian highlands. In a spring cold snap, fleece over the rows protects the flowers and young pods.
world.ready: For shelling, pick when the pods are full but still fairly small, while the scar on each bean, where it joins the pod, is still white or green; once the scar turns black, the beans are tough. Whole young pods can be cooked when about 5 cm long. The lowest pods mature first. For dry beans, leave the pods until pods and seeds have dried on the plant, then harvest before they split in the rain.
world.pick: Cut the pods with scissors or secateurs rather than pulling, which damages the plants, and pick every few days: regular picking keeps new pods coming. When the lowest flowers have set small pods, pinch out the shoot tips — it puts the plant’s effort into the pods and discourages blackfly, which colonise the soft tips — and cook the tips like spinach.

store.how: Young beans lose their sweetness quickly after picking; shell and cook or freeze them soon.
Dried to 11–14% moisture and kept cool, dry and free of pests.

world.preserveNote: Freezing keeps young broad beans best, though there is no officially tested blanching time for them: UC Master Food Preservers boil shelled beans for about 4 minutes, cool them, tray-freeze and bag them, and slip the beans out of their pale skins after thawing — close to the 2–4 minutes by size tested for lima beans. Dry beans are the staple form around the Mediterranean and in Ethiopia — ful medames, shiro, kik wot — and dried to 11–14% moisture they keep for years. They can be pressure-canned like any dried bean: soak 12–18 hours, boil 30 minutes, pack in the cooking liquid and process 75 minutes for 500 ml jars or 90 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge. Never water-bath beans. One safety rule matters more than any recipe: people with G6PD deficiency must not eat broad beans. The vicine and convicine in the beans, especially immature ones, trigger favism — a rapid destruction of red blood cells — and cooking does not remove them; even the pollen can affect very sensitive people.

seeds.how: Broad beans sit between self- and cross-pollinating: bees usually cross 20–50% of the flowers, and occasionally far more. To keep a variety true, grow only one kind for seed or keep varieties well apart. Leave the best plants unpicked until the pods blacken and the seeds rattle, harvest before wet weather splits them, and finish drying the seed indoors.
seeds.viability: 2–7 years at 5–10 °C, or 1–4 years at 10–20 °C, if dried to 11–14% moisture.

world.nextYear: Broad beans fix their own nitrogen and leave the bed richer, so follow them with brassicas or leafy crops. Give them sun, shelter and well-drained, near-neutral soil with compost dug in; they tolerate neither waterlogging nor drought. Sow seed 5–7.5 cm deep and 15–23 cm apart, in single rows 45 cm apart or double rows 23 cm apart, and stake the taller kinds. A mean daily temperature of about 13 °C suits them best, so they are a cool-season crop everywhere: in the Mediterranean sow in autumn — October–November around Lisbon, April–May in Cape Town — for a spring harvest; in Egypt and Sudan from mid-October to November; in the Ethiopian highlands with the main rains in June and July; in Britain in autumn (hardy varieties, mild areas) or from February to April; in Canada as early in spring as the soil can be worked. In the lowland tropics they may flower but rarely set pods. Water well as flowering starts and again two weeks later.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct in the cool season — autumn where winters are mild, as early in spring as the soil can be worked where the ground freezes, or with the main rains in tropical highlands.

faqs.q: When should I sow broad beans?
faqs.a: In the cool season. Around the Mediterranean, including Lisbon and Cape Town, sow in autumn for a spring harvest; in Britain sow hardy varieties in autumn in mild areas, or from February to April; in Canada sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring. In the Ethiopian highlands they go in with the June–July rains.

faqs.q: Who should not eat broad beans?
faqs.a: Anyone with G6PD deficiency, an inherited enzyme deficiency that affects some 500 million people worldwide. The vicine and convicine in broad beans trigger favism — rapid destruction of red blood cells, with jaundice and dark urine — and cooking does not remove them. If favism runs in your family, get tested before eating them, and keep sensitive children away from the flowering crop.

faqs.q: Do you need to double-peel broad beans?
faqs.a: Not when they are young and small, when the skins are tender. Larger beans have tough, pale skins: blanch them briefly, cool, and pinch each bean out of its skin — or freeze them in the skin and slip it off after thawing.

faqs.q: How do you freeze broad beans?
faqs.a: Shell them, boil about 4 minutes, cool quickly, freeze on a tray and bag them once hard. There is no officially tested blanching time for broad beans; this follows UC Master Food Preservers and is close to the tested times for lima beans.

faqs.q: Can broad beans grow in the tropics?
faqs.a: Only at altitude. They are a cool-season crop that grows best at a mean temperature of about 13 °C; in Ethiopia they are grown at 1,300–3,800 m, mostly 2,000–2,500 m. In the hot lowland tropics they may flower but usually set no pods.

faqs.q: Why are there black aphids on my broad beans?
faqs.a: Blackfly colonise the soft shoot tips in late spring. Pinch out the tips once the lowest flowers have set pods — it removes the aphids’ favourite food and sends the plant’s effort into the pods — and cook the tips like spinach.

world.name: Globe artichokes
world.tagline: A silver thistle that crops for years in a Mediterranean garden — cut the buds while they are tight, and give the crowns a dry winter.
world.frostNote: A frost at or near freezing blisters the outer scales of the buds, which turn whitish and then darken — they look spoiled but eat perfectly well. The plants should be protected below about −4 °C (25 °F), and below about −9 °C (15 °F) they are damaged even under mulch. Before winter, cut the old stems, lay the spent leaves over the crown and add a thick mulch of straw; cold, wet winter soil kills more artichokes than cold alone.
world.ready: Cut the buds when they have reached full size for the variety but the scales are still tightly closed; once they start to open and soften, the bud is past its best and will soon become a purple thistle flower. A mature plant gives up to 12 buds a season, the large main bud first and the smaller side buds after. Plants from seed or offsets crop from their second summer in Britain; grown as annuals from vernalised transplants, they crop 90–100 days after planting out.
world.pick: Cut each bud with secateurs, taking 2.5–4 cm of stem below the base of the bud, or a longer stalk cut just above a leaf joint. Check every few days in warm weather, when buds open quickly. Take the main bud first and the side buds as they size up, and after the last harvest cut the old flower stems to the ground.

store.how: Cool the buds the day they are cut and keep them near 0 °C in a perforated bag. Below freezing the bracts brown.

world.preserveNote: Freeze the hearts: strip away all the leaves and the fuzzy choke, trim the stem just below the heart and cut away any woody parts, wash, water-blanch 7 minutes, cool and pack with no headspace. Whole buds keep two to three weeks near 0 °C in the fridge, which covers most gluts. There is no tested home-canning process for globe artichokes in the USDA and NCHFP guides — the NCHFP artichoke pickle is for Jerusalem artichokes, an unrelated plant — and home-made artichokes in oil kept at room temperature are a botulism risk. Marinate cooked hearts in the fridge and eat them within a few days, or freeze them.

seeds.how: Artichokes can be raised from seed, but seedlings vary, and the reliable way to keep a good plant is to divide it. Every four or five years, or when cropping falls off, lift the clump in spring and split off vigorous outer pieces with roots, or take the young offsets — rosettes around the edge of the clump — and replant them. Divisions and offsets are clones of the parent, which is how named varieties are kept. If you start from seed, Imperial Star and Green Globe are the varieties most likely to bud in their first year.
seeds.viability: Not applicable for named varieties, which are kept by division and offsets.

world.nextYear: Artichokes want warmth, full sun and fertile, free-draining soil — raise the bed on heavy clay, because winter wet kills them. Space plants 75–100 cm apart; they grow 1–1.5 m tall and a metre across. In Mediterranean climates plant offsets or divisions in autumn or early spring and cut buds from spring onwards. In Britain sow indoors from late winter or plant divisions in spring, remove any flower stalk in the first summer, and harvest from the second. In cold-winter places grow them as annuals: sow 6–12 weeks before the last frost, then give the young plants a cold spell so they will form buds — roughly 200–500 hours at 2–10 °C, either in a cool room or by planting out early in a cool spring — and transplant after frost. Give them 25–50 mm (1–2 in) of water a week.

sow.outdoors: In mild climates plant offsets or divisions in autumn or early spring; where winters are hard, transplant vernalised seedlings after the last frost.

faqs.q: When do you harvest globe artichokes?
faqs.a: When the buds have reached full size but the scales are still tightly closed — from spring around the Mediterranean, from June in Britain, and from late July to frost when grown as annuals in Canada. Cut with 2.5–4 cm of stem; once the scales loosen, the bud is past its best.

faqs.q: Can I grow artichokes in Ontario?
faqs.a: Yes, as annuals. Ontario growers start transplants in February–April, give them a cold treatment — Imperial Star and Green Globe reach about 80% vernalisation after 200 hours at or below 10 °C — and plant out from April to June. Overwintering is possible only with heavy protection in the warmest parts of the province.

faqs.q: Are frost-blistered artichokes safe to eat?
faqs.a: Yes. Frost ruptures the outer skin of the bud scales, giving them a whitish, blistered look that darkens after a few days, but the eating quality is unaffected.

faqs.q: How do you freeze artichoke hearts?
faqs.a: Remove all the leaves and the fuzzy choke, trim the stem and woody parts, wash the hearts, water-blanch them 7 minutes, cool, and pack with no headspace. Freeze whole buds only if you have no time to trim them; the hearts take far less room.

faqs.q: How do you propagate globe artichokes?
faqs.a: By division or offsets in spring. Lift an established clump every four or five years, split off vigorous outer pieces with roots, or cut away the young rosettes growing at the edge, and replant them 75–100 cm apart. They are clones of the parent plant, unlike seedlings.

faqs.q: Why hasn’t my artichoke made any buds?
faqs.a: Either it is in its first year — plants usually crop from their second summer — or, in a cold climate, the young plants were never chilled enough. Grown as annuals, artichokes need a few hundred hours below about 10 °C as young plants to set buds the same year.

world.name: Florence fennel
world.tagline: An aniseed bulb that wants steady water and no surprises — sown as the days shorten, it swells instead of bolting.
world.frostNote: Florence fennel tolerates light frost, which is why it can be sown in summer for an autumn crop, but mature bulbs are damaged by a hard one. When −2 °C or colder is forecast, harvest every bulb of a usable size and cover younger plants with fleece.
world.ready: Harvest when the bulb is round and pale and about 6–15 cm (2½–6 in) across — tennis-ball size or larger — roughly 90–100 days from sowing, or 70–80 days from transplanting. It can be cut at any size from about 5 cm as a baby vegetable. Harvest before the bulb elongates and sends up a flower stem, after which it turns woody and inedible.
world.pick: Cut just below the swollen bulb with a sharp knife, leaving the base and roots in the ground: it sends up small, feathery shoots for salads, though not another bulb. Or lift the whole plant. Trim off the stalks, and keep some of the fronds to use as a herb.

store.how: Trimmed bulbs, unwashed, in a perforated bag; commercial storage is 0–2 °C at 90–95% humidity for 14–21 days.

world.preserveNote: Florence fennel is a vegetable to eat fresh — shaved raw or braised — and the fridge is its store: trimmed bulbs keep two to three weeks near 0 °C. The fronds lose their flavour when dried, so use them fresh, or wrap and freeze them as you would other fresh herbs for cooked dishes. The seeds are the part that dries well: cut the umbels when the first ripe seeds begin to fall, dry them in an airy place, rub out the seed and keep it in a jar for cooking. There is no tested canning or pickling recipe for fennel bulb in the USDA guides, so keep pickled fennel in the fridge and eat it within a few weeks.

seeds.how: Florence fennel is grown for seed as a biennial: plants sown in midsummer form bulbs, stand through a mild winter — or are lifted and stored where winters are hard — and flower the following year. The flowers are insect-pollinated and cross freely with other fennel varieties and with herb and wild fennel, so for pure seed keep varieties about a kilometre apart, or 500 m with a hedge between. Cut the umbels as the first seeds fall, dry them, then rub out and winnow the seed.
seeds.viability: About four years, sometimes seven; longer in the freezer.

world.nextYear: Fennel’s problem is bolting — running to flower instead of making a bulb — and the causes are cold spells in spring, root disturbance at transplanting and dry soil. So sow direct, or singly in modules so the root ball moves intact; choose bolt-resistant varieties for early sowings; and never let the soil dry out. Give it a warm, sunny site with fertile, free-draining soil, not heavy clay. In Britain and Canada sow in early to midsummer, June or July, for autumn bulbs, thinning to 30 cm apart, and earth up the swelling bulb to keep it pale. In Mediterranean climates — Lisbon, Cape Town — sow in late summer and autumn as the days shorten, for bulbs through the winter and spring; spring sowings there bolt in the lengthening, hotter days.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct, or singly in modules, as the days shorten — early to midsummer in cool-summer countries, late summer to autumn in Mediterranean climates — once the soil is 15–18 °C.

faqs.q: Why does my Florence fennel bolt instead of making a bulb?
faqs.a: Cold spells in spring, root disturbance when transplanting, and dry soil are the usual causes. Sow later — midsummer in Britain and Canada, late summer or autumn around the Mediterranean — choose a bolt-resistant variety, sow direct or in modules, and water generously so the soil never dries out.

faqs.q: When should I sow Florence fennel?
faqs.a: As the days are getting shorter. In Britain sow outdoors in June or July; in Ontario seed from late April for a 90–100-day crop works with bolt-resistant varieties, but a midsummer sowing for autumn is more reliable; in Mediterranean climates sow from late summer into autumn for winter and spring bulbs.

faqs.q: How do you know when fennel is ready?
faqs.a: When the bulb is round, pale and at least 6–8 cm across — tennis-ball size or bigger — usually 90–100 days from sowing. Harvest before it starts to elongate and push up a flower stem, which makes it woody.

faqs.q: Is Florence fennel the same as herb fennel?
faqs.a: Same species, different variety. Florence fennel forms a swollen bulb of leaf bases and is grown as an annual vegetable; herb fennel is a tall perennial grown for its feathery leaves and seeds. They cross freely, so do not let both flower near each other if you save seed.

faqs.q: Can you freeze fennel?
faqs.a: The bulb is best fresh and keeps two to three weeks in the fridge; braised fennel dishes freeze well once cooked. The fronds can be wrapped and frozen for cooked dishes, and the seeds dry perfectly.

faqs.q: Can I grow fennel in Ontario?
faqs.a: Yes, as an annual. Ontario growers seed from late April or transplant 4–6 weeks after seeding into soil at 15–18 °C, and harvest 90–100 days from seed or 70–80 from transplanting, before bolting begins; it grows best at 20–24 °C.

world.name: Rocket (arugula)
world.tagline: The peppery salad leaf of the Mediterranean winter — ready in a month, finished by the first hot spell, so sow a little and often.
world.frostNote: Rocket is a hardy little plant that crops through a mild winter in a cold frame, greenhouse border or under a cloche, and wild rocket keeps cropping into winter under cover and starts again in spring. A hard frost scorches the leaves of an uncovered row, so throw fleece over it when one is forecast.
world.ready: Leaves are ready three to six weeks after sowing, when they are 5–10 cm long; young leaves are milder and more tender. Salad rocket gives two or three cuts over a month or two before it flowers; once the flower stem shoots up, the leaves turn hot and tough and the crop is over.
world.pick: Pick individual leaves, or cut whole plants a few centimetres above the soil and let them regrow, always leaving the bottom set of leaves — cut too low and the plant dies. Pick in the cool of the morning. The flowers are edible too, with the same peppery bite.

store.how: Unwashed, loosely packed in a box or bag lined with paper. At 0 °C, commercial packs keep two or three days in top condition; home-grown leaves often last a week.

world.preserveNote: Rocket does not keep as a leaf — like lettuce and cress, it thaws limp, water-logged and off-flavoured — so it is a crop to sow little and often and eat fresh. The way to keep a glut is pesto: blend the leaves with oil, garlic, nuts and cheese and freeze it in jars or freezer boxes with 1 cm headspace. Fresh pesto keeps no more than three days in the fridge, and home-made pesto or herbs in oil should never be kept at room temperature.

seeds.how: Rocket flowers draw many insects and varieties cross, so Seed Savers Exchange advises 250–800 m (800 ft to ½ mile) between varieties for pure seed. Save from at least five plants, sown early enough to make a good rosette before heat triggers flowering. Cut the stalks when most of the pods are light brown and brittle, finish drying them under cover until the seed is too hard to dent with a fingernail, then thresh and winnow. Plants left to flower often seed themselves.
seeds.viability: About six years cool, dark and dry.

world.nextYear: Rocket belongs to the cabbage family, so rotate it with cabbages, kale and radishes, and cover young plants with fine mesh or fleece where flea beetles pepper the leaves. It wants moist, fertile soil — wild rocket tolerates poorer, drier ground — and full sun in spring and autumn, light shade in summer. Sow thinly in drills 1 cm deep, thinning to 15 cm apart, and sow again every two or three weeks. In Mediterranean and subtropical climates sow from autumn to spring, through the cool, wet season, and stop when the summer heat arrives; Florida gardeners sow from September to March. In Britain and Canada sow from early spring to late summer, give midsummer sowings light shade and plenty of water, and keep a late sowing under cover for winter. In the lowland tropics grow it in the coolest months or in highland gardens such as Nairobi.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct, 1 cm deep, every 2–3 weeks through the cool season — autumn to spring in Mediterranean and subtropical climates, early spring to late summer in cool-summer countries.

faqs.q: Why does my rocket bolt so fast?
faqs.a: Heat, dry soil and crowding all push salad rocket to flower, which ends the leaf harvest. Sow in the cool season, thin plants to 15 cm, keep the soil moist, and grow summer sowings in light shade; sowing a short row every two or three weeks keeps young plants coming.

faqs.q: What is the difference between wild rocket and salad rocket?
faqs.a: Salad rocket, Eruca vesicaria, is an annual with broader, milder leaves that crops for a month or two before flowering. Wild rocket, Diplotaxis tenuifolia, is a perennial with narrow, deeply cut, hotter leaves that keeps cropping through summer and autumn and goes on producing leaves even after it flowers.

faqs.q: How long does rocket take to grow?
faqs.a: Three to six weeks from sowing to the first picking of young leaves, depending on warmth. Florida’s gardening guide gives 30–40 days to harvest.

faqs.q: Why are there tiny holes in my rocket leaves?
faqs.a: Flea beetles, small jumping beetles that feed on the cabbage family. The damage is mostly cosmetic, but heavy attacks set seedlings back; cover sowings with fine mesh or fleece from the day you sow.

faqs.q: Can you freeze rocket?
faqs.a: Not as leaves — they thaw limp and water-logged, like lettuce. Make it into pesto and freeze that in jars or small tubs with 1 cm headspace; fresh pesto keeps only about three days in the fridge.

faqs.q: Can I grow rocket in the tropics?
faqs.a: Yes, in the cool season or at altitude. The plant itself tolerates heat and drought, but in hot weather it flowers within weeks, so leaf crops are best sown in the coolest months or in highland gardens, where it grows much as it does in a Mediterranean winter.
