world.name: Figs
world.tagline: Ripe when it droops — a fig must ripen on the tree, so the tree decides when you eat, and the surplus goes to jam, the dryer or the freezer.
world.frostNote: Fig trees are deciduous and hardy to about −8 °C (18 °F); a tree cut down by a harder freeze usually regrows as a bush. The embryo figs that form at the shoot tips in late summer, which carry over winter to make next year’s first crop, are easily killed by frost, so in cold areas fleece the tree in winter or bring potted figs into a frost-free place. Pick any soft, ripe figs before a frost.
world.ready: A ripe fig is soft, hangs limply on its stalk, and may split slightly when gently squeezed or show a drop of sugary nectar at the ‘eye’ at its base; the skin has reached its full colour — purple, brown or greenish-yellow, by variety. Figs must ripen on the tree, so wait for these signs rather than picking early.
world.pick: Hold the stalk and tear or snip it from the branch so the skin of the fruit does not tear. Pick every day or two through the season. Wear gloves and long sleeves when picking or pruning: the milky sap of the leaves and stems is an irritant. Net the tree as the fruit begins to ripen, held clear of the fruit on canes, to keep off birds and squirrels.

store.how: Ripe figs are best eaten the day they are picked; chill them in a single layer and eat them soon.

world.preserveNote: Figs freeze well: tray-freeze washed, fully ripe fruit and bag it, or pack it in a 40% syrup with ¾ teaspoon (2,250 mg) of ascorbic acid or 125 ml (½ cup) of lemon juice per litre (quart) of syrup; for pale figs in a dry pack, sprinkle the ascorbic acid, dissolved in a little water, over the fruit. To dry, crack the skins of small whole figs by dipping them in boiling water for 30 seconds, or halve large ones and dip them for 10 minutes in an ascorbic acid solution, then dry at 60 °C (140 °F) for 12–24 hours until leathery and pliable. Every tested canning recipe adds acid to figs: whole, unpeeled figs, boiled 2 minutes and then simmered 5 minutes in light syrup, need 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice per 500 ml (pint) jar or 2 per litre (quart) — or ¼ and ½ teaspoon of citric acid — and are processed 45 minutes for 500 ml jars or 50 minutes for litre jars in a boiling-water canner at 0–300 m. Fig jam, made with lemon juice and processed 5 minutes, and spiced fig pickles are tested NCHFP recipes too. Do not leave out the lemon juice or citric acid.

seeds.how: The common figs grown in gardens — Brown Turkey, Celeste, White Marseilles and the rest — set fruit without pollination, so their seeds are not fertile. Smyrna and San Pedro figs need a tiny fig wasp that lives only in warm fig-growing regions. Figs are propagated from cuttings of dormant wood, which root readily, or by layering a low branch into the soil.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — named varieties are propagated from cuttings.

world.nextYear: Figs want the warmest, sunniest, most sheltered spot you have and free-draining soil; they will not tolerate wet soil, but need plenty of water while fruiting, so mulch them. Plant bare-root trees in the dormant season, ideally in late winter or early spring, and container trees at any time. Prune only to keep the size you want, and only after fruiting: the crop forms on last year’s wood, so a hard winter pruning removes it. In cool climates such as Britain, restrict the roots — a 60 cm pit lined with paving slabs, or a large pot — and fan-train the tree against a south-facing wall; there only the first crop, the embryo figs carried through winter, usually ripens, so remove hard green figs larger than a pea at the end of summer. In Mediterranean climates figs need little care beyond watering in dry summers. They need about 100 hours of winter chilling to grow and fruit well.

sow.outdoors: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter or early spring, and container trees at any time; in the tropics, at the start of the rains.

faqs.q: How do I know when a fig is ripe?
faqs.a: It is soft, hangs limply from the branch, has reached its full colour for the variety, and may split slightly when squeezed or show a drop of nectar at the eye. A firm fig that stands up from the branch is not ready.

faqs.q: Do figs ripen after picking?
faqs.a: Not usefully — figs ripen on the tree, which is why they are hard to buy at their best. Pick them fully ripe and eat or preserve them within a day or two.

faqs.q: Why don’t my figs ripen?
faqs.a: In a cool climate, only the first crop — the tiny figs that overwinter at the shoot tips — usually has time to ripen; the second crop, formed in spring and summer, stays hard and green. Grow the tree in the warmest, most sheltered spot against a sunny wall, protect the overwintering fruitlets from frost, and remove the hard green figs at the end of summer.

faqs.q: Can I grow a fig tree in Canada?
faqs.a: In the mildest coastal parts, outdoors against a warm wall; elsewhere, in a large pot. The tree is hardy to about −8 °C, and a frost-killed tree often regrows as a bush, but the overwintering fruitlets are tender, so in most of Canada move a potted fig into an unheated garage or cool basement for the winter and back out after frost.

faqs.q: Do you need lemon juice to can figs?
faqs.a: Yes. Every tested recipe adds acid: 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice per pint jar or 2 per quart (or ¼ and ½ teaspoon of citric acid), with whole figs in light syrup processed 45 minutes for pints and 50 for quarts in a boiling-water canner near sea level.

faqs.q: Is fig sap harmful?
faqs.a: It is an irritant to skin, so wear gloves and long sleeves when picking or pruning, and prune from the bottom of the tree upwards so the sap does not drip on you.

world.name: Olives
world.tagline: Bitter beyond eating straight from the tree — every olive you have ever tasted was cured first, in lye, brine, water or salt.
world.frostNote: Olive trees need winter cold to flower but are hurt by hard frost: new growth and fruit are harmed below about −1.7 °C (29 °F), trees are damaged below about −5.6 °C (22 °F) — especially if late feeding or watering kept them growing into autumn — and they cannot survive below about −12 °C (10.5 °F). Pick fruit for curing before the first frost, while it is firm. In cold districts, potted olives belong in a frost-free place for winter.
world.ready: Olives are picked at three stages: green-ripe, full-sized and evenly yellow-green to straw-coloured; turning, rose to red-brown; and naturally black-ripe, dark red to purple-black, about three to four months after the green-ripe stage. In California green-ripe olives come from mid-September and black-ripe ones from mid-November. Pick for the cure you plan: green-ripe fruit for lye-cured and Spanish-style green olives, fully ripe fruit for dry-salt and Greek-style black olives.
world.pick: Pick by hand, or comb the fruit gently onto a sheet spread beneath the tree, and set aside any bruised olives: bruises show after curing. Sort by ripeness and size, because each cure suits a stage and even-sized fruit cures evenly. Process fresh olives within a few days of picking, especially black-ripe ones.

store.where: Cool room, fresh olives awaiting curing
store.how: Cure olives as soon as you can; green-ripe fruit holds better than black. Held at 0–2 °C for two weeks or more they suffer chilling injury.

store.where: In finish brine, cool and dark, or the fridge
store.keeps: Up to a year for water- and brine-cured styles; about 2 months for lye-cured; 6 months for dry-salt-cured, refrigerated
store.how: Cured olives in airtight food-grade containers, covered with brine; some styles must be refrigerated.

world.preserveNote: Raw olives are inedible: they contain oleuropein, an intensely bitter compound that must be leached out before the fruit can be eaten. The tested home methods are in UC Agriculture and Natural Resources publication 8267, Olives: Safe Methods for Home Pickling. Water curing — cut or cracked olives soaked in fresh water changed daily for one to three weeks, then kept in a salt-and-vinegar finish brine — is ready in weeks but leaves the olives slightly bitter. Brine curing ferments the olives in salt brine for at least three months, often six or more, as for Greek-style black and Sicilian-style green olives. Dry-salt curing packs fully ripe, oil-rich olives with about 1 part pickling salt to 2 parts fruit by weight for several weeks, giving soft, shrivelled, salty olives that keep up to six months in the fridge. Lye curing, with 57 g (2 oz) of pure lye per 3.8 L (1 gallon) of cold water, debitters green-ripe olives in days, giving the mild, firm California style — but lye is extremely corrosive: wear rubber gloves and eye protection, add lye to water and never water to lye, use only glass, stainless steel, food-grade plastic or wood — never aluminium, tin or galvanised metal — and keep it away from children and pets. Olives are a low-acid food: home canning of cured olives needs a pressure canner — whole olives in brine, 60 minutes for 500 ml jars or 70 minutes for litre jars at 10 lb weighted gauge near sea level — and must never be done in a boiling-water or steam canner, because of botulism. Dry-salt and lye-cured olives of small, oily varieties also freeze. Throw out any batch that becomes mouldy, soft or foul-smelling.

seeds.how: Olive seedlings do not come true, so named varieties are propagated from rooted cuttings or by grafting; buy a named variety from a nursery. Most olives crop better with a second, compatible variety nearby to cross-pollinate, so plant two kinds, or check what grows in neighbouring gardens.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — named varieties are kept by cuttings and grafting.

world.nextYear: Olives need a long, hot, dry summer to ripen their fruit and a cool winter to flower: 200–300 hours between about 0 and 8 °C (32–47 °F) set the flower buds, and long spells near 24 °C (75 °F) in winter spoil flowering. That is why they crop across the Mediterranean, in South Africa’s Western Cape and in California, and do not fruit in the humid lowland tropics. Give them full sun, shelter, and well-drained soil, even poor and stony ground; they hate wet roots. Plant in spring. Stop feeding and watering by late summer so the tree hardens off before winter. Olives tend to bear heavily one year and lightly the next, and reach full production in seven to ten years. In Britain, plant in the ground only in a very sheltered town garden near a sunny wall, or grow them in large pots of gritty, loam-based compost moved under cover for the winter.

sow.outdoors: Plant container trees in spring, in full sun and free-draining soil, once the risk of hard frost has passed.

faqs.q: Can you eat olives straight from the tree?
faqs.a: No. Fresh olives contain oleuropein, a compound so bitter that the fruit is inedible until it has been cured in water, brine, salt or lye to leach it out. Even black, fully ripe olives on the tree are bitter.

faqs.q: How do you cure olives at home?
faqs.a: Choose a tested method from UC publication 8267: water-curing cracked olives with daily changes of water for one to three weeks; fermenting them in salt brine for three to six months or more; packing fully ripe olives in dry salt for several weeks; or lye-curing green-ripe olives, which takes days. Each style has its own finish brine and storage rules.

faqs.q: Is it safe to cure olives with lye?
faqs.a: Yes, if you follow a tested method and treat the lye with respect: it is extremely corrosive. Wear rubber gloves and eye protection, always add lye to cold water and never the reverse, use glass, stainless steel, food-grade plastic or wood — never aluminium, tin or galvanised metal — rinse and soak the olives as directed, and keep children and pets away.

faqs.q: How long do home-cured olives keep?
faqs.a: It depends on the style. Water- and brine-cured olives keep up to about a year in their finish brine in a cool, dark place or the fridge, as the recipe directs; lye-cured olives about two months in brine; dry-salt-cured olives up to six months refrigerated. For longer storage, cured olives can be pressure-canned in brine or, for some styles, frozen or dried.

faqs.q: Why doesn’t my olive tree fruit?
faqs.a: Usually because the winter was too warm for the tree to form flower buds — olives need 200–300 hours between about 0 and 8 °C — or because it is still young: full production takes seven to ten years. A second, compatible variety nearby improves fruit set, and olives naturally crop heavily and lightly in alternate years.

faqs.q: Can I grow an olive tree in Canada or Britain?
faqs.a: In a pot, yes, and in the ground only in the most sheltered spots of southern Britain. Many olives are hardy to several degrees of frost, but severe frosts damage the branches; grow them in large pots of gritty compost outdoors in summer and move them into a frost-free, bright place for winter.

world.name: Lemons and oranges
world.tagline: The tree is the larder — citrus never sweetens after picking, so leave it hanging until you want it, for months if need be.
world.frostNote: Lemons are the most cold-sensitive: flowers and young fruit are killed at about −1.7 °C (29 °F), nearly mature fruit is badly damaged below −2.2 °C (28 °F), and the tree loses its leaves at −4 to −6 °C. Oranges are a little hardier — fruit is damaged between about −1 and −3 °C, and mature, dormant trees have survived ten hours below −4 °C — but young trees can be killed by even a brief frost. When frost is forecast, pick ripe fruit, cover young trees to the ground, and bring potted citrus under cover.
world.ready: Citrus is ready when it has full colour and, above all, full flavour — taste one. Colour is not a reliable guide: some varieties do not colour until autumn cold, though that does not affect sweetness, and Valencia oranges can look greenish when fully ripe. Navel oranges ripen in late winter and Valencias in summer, while lemons carry flowers and fruit through much of the year.
world.pick: Clip the fruit with secateurs close to the button, or lift and twist it off gently; a torn peel at the stem end lets in rot. Pick ripe fruit as you need it, because once picked it gets no sweeter. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft: they are the rootstock and will not bear good fruit.

store.how: The best store of all: ripe fruit holds its quality on the tree, so pick as you need it.
Picked fruit in a bag in the crisper keeps about four to six weeks.

world.preserveNote: Marmalade is citrus’s great preserve and a tested water-bath recipe: thin-sliced peel — keep some of the white pith, which holds the pectin — simmered until tender, then boiled with the pulp and sugar to 8 °C above the boiling point of water (104 °C, 220 °F, at sea level) and processed 5 minutes for 250 or 500 ml jars at 0–300 m. Orange and grapefruit sections, stripped of all white tissue, can be packed raw in water, juice or syrup and water-bath canned 10 minutes for 500 ml or litre jars. Juice freezes well — lemon, lime and Valencia juice keeps about four months frozen — and is best frozen in glass, squeezed with a juicer that does not press oil from the rind. Sections freeze in a 40% syrup. Thinly pared outer peel, scrubbed and cut free of the bitter white pith, dries in 8–12 hours at 60 °C (140 °F) for baking and tea.

seeds.how: Garden citrus is grafted onto rootstocks chosen for soil, vigour and disease resistance, and trees should be bought grafted: ungrafted seedlings can take up to ten years to fruit and may not resemble the parent. A pip from a shop orange is a long experiment, not a quick crop. Keep the graft union above the soil and remove any shoots that grow from below it.
seeds.viability: Not applicable — named varieties are propagated by grafting.

world.nextYear: Citrus wants full sun, shelter from cold wind and free-draining soil. It is hungry: feed regularly through the growing season — the RHS uses a nitrogen-rich summer feed from late March to October and a balanced winter feed after that — and keep young trees watered. Mature trees need little pruning beyond dead wood and rootstock suckers; thin heavy crops, since a tree about 1 m tall should carry no more than about 20 fruit at once. In Mediterranean climates — Lisbon, Seville, Cape Town — lemons and oranges grow outdoors with little fuss, and they crop well in tropical highlands such as Nairobi; in the hot lowland tropics oranges ripen but stay greenish, because colour comes with cool nights. Where winters bring frost, grow the hardier types, plant against a sunny wall, or keep citrus in pots that winter in a bright, cool, frost-free place: citrus will not reliably survive British winters outdoors.

sow.outdoors: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in Mediterranean climates, or at the start of the rains in the tropics, in full sun and free-draining soil.

faqs.q: Do lemons and oranges ripen after picking?
faqs.a: No. Once picked, citrus does not get any sweeter or riper, so taste one before picking the rest. The best place to store ripe fruit is on the tree; picked fruit keeps about four to six weeks in the fridge.

faqs.q: Why are my ripe oranges still green?
faqs.a: Orange colour develops with cool weather, so in warm climates, and early in the season, fully ripe fruit can stay green or partly green, and Valencias can turn greenish again on the tree. Colour does not affect sweetness — taste is the test.

faqs.q: How long can citrus stay on the tree?
faqs.a: Weeks to months, depending on the variety — the tree is the best store. Valencia oranges, for example, are picked in summer but can hang well beyond that; eventually quality falls as the fruit dries out or drops, so keep picking through the season.

faqs.q: How cold can a lemon tree take?
faqs.a: Not much. Lemon flowers and young fruit die at about −1.7 °C, nearly ripe fruit is damaged below −2.2 °C, and the tree is defoliated at −4 to −6 °C. Oranges are slightly hardier. Cover young trees on frost nights and bring potted ones under cover.

faqs.q: Can I grow a lemon tree in Canada or the UK?
faqs.a: Yes, in a pot. Keep it outdoors in a sunny, sheltered spot in summer and bring it into a bright, cool, frost-free room or conservatory for winter — citrus prefer a cool winter spell and more humidity than a centrally heated house gives. Water sparingly in winter and feed with citrus fertiliser all year.

faqs.q: Can I grow citrus from a pip?
faqs.a: You can grow a tree, but it may take up to ten years to fruit and the fruit may not resemble the parent. For a reliable crop within a few years, buy a grafted tree, ideally one already flowering or fruiting.

world.name: Pomegranates
world.tagline: A tough, long-lived shrub for hot summers — and a fruit that keeps for months in a cold store, growing juicier as it waits.
world.frostNote: Pomegranates are adapted to cool winters and hot summers, and the shrub is severely injured only below about −11 °C (12 °F). Pick the fruit before a hard frost. In a cold district, plant against a sunny wall: the shrub grows as far north as Washington, D.C., though it does not fruit there.
world.ready: Fruit ripens six to seven months after flowering and cannot be ripened off the tree, so pick it fully coloured for the variety — red, pink or yellow blushed with pink — and when it gives a metallic sound if tapped. Do not leave it to become over-mature: ripe fruit splits open after rain, drying winds or irregular watering.
world.pick: Clip the fruit close to its base with secateurs, leaving no stalk to bruise other fruit in the basket; pulling tears the shrub. The branches are spiny, so wear gloves.

store.how: Whole, sound fruit at 0–5 °C and 80–85% humidity keeps up to seven months without shrinking or spoiling, and grows juicier and more flavourful; at 95% humidity it keeps only about two months at 5 °C.

world.preserveNote: A sound, whole pomegranate is its own preserve, keeping for months cold. For the freezer, halve the fruit, set it cut side down and rap the shell with a wooden spoon handle to break the inner walls and release the seeds and juice; pack the seeds and juice in a cold 30% syrup or unsweetened, with headspace, and freeze. Juice is best pressed from the seeds alone — pressing whole fruit pulls bitter tannin from the rind — and it freezes well or can be boiled down to a syrup, the original grenadine. There is no tested home-canning recipe for plain pomegranate juice in the NCHFP guides; freeze it.

seeds.how: Pomegranate seed germinates readily, even scattered on loose soil, but seedlings vary, so selected varieties are grown from hardwood cuttings 25–50 cm long, set with one or two buds above the soil; they root in a year. Rooted suckers and air-layers also work. Pomegranates are self-pollinating, so a single shrub will fruit.
seeds.viability: Not applicable for named varieties, which are propagated from cuttings.

world.nextYear: Pomegranates need hot summers and favour a semi-arid climate; in humid summers, leaf blotch and fruit spot are common. Give them full sun and deep soil, and water every seven to ten days in dry weather while the fruit develops — keeping the soil evenly moist in late summer and early autumn is the main defence against split fruit. Grow them as a bushy, multi-stemmed shrub or train a single trunk by removing suckers; fruit forms at the tips of new growth, so shorten the branches for the first three years to encourage plenty of shoots. Plants may bear a year after planting, but two and a half to three years is usual. Plant in the dormant season or early spring in Mediterranean climates. Pomegranates thrive from Lisbon to Cairo and in South Africa’s Western Cape, and are grown in tropical gardens too, though they fruit best after a cool winter.

sow.outdoors: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in the dormant season or early spring, in full sun; in the tropics, at the start of the rains.

faqs.q: When is a pomegranate ripe?
faqs.a: When it has full colour for its variety and gives a metallic sound when tapped, six to seven months after flowering. It will not ripen once picked, so do not pick early — but do not leave it so long that rain splits it.

faqs.q: Why do my pomegranates split?
faqs.a: Over-mature fruit cracks when it gets a sudden drink after dry weather, or in rain or drying winds. Water evenly — about every seven to ten days without rain — through late summer and early autumn, and pick fruit as soon as it is ripe.

faqs.q: How do you get the seeds out of a pomegranate?
faqs.a: Cut it in half, hold it cut side down over a bowl and rap the skin firmly with a wooden spoon handle; the seeds drop out with the juice. Picking out the bitter white membrane afterwards is easier in a bowl of water, where the seeds sink and the membrane floats.

faqs.q: How long do pomegranates keep?
faqs.a: Remarkably long: whole, sound fruit keeps up to seven months at 0–5 °C and 80–85% humidity, becoming juicier as it stores. In a very humid fridge drawer expect about two months.

faqs.q: Can you freeze pomegranate seeds?
faqs.a: Yes. Freeze the seeds and juice unsweetened or in a cold 30% syrup, with headspace in a rigid container. They thaw softer than fresh, so use them for juice, sauces and baking rather than garnish.

faqs.q: Can I grow pomegranates in a cold climate?
faqs.a: Only where summers are long and hot. The shrub survives to about −11 °C and grows as far north as Washington, D.C., but it does not fruit there; in Canada or northern Europe, grow a compact variety in a pot and bring it into a cool, bright place for winter.

world.name: Watermelons
world.tagline: Born in the dry sands of southern Africa — it wants heat, room and dry air, and tells you it is ripe with a yellow belly and a dead tendril.
world.frostNote: Watermelon vines die at the first frost and stop growing well before it, and the seed will not germinate below 15 °C. Pick every ripe melon before a frost; unripe ones do not ripen after picking, so there is no point bringing them in green.
world.ready: A ripe watermelon has a creamy-yellow ground spot where it rests on the soil, a shrivelled, browning tendril on the vine just opposite the fruit stalk, a skin that has lost its gloss and turned dull and waxy, and a muffled, hollow sound when tapped with a knuckle. Fruit is mature 30–50 days after pollination, and most varieties take 80–100 days from sowing. Watermelons do not ripen further after picking.
world.pick: Cut the stalk with a sharp knife, leaving about 5 cm on the fruit, rather than pulling the melon from the vine. Fruit picked in the afternoon is less turgid and less likely to crack. Handle them gently: watermelons crack and bruise easily.

store.where: Cool room or shaded veranda, whole fruit
store.how: Whole, unblemished fruit at 10–15 °C and about 85% humidity. Cut melon goes in the fridge, covered, and is best eaten within a few days.

world.preserveNote: Watermelon is a fruit for eating fresh, but both flesh and rind can be kept. Seeded cubes or balls of firm, ripe flesh freeze unsweetened or in a cold 30% syrup; they thaw soft, so use them for sorbets and drinks. The rind makes two tested NCHFP preserves: watermelon rind pickles — the green skin and pink flesh trimmed away, the white rind soaked in a salt brine with ice, simmered tender, steeped overnight in a spiced syrup of sugar and 5% vinegar, cooked an hour and processed 10 minutes for 500 ml jars — and watermelon rind preserves. Do not can plain watermelon flesh or juice: there is no tested process for it.

seeds.how: Watermelons are bee-pollinated and cross with other watermelons, including the egusi seed melons of West Africa, which belong to the same species, but not with cucumbers, squash or sweet melons. For pure seed keep varieties at least 250 m (800 ft) apart or hand-pollinate a few fruits. Seed from an ordinary eating-ripe melon is mature: rinse it, dry it in a thin layer on paper plates or screens, and store it airtight. Seedless watermelons give no seed and need a seeded variety planted nearby to pollinate them; F1 hybrids will not come true.
seeds.viability: About five years cool, dark and dry in an airtight container; kept dry below 18 °C, at least eight.

world.nextYear: Watermelons are cucurbits: keep them off beds that grew cucumbers, melons, squash or pumpkins in the last two years. They want full sun, a long hot season, room to sprawl — hills at least 1.8 m apart — and well-drained sandy loam at pH 6–7; heavy rain and humidity bring rampant leaves and leaf and fruit rots, and waterlogged soil invites anthracnose. Sow three or four seeds per hill, 2–4 cm deep, once the soil is warm, thinning to the strongest two, or transplant pot-raised seedlings at three or four true leaves without disturbing the roots. In the West African savanna and the Sahel sow early in the rains, or under irrigation in the dry season, when yields are higher; in summer-rainfall southern Africa from September to December; around the Mediterranean from late April into May. In Canada start seed in pots 4–6 weeks before the last frost, plant out on black plastic once nights are warm, and grow small ‘ice-box’ varieties.

sow.outdoors: Sow direct once the soil is above about 20 °C — early in the rains, or in the irrigated dry season, in the tropics; after the last frost elsewhere.

faqs.q: How do you tell when a watermelon is ripe?
faqs.a: Look for four signs together: the ground spot underneath has turned from white to creamy yellow, the curly tendril opposite the fruit stalk has shrivelled and browned, the rind has gone from glossy to dull, and the fruit sounds hollow and taut when you knock on it.

faqs.q: Will a watermelon ripen after picking?
faqs.a: No. Watermelons do not continue ripening once cut from the vine, so an under-ripe melon stays pale and bland. Wait for the ripeness signs before you cut.

faqs.q: Why do seedless watermelons need another variety nearby?
faqs.a: Seedless watermelons produce too little viable pollen of their own, so they need a seeded variety planted among them, and bees to carry its pollen, to set fruit dependably.

faqs.q: Can I grow watermelons in Canada?
faqs.a: Yes, with a small, early ‘ice-box’ variety and a head start. Sow in pots indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost, plant out after it into soil warmed under black plastic, cover with row cover early on, and give them the sunniest bed; most varieties need 80–100 days.

faqs.q: Can you freeze watermelon?
faqs.a: Yes: cut firm, ripe flesh into cubes or balls, remove the seeds, and freeze unsweetened or in a cold 30% syrup. It thaws soft and watery, so use it for smoothies, sorbets and drinks.

faqs.q: How do you pickle watermelon rind?
faqs.a: Trim off the green skin and pink flesh, cut the white rind into pieces, soak 3–4 hours in salted iced water, simmer until just tender, then steep overnight and cook an hour in a spiced sugar syrup made with 5% vinegar, following the tested NCHFP recipe; process pint jars 10 minutes in a boiling-water canner near sea level.
